Pro-Israel lobby spends big on US midterms as backlash grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
02:20:00 UTC
11:20:00 KST

Pro-Israel lobby spends big on US midterms as backlash grows
WASHINGTON – The most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the United States is spending more than any other outside group on the 2026 midterms – even as its once-coveted backing becomes an increasingly potent weapon for political opponents.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has poured tens of millions of dollars into races nationwide through its main election-spending vehicle, the United Democracy Project (UDP).
The so-called “super PAC” – a group allowed to lavish unlimited sums to influence elections, provided it operates independently of candidates – has spent US$54 million (S$68.6 million) on congressional races, according to campaign finance monitor OpenSecrets.
That has made it the single largest outside spender of the cycle, OpenSecrets said, while the wider pro-Israel donor network spent US$71 million – placing it second only to the cryptocurrency industry.
The extraordinary financial firepower underscores AIPAC’s continued influence in Washington – but also a growing backlash over US policy towards Israel and the role of wealthy interest groups in American elections.
AIPAC has concentrated much of its spending on Democratic primaries, supporting candidates strongly committed to Israel and trying to defeat critics of unconditional US military aid. It did not respond to a request for comment, but it has rejected suggestions that its influence is collapsing, saying hundreds of candidates it backed have won their primaries.
Its money has indeed delivered victories in 2026, but also some expensive failures.
Money meets resistance
In Michigan, AIPAC and allied groups spent around US$30 million in an unsuccessful effort to prevent progressive former health official Abdul El-Sayed from winning the Democratic Senate nomination over establishment-backed Congresswoman Haley Stevens.
Progressives have also defeated candidates supported by AIPAC-linked money in congressional contests in California, Illinois and New York, often turning the group’s spending itself into a campaign issue.
Eli Clifton, of US foreign policy think-tank the Quincy Institute, said UDP was the biggest spender in Michigan, although 97 per cent of its large contributions came from outside the state, and its biggest donors are Republican billionaires.
“This is a special interest that participates outside of the partisan framework, and it’s really all about advancing the interests of a foreign country,” he told AFP.
Unease over the group is no longer confined to Democrats.
Allies of Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, recently asked AIPAC not to run advertisements publicly on his behalf, US media reported, fearing its overt involvement would benefit El-Sayed in the Arab-American heartland.
Shifting opinion
The discomfort reflects a broader transformation in US attitudes towards Israel following years of war in Gaza and widening conflict across the Middle East.
A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48 per cent of American voters believed Washington was too supportive of Israel, including 66 per cent of Democrats – the highest overall figure in nine years of the survey.
The change has been clearest on the Democratic left, where candidates increasingly portray AIPAC as too closely aligned with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and emblematic of big-money interests overwhelming ordinary voters.
But criticism has spread to the populist right, where some “America First” conservatives have attacked Washington’s support for Israel and blamed pro-Israel lobbying for drawing the US deeper into foreign conflicts.
AIPAC’s financial strength, meanwhile, continues to grow. OpenSecrets says the organisation itself has contributed US$30 million to UDP.
And its political power remains formidable, with US military aid to Israel continuing to attract broad support in Congress.
But the primaries have demonstrated that record spending cannot guarantee victory – and a once-prized endorsement can now, in some races, be something candidates would rather their opponents talked less about.
“That’s precisely why they never mention US foreign policy and Israel in their ads,” Casey Kennedy, co-founder of the Track AIPAC advocacy platform, told AFP. “AIPAC knows AIPAC is toxic, and the more they spend, the more toxic they become with voters across the political spectrum.” AFP

Drones attack thermal power plant in Shchastia, causing major blackout in Russian-occupied territories

Drones attack thermal power plant in Shchastia, causing major blackout in Russian-occupied territories
A major blackout occurred on the night of 27-28 August across temporarily occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. The power cuts followed a drone attack on the Luhansk Thermal Power Plant in the city of Shchastia.
Source: a Russian media outlet Astra; monitoring Telegram channels
Details: Local sources began warning of a possible drone attack as early as 21:00 on 27 August.
Around midnight, posts on social media about power outages began appearing in large numbers. In particular, the power went off in occupied Donetsk at around 01:00 on 28 August.
Local residents reported that the drone strike had caused a fire at the thermal power plant in Shchastia. Photos were also posted online that reportedly showed a fire at the facility.
Shortly afterwards, reports of widespread power outages began coming in from the so-called Donetsk People's Republic and occupied parts of Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. Meanwhile, local Telegram channels said there was "no precise or official information".
For reference: Russian forces fully occupied the city of Shchastia on 28 February 2022. After seizing the city, the Russians announced the so-called "nationalisation" of the power plant. They used the plant's generating units to cover the power shortfall in the so-called Luhansk People's Republic.
The Luhansk Thermal Power Plant is also a key facility supporting Russia's defence industry in Ukraine's east. The plant supplies electricity to military bases, repair facilities, coal mines and railway infrastructure used by the Russian military to supply its forces.

Fired Stars and Stripes journalists sue Trump administration for censorship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
02:16:50 UTC
11:16:50 KST

Fired Stars and Stripes journalists sue Trump administration for censorship
Staff at the military newspaper allege that the US government seeks to violate their First Amendment rights to free speech.
Three staff members from the Stars and Stripes military newspaper have filed a lawsuit against the United States Department of Defense, alleging that their recent firing was part of an effort to erode the paper’s independence.
In Thursday’s court filings, the newspaper’s publisher Max Lederer, editor-in-chief Erik Slavin and Middle East reporter Lara Korte argued that their First Amendment rights to free speech had been infringed.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Editor of US newspaper Stars and Stripes reportedly fired under Trump
- list 2 of 3Trump’s war on Stars and Stripes: Why has military newspaper chief quit?
- list 3 of 3Publisher of US military newspaper resigns over differences with government
The Stars and Stripes has long billed itself as an independent source for military news, though it receives government funding for its operations.
But last week, the three journalists received notices of termination from the Pentagon that reportedly accused them of insubordination.
That has raised questions about the Defense Department’s longtime commitment to respecting the newspaper’s editorial independence.
Thursday’s complaint accuses the department and several of its leaders, including Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, of engaging in “extraordinary censorship efforts”.
“Defendants are attempting to fire Plaintiffs for speaking up as private citizens in support of the press’s freedom to cover military operations,” the lawsuit says.
“This [legal] action seeks to prevent the blatant violation of the First Amendment rights of these journalists.”
The case is set to be heard in a district court in Washington, DC.
Korte explained the journalists’ reason for filing the lawsuit in a social media post.
“Everyone deserves the right to a free and independent press, especially our service members,” she wrote. “This lawsuit is about safeguarding the mission of Stars and Stripes journalists so they can continue to do their jobs without fear or retaliation.”
The legal battle is the latest instance under President Donald Trump of the executive branch being sued for allegedly penalising reporters and media personalities who do not comply with the administration’s viewpoints.
The lawsuit points to a July interview on CBS Sunday Morning as the “genesis” of the friction between the Stars and Stripes journalists and the Trump administration.
Both Korte and Slavin were featured in the segment. A reporter for the morning news show asked them about their work and recent statements from the Pentagon indicating it would seek to redirect the newspaper’s focus.
“You have a sign on your desk: Pick your battles,” CBS News reporter David Martin asked Slavin. “Which foxholes are you willing to die in?”
“We need to be able to provide independent news to service members,” Slavin responded. “If we can’t do that, if we were turned into something other than that, if we were public relations, that’s the foxhole.”
The CBS interview followed a statement in January, in which Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said his department would return Stars and Stripes “to its original mission: reporting for our warfighters”.
“We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members,” Parnell wrote.
“It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability, and ALL THINGS MILITARY.”
But critics have denounced the modernisation initiative as a smokescreen through which the Pentagon is seeking to reshape the Stars and Stripes’ coverage.
The lawsuit points to the newspaper’s key role in breaking coverage about deteriorating conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln, an aircraft carrier that has been on deployment, without a port stop, since November of last year.
The Stars and Stripes was one of the first media outlets to cover the supply shortages on the ship, as well as the mental health struggles of the sailors working through the record-long deployment.
But Trump and Hegseth have both denied reports of poor living conditions on the USS Lincoln, calling such news “fake”.
The lawsuit suggests the recent firings may be retaliation for the Stars and Stripes reporting on the subject.
A day after one of its articles was published, the lawsuit alleges that the Defense Department contacted Lederer, the publisher, about firing Korte and Slavin. The department allegedly pointed to the CBS interview from weeks earlier as justification.
Lederer did not follow through with the order to deliver the termination notices. Instead, he announced his intention to retire in September.
His memo to the Stars and Stripes staff suggested he had disagreements with the “direction the leadership of the Department of Defense has for the organization”.
But on August 21, the Department of Defense had issued termination notices to all three employees, including Lederer.
In April, the newspaper’s ombudsman, Jacqueline Smith, was also fired. Her role, in part, was charged with safeguarding the independence of the Stars and Stripes, a newspaper with a storied history, stretching back to the US Civil War.
Korte has worked at the paper since 2024. Her colleagues Slavin and Lederer have been with the Stars and Stripes for 21 and 25 years, respectively.
“Defense officials and military commanders have long made clear that Stripes would not be subject to interference by military officials,” the lawsuit says.
“Stripes’ historical editorial independence is critical to its core mission of gathering and providing unbiased, credible journalism to the US military community.”

PM Modi on 4-day visit to Uzbekistan, Kyrgyz Republic - what's on agenda

PM Modi on 4-day visit to Uzbekistan, Kyrgyz Republic - what's on agenda
Edited by: Vijaya Srivastava / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 28, 2026, 07:33 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
PM Modi will begin the trip in Tashkent and will then travel to Bishkek to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will embark on a four-day visit to Uzbekistan and the Kyrgyz Republic from August 29 to September 1, with Central Asia's strategic and economic importance high on India's agenda. He will begin the trip in Tashkent, where he is expected to hold talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on strengthening bilateral ties.The discussions will cover a broad range of areas, including trade and investment, critical minerals, defence, healthcare, energy, digital connectivity, education and technology.India and Uzbekistan are also expected to explore new opportunities in pharmaceuticals, space and business-to-business cooperation, as both sides look to expand their economic partnership.PM Modi will then travel to Bishkek to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit. There, he will highlight India's priorities of security, connectivity and opportunity, while holding bilateral meetings with leaders of SCO member states on the sidelines. His visit will also include the opening ceremony of the sixth World Nomad Games.
PM Modi's Uzbekistan visit: Strategic partnership in focus
PM Modi will begin his visit in Tashkent, where he will hold delegation-level talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev on August 29 and 30.
The visit is being undertaken at the invitation of Mirziyoyev and will be PM Modi's fourth visit to Uzbekistan and his second bilateral visit to the country, according to MEA Secretary (West) Sibi George.The two leaders are expected to review the full spectrum of India-Uzbekistan cooperation and discuss ways to further strengthen their strategic partnership.The talks will cover trade and investment, defence, digital connectivity, energy, education and people-to-people ties.PM Modi and Mirziyoyev are also expected to discuss ways to advance their respective long-term development visions, Viksit Bharat 2047 and Uzbekistan-2030.
Trade, critical minerals and healthcare on agenda
Economic cooperation is expected to be a key component of PM Modi's discussions in Tashkent, with the two sides looking to identify new avenues for trade, investment and business-to-business engagement.India is among Uzbekistan's top 10 trading partners, while bilateral trade and investments together are close to USD 1 billion.Critical minerals, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, information technology and technology are among the areas where the two countries already have cooperation and are expected to explore further opportunities."We have wide-ranging cooperation in the fields of critical minerals, pharma, education, information technology, and the health sector," George said.The two sides are also expected to explore cooperation in space, technology and other emerging sectors as they seek to expand the economic relationship beyond traditional areas.
16,000 Indian students, 4 university campuses
Education and people-to-people ties are another important component of the India-Uzbekistan relationship.George said more than 16,000 Indian students are currently studying in Uzbekistan, while four Indian university campuses have been established in the country.Major Indian investments in Uzbekistan are spread across pharmaceuticals, amusement parks, automobile components and education, reflecting the expanding commercial relationship between the two countries.
PM Modi to visit Shastri Memorial, Gandhi Centre
PM Modi's Tashkent programme will also include engagements highlighting India's historical and cultural links with Uzbekistan.The Prime Minister is expected to visit the Shastri Memorial in Tashkent as well as the Mahatma Gandhi Centre at the Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies.His programme will also include a banquet lunch hosted by Mirziyoyev in his honour."The Prime Minister's visit will reaffirm the close, multi-faceted, and growing strategic partnership between India and Uzbekistan," George said.
From Tashkent to Bishkek for SCO Summit
After his bilateral engagements in Uzbekistan, PM Modi will travel to Bishkek from August 31 to September 1 at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov to attend the 26th SCO Summit."The Prime Minister will travel to Bishkek from 31st August to 1st September" George said.The summit comes as the SCO marks the 25th anniversary of its establishment. India became a full member of the grouping in 2017, after holding observer status since 2005.
Security, connectivity and opportunity to guide India's SCO agenda
At the Bishkek summit, PM Modi will address SCO leaders and underline India's priorities of security, connectivity and opportunity. He is also expected to hold bilateral meetings with leaders of SCO member states on the sidelines of the summit.The SCO currently comprises 10 member states, along with dialogue partners and observers. The grouping was originally established to address the three "evils" of terrorism, separatism and extremism, but its cooperation has since expanded into a wider range of regional issues.India has previously chaired the SCO Council of Heads of Government in 2020 and the SCO Council of Heads of State during 2022-23.India's engagement with the grouping has been guided by the SECURE framework articulated by PM Modi at the 2018 SCO Summit. SECURE stands for "Security, Economy and Trade, Connectivity, Unity, Respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, and Environment".
More recently, at the SCO Summit in China's Tianjin, PM Modi highlighted security, connectivity and opportunity as three key elements of India's engagement with the organisation.
World Nomad Games on PM Modi's Bishkek itinerary
PM Modi will also attend the opening ceremony of the sixth World Nomad Games in Bishkek, which celebrates the cultural heritage of Central Asia.The four-day visit will give India an opportunity to simultaneously deepen its bilateral relationship with Uzbekistan, strengthen ties with Kyrgyzstan and advance its wider engagement with Central Asia through the SCO.

Federal US judge faces complaint over staunch pro-Israel advocacy

Federal US judge faces complaint over staunch pro-Israel advocacy
A lawyer has accused Judge Roy Altman, who calls the keffiyeh a ‘terror scarf’, of anti-Palestinian bias in his remarks.
A federal judge in the United States is facing a formal complaint over anti-Palestinian comments and alleged association with Islamophobic groups, in a case that highlights growing concern about possible pro-Israel bias in the judicial system.
Florida lawyer Katherine Giannamore filed the judicial complaint against District Judge Roy Altman earlier this month, accusing him of eroding “public confidence in the integrity, impartiality, and independence of the federal judiciary”.

The complaint, filed with the Eleventh Circuit Court, also says Altman used judicial resources to promote Israel, including by making media appearances from his chambers in Miami.
“Since at least April 2026, Judge Altman has consistently engaged in this conduct during business hours, broadcasting himself live from chambers and has utilized law clerks during public talks during business hours,” the complaint reads.
“These activities have been persistent, almost daily and spanned several months.”
‘The terrorism scarf’
The complaint points to several examples of what it considers to be worrying behaviour.
In April, for instance, Judge Altman appeared on a podcast with the Middle East Forum, a right-wing group whose stated mission is to combat “the infrastructure of lawful Islamism”. During the interview, he called the keffiyeh, a symbol of Palestinian identity, a “terrorism scarf”.
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Giannamore pointed to such remarks as a reason for concern.
“This kind of blatant use of the judicial office for your own political aspirations or your beliefs, it’s bad for the judiciary. It’s bad for public opinion as far as the legitimacy of the judiciary,” Giannamore said.
She acknowledged that the complaint is unlikely to lead to a reprimand against Altman, but she said it was important to raise the issue.
Federal judges are appointed for life. Judicial misconduct complaints go to the chief judge of a court of appeals, who can either dismiss them or appoint a special committee to investigate the claims.
In rare cases, the complaints can lead to sanctions, including the decision to suspend case assignments to a given judge or a request for voluntary resignation.
Giannamore believes complaints like hers can help spark a discussion about acceptable behaviour within the judicial system, particularly for lifelong office-holders.
“It’s important to bring awareness to that, and maybe give them a moment to take a step back and say, ‘Is this worth it? Is this something that we accept? And would we accept it if it was other issues that a judge was using the office to speak on?'” Giannamore said.
Altman, a staunch supporter of Israel who was appointed by President Donald Trump in 2019, is currently promoting a self-published book defending the US ally.
During his remarks with the Middle East Forum in April, he explained that he had been touring college campuses and churches to dismiss accusations of rights abuses against Israel, which has been carrying out a genocidal war on Gaza.
The judge uses “Jews” and “Israel” interchangeably throughout his talks.
“I say on college campuses, ‘You think you’re counterculture? You think you’re cool and unique because you wear the terrorism scarf, the keffiyeh, and you chant against the Jews? Get in line, get a ticket. You’re the most mainstream, boring thing history has ever seen,'” Altman said.
That was one of several incidents in which the judge demonised the symbol of Palestinian nationalism.
“At Yale Law School, for example, in three years, I graduated in 2007, I never once saw a single person wearing a keffiyeh,” he said on a recent podcast.
“And so that tells you that, at one of the most liberal law schools on the planet, not one student thought it was appropriate to wear a scarf that is a symbol of terrorism and the deaths — the violent deaths of thousands and thousands of innocent Jews.”
Altman is also a prolific social media user, and most of his posts are about Israel. He has also made frequent appearances on podcasts and in YouTube clips.
In one interview, he declared that “there is no distinction” between anti-Semitism and anti-Zionism.
The judge’s pro-Israel advocacy at times drifts into comments that could be seen as hostile towards Arabs and Muslims.
“The real geo-strategic conflict here isn’t seven million Jews against six million Palestinians,” he said in June.
“It’s seven million Jews surrounded by two billion Muslims — hundreds of millions of whom have been raised to believe that divine providence requires them to devote their lives to the destruction of that teeny, tiny Jewish state.”
The judge did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment by the time of publication.
Israel trips
It is highly unusual for a judge to be so outspoken about a divisive political issue.
Altman’s advocacy comes at a time when the federal judiciary is assessing several cases relating to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including Trump’s push to deport student activists who protested against the war on Gaza.
Altman often promotes a travel programme by the World Jewish Congress to take fellow judges on trips to Israel — visits akin to the junkets the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) gives to members of Congress.
“One of the reasons our judges in America give for why trips to Israel are so profoundly transformative for them is that, in Israel, you can feel our joint Judeo-Christian heritage, our history, our home,” he wrote in a social media post earlier this month.
According to Giannamore’s complaint, Altman said in a speech at Florida International University that he has taken 10 percent of the federal judiciary on such trips.
Such a large number of judges “coming away from foreign state-sponsored trips, where they meet with foreign political officials, is truly frightening”, the complaint said. It pointed out that some of those judges may rule on cases related to Israel.
Giannamore suggested that possible bias acquired from the “propaganda” visits to Israel may extend beyond issues related to the conflict, but to cases involving Palestinians, Arabs and Muslims more broadly.
“It goes into biases that they at least can be perceived to hold versus Palestinians, Arabs, Muslims, peace advocates,” she said.
“So if you’re taking 10 percent of the judiciary right now and they’re spread all across the country, that’s a huge number, and I think that ultimately undermines public confidence in one of our branches of government. So, it’s really bad for everyone.”

Why Filipino migrants are rethinking their futures in Japan
The weak yen, rising costs and uncertainty over immigration rules have made staying long term in Japan difficult for foreign workers
The need is especially acute in care work: Japan will require about 2.72 million care workers by financial year 2040, roughly 570,000 more than in 2022, according to Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare estimates, while one think tank projection has warned the country could be nearly 1 million foreign workers short by then if current inflows continue.
For the Filipino care workers, nurses and other professionals who came to Japan seeking greener pastures, the contradiction has become personal: the country needs them, but high living costs, a weak yen and uncertainty over immigration rules make it harder to imagine staying long-term.
Job Galutan Andawey, a licensed nurse from the Philippines working as a carer in Kanagawa prefecture, is in his sixth year in Japan after arriving through the Japan-Philippines Economic Partnership Agreement, a treaty that includes career placement and language training programmes for nurses and care workers.
“I chose Japan because I was influenced by Japanese culture. I dreamed of working here in Japan since I was little,” Andawey told This Week in Asia.

Thirty years of advancing equal opportunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
02:00:08 UTC
11:00:08 KST

Thirty years of advancing equal opportunity
From law enforcement and public education to promoting accessibility and workplace inclusion, the EOC marks three decades of putting equal opportunity into practice 
 
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
Thirty years after Hong Kong established a statutory body to combat discrimination, equal opportunity has become increasingly embedded in laws, workplaces and community.
As the Equal Opportunities Commission (EOC) marks its 30th anniversary this year, its record offers much to reflect on, but the work is far from finished considering the challenges brought by changing social needs.
Following the enactment of the Sex Discrimination Ordinance in 1995, the EOC was established in May 1996. Over the past three decades, it has implemented and enforced four anti-discrimination ordinances covering sex, marital status, pregnancy, breastfeeding, disability, family status and race, while carrying out policy advocacy, public education and community engagement.
Linda Lam Mei-sau EOC Chairperson said, “The anniversary offers us a moment to reflect on the EOC’s sustained efforts and achievements, and consolidate our experience to respond to increasingly complex social needs.”
The figures give some indication of the reach of that work. As of end-2025, the EOC had handled 22,548 complaints and secured more than HK$134mn for complainants through conciliation or legal assistance.
Some of the most important changes are harder to capture in numbers, says Lam. Years of law enforcement, education and advocacy have raised public awareness and more importantly helped equal opportunity values gradually take root across the community and translate into tangible social change.
A case in point is gender-specific recruitment advertising. When the EOC was established, job advertisements explicitly stating a preference for male or female applicants were common. Through education and reminders to publishers and advertisers about their legal responsibilities, such adverts fell to below 1 per cent within a relatively short period and have remained rare to this day.
Legal safeguards have also been strengthened over the years. Amendments to the anti-discrimination ordinances have introduced protection against breastfeeding discrimination and harassment, sexual harassment of service providers by customers, and sexual, disability and racial harassment among workplace participants without a direct employment relationship.
Putting accessibility into practice
Accessibility provides another good example of how advocacy and research can lead to concrete action.
Between 2007 and 2008, the EOC inspected 60 publicly accessible premises to identify barriers faced by people with disabilities and gather responses from premise owners and managers. The work led to the 2010 “Formal Investigation on Accessibility in Publicly Accessible Premises”, which put forward policy and operational recommendations to the Government.
A HK$1.3bn retrofitting programme covering 3,500 government premises and facilities followed, while accessibility was improved at around 240 Housing Authority properties. Accessibility coordinators and officers were also appointed, and the Universal Accessibility Programme was further introduced in 2012 to improve access to public walkways.
While some discriminatory practices are outright and easy to spot, dismantling subtle biases embedded in routine working practices demands true cultural change.
According to Lam, family-friendly employment is an area where further effort is needed. Many organisations, she notes, still lack formal policies supporting employees with family responsibilities and may regard such arrangements as optional staff benefits. Traditional gender roles and bias towards working mothers can also affect career opportunities.
Such barriers require workplace culture and practice to change in conjunction with legal protection. The EOC has been working with organisations from various sectors to promote the importance and benefits of fostering inclusive and respectful workplace cultures.
The EOC’s Racial Diversity and Inclusion Charter for Employers encourages businesses to promote racial diversity and inclusion in the workplace, while the “Safe Spaces for All: Anti-Sexual Harassment Community Partner Programme” provides structured training on legal protections and prevention strategies. Participants from 17 organisations are encouraged to bring anti-sexual-harassment awareness back into their own organisations.
Education remains vital to driving cultural change and shifting societal perspectives. Since 2001, more than 480,000 participants from companies and organisations have attended EOC training programmes on equal opportunities.
As the EOC enters its fourth decade, Lam sees greater value in working closely with different sectors across the region.
That forward-looking vision guides the EOC’s 30th anniversary campaign, “30 Years of Building a Vibrant City Through Equality”.

Pro-Israel lobby AIPAC spends big on US midterms as backlash grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
02:00:01 UTC
11:00:01 KST

The most powerful pro-Israel lobby in the United States is spending more than any other outside group on the 2026 midterms — even as its once-coveted backing becomes an increasingly potent weapon for political opponents.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has poured tens of millions of dollars into races nationwide through its main election-spending vehicle, the United Democracy Project (UDP).
The so-called "super PAC" — a group allowed to lavish unlimited sums to influence elections, provided it operates independently of candidates — has spent $54 million on congressional races, according to campaign finance monitor OpenSecrets.
That has made it the single largest outside spender of the cycle, OpenSecrets said, while the wider pro-Israel donor network spent $71 million — placing it second only to the cryptocurrency industry.
The extraordinary financial firepower underscores AIPAC's continued influence in Washington — but also a growing backlash over US policy toward Israel and the role of wealthy interest groups in American elections.
AIPAC has concentrated much of its spending on Democratic primaries, supporting candidates strongly committed to Israel and trying to defeat critics of unconditional US military aid.
It didn't respond to a request for comment, but it has rejected suggestions that its influence is collapsing, saying hundreds of candidates it backed have won their primaries.
Its money has indeed delivered victories this year, but also some expensive failures.
Money meets resistance
In Michigan, AIPAC and allied groups spent around $30 million in an unsuccessful effort to prevent progressive former health official Abdul El-Sayed from winning the Democratic Senate nomination over establishment-backed Congresswoman Haley Stevens.
Progressives have also defeated candidates supported by AIPAC-linked money in congressional contests in California, Illinois and New York, often turning the group's spending itself into a campaign issue.
Eli Clifton, of US foreign policy think tank the Quincy Institute, said UDP was the biggest spender in Michigan, although 97 percent of its large contributions came from outside the state — and its biggest donors are Republican billionaires.
"This is a special interest that participates outside of the partisan framework, and it's really all about advancing the interests of a foreign country," he told AFP.
Unease over the group is no longer confined to Democrats.
Allies of Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, recently asked AIPAC not to run advertisements publicly on his behalf, US media reported, fearing its overt involvement would benefit El-Sayed in the Arab-American heartland.
Shifting opinion
The discomfort reflects a broader transformation in US attitudes toward Israel following years of its genocide in Gaza and widening conflict across the Middle East.
A June Quinnipiac University poll found 48 percent of American voters believed Washington was too supportive of Israel, including 66 percent of Democrats — the highest overall figure in nine years of the survey.
The change has been clearest on the Democratic left, where candidates increasingly portray AIPAC as too closely aligned with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and emblematic of big-money interests overwhelming ordinary voters.
But criticism has spread to the populist right, where some "America First" conservatives have attacked Washington's support for Israel and blamed pro-Israel lobbying for drawing the United States deeper into foreign conflicts.
AIPAC's financial strength, meanwhile, continues to grow. OpenSecrets says the organisation itself has contributed $30 million to UDP.
And its political power remains formidable, with US military support to Israel continuing to attract broad support in Congress.
But the primaries have demonstrated that record spending cannot guarantee victory — and a once-prized endorsement can now, in some races, be something candidates would rather their opponents talked less about.
"That's precisely why they never mention US foreign policy and Israel in their ads," Casey Kennedy, co-founder of the Track AIPAC advocacy platform, told AFP.
"AIPAC knows AIPAC is toxic, and the more they spend, the more toxic they become with voters across the political spectrum."

Singapore keen to build on goodwill, deepen ties with Kazakhstan: SM Lee
- Singapore aims to strengthen ties with Kazakhstan, focusing on business growth, increased trade, and improved connectivity, including exploring direct flights.
- Singapore companies are expanding in Kazakhstan, especially in services and investments, with opportunities in logistics, education, and the Middle Corridor trade route.
- Both countries value cooperation as small nations, promoting a rules-based international system and Kazakhstan's efforts to join ASEAN’s Treaty of Amity and Cooperation.
AI generated
ASTANA – Singapore wants to build on the goodwill it enjoys in Kazakhstan and deepen ties in areas ranging from business to connectivity, Senior Minister Lee Hsien Loong said as he wrapped up his first visit to the Central Asian country.
Lee said on Aug 27 that Singapore’s relationship with Kazakhstan was “an account well worth cultivating”, with Singapore companies showing growing interest in the country and trade and investments increasing significantly in recent years.
“We enjoy a lot of goodwill,” he told Singapore media in a doorstop interview at the St. Regis Astana Hotel, noting that Kazakhstan remembers warmly founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew’s first visit in September 1991, three months before the country became an independent republic.
One area where Lee saw room for improvement was connectivity. He said Kazakh businesses had cited the lack of direct flights between Singapore and either Astana, the capital, or Almaty, its largest city, as an obstacle to closer links.
“It’s something which we would look at, and we would encourage SIA to look at,” he said. “I hope there’s a business case at some point.”
Lee noted Kazakhstan’s growing winter tourism industry as one potential source of demand. The country is developing the Shymbulak ski resort near Almaty as it prepares to host the Asian Winter Games in 2029.
Singaporeans are keen on winter sports and travel to Japan, South Korea and China to ski, he said, adding that further development of the resort in the next few years would bring more business.
Growing business interest
Beyond connectivity, Lee said Singapore companies were showing growing interest in Kazakhstan, with trade and investments rising significantly in recent years.
Singapore firms in sectors ranging from law and logistics to education and venture capital are already present in the country, Lee said, adding that PSA International and Changi Airport Group are also there.
“There will be these opportunities where the Kazakhs are building their economy, and our firms can participate in this,” Lee said.
Kazakhstan is Singapore’s largest trading partner in Central Asia. Bilateral trade in goods amounted to $326.6 million, while trade in services was $159 million. Singapore’s stock of direct investment in Kazakhstan stood at $2.1 billion, with 158 Singapore overseas affiliates operating there.
Lee said the physical distance means direct trade and investment may not be enormous. “But if we are talking about services trade, or talking about investments, doing business in each other’s countries, there is good potential,” he noted.
Another potential area of cooperation is the Middle Corridor, a route connecting China, via Central Asia and the Caspian Sea, to Europe.
Lee said that the route would complement, rather than replace, maritime routes between Asia and Europe, given the vastly different costs and volumes involved.
The Trans-Caspian Transport Corridor, commonly known as the Middle Corridor, carried about 4.5 million tonnes of goods in 2024, up 62 per cent from the year before, according to the OECD.
Singapore could contribute logistics, transportation management and IT expertise, he said, citing the possibility of PSA International helping to make operations along the corridor smoother.
“It’s an advantage to them. It’s business for us,” he said.
A relationship between the two countries would offer broader strategic advantages, Lee said. While Kazakhstan is vast in land area, it has a population of about 20 million, making both countries relatively small in the international scheme of things.
Small and medium-sized countries need to work together to support a rules-based international system rather than one governed by “might is right” arrangements, he said.
Lee also noted parallels between how Singapore and Kazakhstan navigate their respective regions.
Kazakhstan has two much larger neighbours, Russia to the north and China to the east. Singapore, meanwhile, understands what it means to be a small country that seeks to maintain friendly relations with its neighbours while pursuing its own course.
“We understand what it is we need to do in order to keep on friendly terms with our neighbours and yet maintain a consistent direction so that people find us trustworthy, reliable, and something they can depend on and are happy to do business with,” he said.
“We compared notes on this.”
Aside from doing business in South-east Asia, Kazakhstan is also looking to deepen its links with the region more broadly. Lee has previously said that Singapore, which will assume the ASEAN chair in 2027, will create more opportunities for ASEAN to engage with partners beyond its traditional networks.
When asked about prospects for closer engagement with the grouping, Lee noted that Kazakhstan was “very serious” about joining the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (TAC).
The TAC is a regional pact that sets out principles for peaceful relations and cooperation, and accession is a prerequisite for formal partnerships with ASEAN.
He said there was a process underway for Kazakhstan to join the treaty, adding: “I hope it will reach a good conclusion and not take too long.”
Desire for progress
During Lee’s visit from Aug 24 to 27, he met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and other senior Kazakh leaders, as well as business representatives in Almaty.
He was also conferred Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk, or Order of Friendship, First Class, by Tokayev on Aug 26.
On Aug 27, Lee delivered a lecture at Nazarbayev University in Astana, where he was conferred an honorary professorship.
Reflecting on his first visit to Kazakhstan, Lee said he was impressed by the country’s “energy” and “determination” to make progress in a complicated world, through investments in education, IT and artificial intelligence.
He also pointed to Kazakhstan’s considerable mineral and energy resources, with extractive industries accounting for about a quarter of its economy. If the country could complement these resources with its human talent, “I think they have many things going for them”, he said.
“The impression is that these are people who know what they want, and who are moving quite fast to get there,” Lee added.

Private credit stress deepens as CVS Lane suspends investor redemptions
Unknown

Private credit firm CVS Lane joins list of firms limiting investor pullouts
Stress in Australia's private credit sector is intensifying.
A private lender with significant loans to collapsed developer Bathla called CVS Lane is the latest private credit firm to limit "investor redemptions".
The ABC has confirmed that the investment manager told investors on Thursday that its CVS Lane First Mortgage Fund and CVS Lane Property Finance Fund had exposure to Bathla across nine different loans.
Investor redemptions are when investors in private credit firms seek to get some or all of their money returned in the face of concerns about the safety of their investment because of potentially overly risky lending.
Major Sydney residential developer Bathla Group announced earlier this week that it was going into administration after months of mounting financial pressure, owning more than $3.5 billion.
Administrators from Teneo were appointed to its main corporate entity, Universal Property Group, as well as Raj & Jai Construction, a company linked to the Bathla Group, documents lodged with ASIC show.
CVS Lane is reported to have told investors it had "determined to temporarily suspend the processing of application and redemption requests across the funds".
"The funds' redemption provisions are designed to balance investor liquidity with the interests of all investors in the funds," it told clients.
Temporary suspension 'in best interests'
CVS Lane has $2.1 billion under management.
"The trustee considers a temporary suspension to be in the best interests of investors as a whole, with relevant factors including the current uncertainty surrounding the Bathla administration and the need to ensure any decisions … are made on the basis of the best available information," CVS Lane is reported to have told investors.
There are about 40 private credit funds invested in Bathla, with exposures ranging from $1.5 million to $340 million.
CVS Lane told investors it would update them next week and reassess its position by the end of October.
Among the other private credit firms exposed to Bathla, the ABC has contacted Balmain, Centuria Bass, Credit Connect, CVS Lane, Keyview, La Trobe, Ray White Capital and Trilogy for comment.
The ABC understands private credit firm Keyview's loans are at the stage of being repaid through the settlement of completed assets rather than having any exposure to Bathla's ongoing viability.
The Sydney-based firm, according to its website, oversees more than $800 million across its funds.
The ABC understand Keyview has no redemption restrictions in place across any of its funds and has no current plans to limit investor liquidity.
La Trobe Financial's total exposure to the Bathla Group is approximately $38.1 million.
"It comprises four residential loans and one development loan," the firm said in a statement.
The development project is approximately 95 per cent complete.
The private credit firm added: "We hold the full costs to complete it, and presales cover 89 per cent of the current loan balance.
"We expect to recover the loan in full."
Trilogy Funds said that, as of yesterday, its exposure to Bathla Group was $29.79 million, relating to two of 131 current loans.
"Trilogy Monthly Income Trust continues to operate in the normal course and there are currently no plans to limit investor redemptions," the private lender said in answer to the ABC News questions about the potential for investor redemptions.
"Redemption procedures remain unchanged and investors continue to have access to their funds in accordance with normal processes."
Concerns more credit provide will limit redemptions
Credit funds not exposed to Bathla have told the ABC they are concerned more private credit providers will limit redemptions to avoid investors pulling money out now in fear of not being able to later on.
Earlier this week MA Financial announced a temporary redemption limit of up to 1 per cent of its funds under management per month.
MA Financial's joint chief executive Chris Wyke told Nine newspapers the action was a "proactive measure in response to the potential for increased redemption activity".
Wall Street is ground zero for the alternative investment market and there are fears this massive, risky US private lending ship is sinking and investors are jumping out.
Financial Services Council trying to head off worries
The Financial Services Council (FSC), the peak body for Australia's financial services industry, is now seeking to head off similar worries taking hold in Australia.
It has released a new industry standard for the private markets and private credit sectors designed, it said, "to strengthen investor confidence and lift industry practices in the growing market".
ASIC told the ABC earlier this year it was concerned about the risks private credit presented to Australia's superannuation industry and therefore all working Australians.
While it does not see systemic financial risk yet, Commissioner Simone Constant said, "FSC's standards mark an important step towards lifting practices across a sector that has grown dramatically in size and breadth and is now facing its first real test".
"The next step is for other industry associations and participants to follow suit in developing, adopting and adhering to strong standards and definitions and, of course, for the funds themselves to step up and adopt them with urgency," she said.

What's next?

Hours after seeing his national record broken by two seconds at the Gold Coast marathon, Andy Buchanan was sitting in his hotel room reflecting.

The record was unattainable for an Australian man for decades.
Rob de Castella's mark stood for 36 years, before Brett Robinson's breakthrough in 2022, then Buchanan in 2024, and now Strintzos.
And while it is unlikely to fall again on Sydney's tricky, hilly course, Buchanan will be the fastest Australian man in the elite field, headlined by reigning world champion, Tanzania's Alphonce Simbu.
They will be amongst more than 40,000 entrants in Sydney's second year as one of the world's eight marathon majors.
It is Buchanan's first marathon at home, and first since London in April last year.
"I had a stress reaction in my femur, and then I tried to get back for World Champs and then re-injured it, tried to get back for Valencia, re-injured it," he said.
"So it's just the same injury three times, which was very frustrating, but you've just got to try and learn something from every injury, and I think I've learned something, but we'll find out."
And as the second fastest male marathon runner in Australian history, the 35-year-old was always destined to go the distance.
"Growing up as a schoolkid, my parents were marathon runners back before running was cool," he said.
"And I grew up thinking the normal family holiday was to go to Gold Coast or go to Adelaide or go to Hobart or Perth, watch your parents run a marathon, then you get to spend a week or two around that state.
"But I'm very thankful for my parents that I got to have that upbringing.
"I fell in love with the marathon just by watching people at 30k and seeing the pain they were going through, and you'd see the same people then crossing the line at 42k and it's such a unique thing."
Pashley leading Australian women
The women's field also boasts the current world champion, Kenya's Peres Jepchirchir, while Ellie Pashley is vying to be the first Australian across the line — a title which pockets $30,000 for men and women.
The Tokyo Olympian won the Ballarat Marathon in April, her first after the birth of her second child.
"I'm really excited to be honest. I think time off from the sport really grows your hunger to get back into it," she said.
"Watching last year, seeing the course, seeing the race amongst the Australian women, I was really pumped to try and get a spot in the race this year and I'm excited to be a part of it."
And she is trying not to measure herself against some of Australia's other leading female marathoners.
"I feel like it takes me a while to get back after having a baby," Pashley said.
"I think some of the Australian women make it look fairly easy with how incredibly they run so soon after childbirth.
"I feel like I'm still building back up and I hope I'm a little bit fitter than I was in Ballarat.
"There's always a few hiccups along the way when you have young children with illness and things like that. But I'm feeling fitter and I'm hoping to give a good time."
Caitlin Scott, 29, is one of the other leading Australian women, having only made her marathon debut in Melbourne last year.
"I feel like I'm quite green and inexperienced as a marathon runner, so I'm really excited for Sunday … just to give the distance another crack and see what we can do," she said.

What is celebrated on August 28 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
04:45:27 EEST
10:45:27 KST

What is celebrated on August 28 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
On August 28, Ukraine honors Moses the Ethiopian, while according to the old calendar, it is the Dormition of the Mother of God. Ternopil celebrates its city day, and people around the world read comics.
On August 28, Orthodox believers traditionally celebrate one of the twelve major feasts — the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos according to the old calendar, while according to the new calendar they commemorate Saint Moses the Black. At the same time, the world celebrates International Read Comics in Public Day, and Ternopil marks its city day, UNN writes.
International Read Comics in Public Day
This creative annual celebration was launched in 2010 to promote comics as a fully fledged literary and artistic genre. The organizers encourage graphic novel fans to go out into the streets, parks, or cafés and openly read their favorite publications. This flash mob helps break down stereotypes that comics are created exclusively for children and brings like-minded people together around the world.
Ternopil City Day
One of the most beautiful cities in western Ukraine traditionally celebrates its birthday on August 28, which historically coincides with the major church feast of the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos. Festive celebrations are usually held that day on the banks of Ternopil Pond, along with folk crafts fairs, concerts, and exhibitions. Local residents and city visitors have an opportunity to enjoy the unique atmosphere, taste Galician delicacies, and join charitable initiatives.
The Commemoration Day of Saint Moses the Black and Saint Augustine
According to the new calendar, on August 28, Orthodox believers commemorate Saint Moses the Black and Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo. Moses the Black (the Ethiopian) is a unique figure in Christianity, as before his sincere repentance and acceptance of monasticism, he was a merciless leader of bandits. His life became a vivid example of profound repentance, extraordinary strength of will, and a person's ability to completely change their path for the sake of spiritual purity. In prayers to Saint Moses, people often ask for healing from destructive passions, particularly addictions.
According to the old calendar, August 28 marks the major twelve-feast celebration of the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos, popularly known as the "First Most Pure Feast." The celebration is dedicated to the end of the earthly life of the Virgin Mary and her blessed passage into the Kingdom of Heaven, where she was reunited with her Son, Jesus Christ. This day also marks the end of the strict two-week Dormition Fast, so hearty meat dishes traditionally appear on the festive table. In folk tradition, the feast symbolized the final completion of the harvest, so people brought ears of the new crop to church for consecration and blessing

Trump plans to mark 9/11 at the Pentagon, not Ground Zero
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
01:45:00 UTC
10:45:00 KST

Trump plans to mark 9/11 at the Pentagon, not Ground Zero
Maggie Haberman, Zolan Kanno-Youngs, Dana Rubinstein and Sally Goldenberg
- President Trump will commemorate the 25th anniversary of 9/11 at the Pentagon, not at Ground Zero, because politicians are barred from speaking at the New York memorial.
- Trump plans to speak at the Pentagon ceremony and will attend a political convention in Texas beforehand, then travel to Ireland; Vice-President J.D. Vance will represent the White House in New York.
- The 2026 Ground Zero event will include former presidents and officials, maintaining a non-partisan, speech-free tradition since 2012.
AI generated
NEW YORK – President Donald Trump is not planning to attend a ceremony in New York for the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attack on the World Trade Center, in part because he wanted to deliver a speech and the annual event has long barred remarks, according to four people with knowledge of the events.
Trump’s team had conducted advance visits at the site and had initially signalled to officials in New York and in Washington that he intended to visit the memorial space known as Ground Zero, two of the people with knowledge of the events said.
The President’s interest in speaking on 9/11 was conveyed to memorial planners in recent weeks, three of the people with knowledge of the events said. But since 2012, politicians have been barred from speaking at the site.
The National September 11 Memorial & Museum, which oversees the site, has worked rigorously to keep the venue non-partisan and focused on the solemnity of the day.
Trump, a native New Yorker who talked often about the 9/11 attacks during his 2016 presidential campaign, is now expected to commemorate them at the Pentagon, two of the people with knowledge of the events said. The Pentagon also came under attack on 9/11.
Vice-President J.D. Vance is expected to represent the White House in New York.
The President will go to the Pentagon after he attends a mid-term political convention in Texas. Officials have discussed some kind of tribute to the terrorist attack victims during that convention, which takes place Sept 9 and 10.
There are other considerations that led to Trump honouring the day in Washington, including that he will depart the next day for his golf course in Doonbeg, Ireland, where the Irish Open tournament will take place.
Leaving from John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City, or from Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey, would snarl air and motor traffic to a much greater extent than with Trump leaving from Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.
Trump last attended the ceremony at Ground Zero in 2024, when he stood alongside Vance, former mayor Michael Bloomberg, president Joe Biden and vice-president Kamala Harris.
None of the officials made formal remarks. Trump visited a fire station in New York City after the event.
The 2026 anniversary marks a quarter-century since the worst attack on the United States after the assault on Pearl Harbor.
Anna Kelly, a spokesperson for the White House, did not address the President’s plans in a response to an e-mail seeking comment.
“On the 25th anniversary of this tragic day, the President will remember those who were killed at the hands of evil terrorists, honour their loved ones, and pay tribute to the brave first responders who put their lives on the line to rescue their fellow Americans,” she said.
At the Pentagon, Trump will be allowed to speak, as he did in 2025 when he attended the remembrances there.
His speech that day came less than 24 hours after conservative activist Charlie Kirk, whose efforts to draw college-age voters into the MAGA movement were seen as significant to Trump’s 2024 victory, was shot and killed while speaking on a campus in Utah.
The ceremony had been intended to be held in a different spot that day but was moved to a new one amid security concerns about Trump after Kirk was assassinated.
“We recall the light of America’s best and bravest and the love that they showed in their final moments,” Trump said at the time.
“In their memory, we make a solemn pledge and a noble promise. We will honour always our great heroes, and you are our heroes.”
Trump has faced two assassination attempts and other murder-for-hire plots by alleged Iranian proxies. He has faced an uptick in threats since he began a war against Iran on Feb 28.
The 2026 event in Manhattan is expected to include former mayor Rudy Giuliani; former president Bill Clinton and his wife Hillary; former president George W. Bush and his wife Laura; and former president Barack Obama, among others, according to several people who have been close to the planning.
In the first decade after 9/11, elected officials would read poems and historic American documents, like the Gettysburg Address, at the ceremony.
But since 2012, the memorial has barred any speeches by politicians. Instead, politicians stand alongside their peers from opposing parties as families step onto a stage to read the names of the dead over the course of hours.
Trump’s advisers have discussed possibly taking federal control of the National September 11 Memorial & Museum, including as recently as in 2025. Families of the Sept 11 victims have in recent years criticised the site over its leadership and finances.
Trump, who was in New York on the day of the attacks, spoke to a New Jersey television station in the aftermath, saying that a building he owned had gained in stature because the twin towers had fallen.
That building, 40 Wall Street, “actually was the second tallest building in downtown Manhattan, and it was actually – before the World Trade Center – was the tallest”.
He went on: “And then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest. And now it’s the tallest.” (The statement was not correct; 70 Pine Street, nearby, was taller than Trump’s building.) NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

US judge blocks Pentagon's Anthropic blacklisting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
01:44:17 UTC
10:44:17 KST

US judge blocks Pentagon’s Anthropic blacklisting
- A US judge blocked the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic, ruling the decision "illegal and baseless" and protecting the company's free speech and due process rights.
- Anthropic was labelled a national security supply-chain risk after refusing military use of its AI chatbot Claude for surveillance and autonomous weapons.
- The Pentagon argues the designation is due to contract issues, not AI safety views, while Anthropic claims it could lose billions and reputational harm from the ban.
AI generated
A US judge on Aug 27 blocked the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic, the latest turn in the Claude maker’s high-stakes fight with the military over AI safety on the battlefield.
Anthropic’s lawsuit in California federal court alleges that Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth overstepped his authority when he designated Anthropic a national security supply-chain risk, a label the government can apply to companies that expose military systems to potential infiltration or sabotage by adversaries.
Hegseth’s unprecedented move, which followed Anthropic’s refusal to allow the military to use AI chatbot Claude for US surveillance or autonomous weapons, blocked Anthropic from certain military contracts. Anthropic executives have said it could cost the company billions of dollars in lost business and reputational harm.
Anthropic says that AI models are not reliable enough to be safely used in autonomous weapons and that it opposes domestic surveillance as a violation of rights, but the Pentagon says private companies should not be able to constrain military action.
US District Judge Rita Lin, an appointee of former democratic president Joe Biden, made the ruling in a 59-page order where she found that the Pentagon’s decision was “illegal and baseless”.
“The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” she wrote.
Anthropic’s designation was the first time a US company has been publicly designated a supply-chain risk under an obscure government-procurement statute aimed at protecting military systems from foreign sabotage.
In its March 9 lawsuit, Anthropic alleged the government violated its right to free speech under the First Amendment of the Constitution by retaliating against its views on AI safety. The company said it was not given a chance to dispute the designation, in violation of its Fifth Amendment right to due process.
The lawsuit says the decision was unlawful, unsupported by facts and inconsistent with the military’s past praise of Claude.
The Justice Department countered that Anthropic’s refusal to lift the restrictions could cause uncertainty in the Pentagon over how it could use Claude and risk disabling military systems during operations, according to a court filing.
The government said the designation stemmed from Anthropic’s refusal to accept contractual terms, not its views on AI safety.
Anthropic has a second lawsuit pending in Washington DC, over a separate Pentagon supply-chain risk designation that could lead to its exclusion from civilian government contracts. REUTERS

Iran war diplomacy turns towards reopening Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
01:39:33 UTC
10:39:33 KST

Iran war diplomacy turns towards reopening Strait of Hormuz
- Iran and Qatar are working to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran preparing conditions to restore normal shipping after mediation efforts.
- Iran and Oman have agreed on a shared shipping corridor, pending US acceptance of Iran's demands including lifting sanctions.
- US forces have cleared sea mines and maintained some shipping flow, but vessel traffic remains low due to Iranian threats and ongoing tensions.
AI generated
DUBAI – Iran war mediators have placed renewed emphasis on reopening the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran agreeing to draw up a list of conditions to restore normal traffic after a Qatari emissary pressed the Iranians to respect freedom of navigation.
With the US having disengaged from talks in favour of an economic pressure campaign, the prime minister of Qatar met senior Iranian leaders in Tehran on Aug 27, stressing the importance of returning to the pre-war status of open shipping through an international waterway.
Qatar, a US ally and Gulf neighbour of Iran, and Pakistan helped broker a memorandum of understanding in June that led to a ceasefire and set terms for shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow stretch between Iran and Oman that before the war was the conduit for 20 per cent of the world’s oil supply.
After the US and Israel launched the war six months ago, Iran threatened to strike any vessel transiting the strait without its authorisation, driving down traffic and sending up the price of oil, providing Iran with leverage in the bargain.
In his mission to Tehran on Aug 27, Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said on X that he underscored to senior Iranian officials “the importance of respecting freedom of navigation in the Strait of Hormuz in accordance with international law”.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, later said Iran was preparing a list of conditions for reopening the strait after mediators asked Tehran to set them out.
Speaking through an interpreter in an Al Manar TV interview, Rezaei said Iran had agreed with Oman on a shipping corridor through the strait, with parts of the route in Omani waters and parts in Iranian waters. Ships would use a designated central channel if the US met Iran’s conditions, he said.
In the past Iran’s conditions have included an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, compensation and removal of sanctions. It remained unclear whether Iran intended to amend those demands in a way that might be acceptable to the Americans.
Tehran and Washington have exchanged little more than bellicose statements in recent weeks, leaving the diplomacy to third parties.
So far Iran has insisted on returning to the June memorandum of understanding that established a ceasefire within a 60-day window for negotiations.
But that deal quickly fell apart over differing interpretations of Iran’s authority over shipping arrangements, and US President Donald Trump declared the MOU was “over” three weeks after it was signed.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said on Aug 26 that Iran and Oman had agreed in principle on administering traffic in the strait and sharing revenues, but a senior Iranian source later said the two countries were still working on the details of an agreement.
Meanwhile, US military commanders say American forces have cleared sea mines from the strait that had been laid months ago by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
“Bottom line: today, international shipping lanes are open and momentum is building,” Admiral Brad Cooper, commander of the US military’s Central Command, said in a video message posted on social media.
US forces have in recent months helped 1,500 commercial vessels carrying nearly 750 million barrels of crude oil to transit the strait, Cooper said.
Trump has repeatedly said the strait was open, but many vessels have opted against sailing through it because of Iranian threats, and ship tracking services have estimated activity at roughly 5 per cent to 15 per cent of normal volumes.
The UN’s International Maritime Organisation has reported 70 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the war that have killed 19 seafarers. REUTERS

Dolly Parton's legacy lives on through book deliveries to kids

Dolly Parton's legacy lives on through book deliveries to kids
CLEVELAND, Georgia, Aug 27 - For 3-year-old Simon Dockery, a trip to the mailbox can mean a new adventure.
Since he was a baby, books from Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library have arrived at his family’s Georgia home each month. Now his younger brother, 11-month-old Samuel, also receives books of his own.
The deliveries have helped turn reading into a family tradition, their mother Olivia Dockery said.
“It’s so exciting and for our family it was like a launch point for just the love of books,” Dockery, 30, said in an interview. “Each month, the oldest looks forward to going to the mailbox and getting that book out.”
Parton, the country music star and philanthropist who died on Tuesday at age 80, founded the Imagination Library in 1995, inspired in part by her father’s inability to read or write. The program sends free books each month to enrolled children from birth until age five.
What began by serving children in Parton’s home county in Tennessee grew into an international literacy initiative operating across five countries. The program has distributed more than 300 million free books worldwide.
Dockery said she did not have an enthusiasm for reading as a child and hopes the monthly deliveries will help give her sons something different.
“I didn’t grow up with a love for books,” she said. “Something that we want to instill is just a love for literature. And having these books provided for us each month just kind of continues that fire.”
The books are selected based on a child’s age, personalized with the child’s name and mailed directly to his or her home, helping make receiving a new book an event of its own.
In the U.S. capital city of Washington, more than 100,000 children have participated in the program through a joint effort with the Imagination Library and the D.C. Public Library, according to D.C. Public Library Executive Director Richard Reyes-Gavilan.
Shami Chimonyo enrolled her 7-month-old daughter shortly after she was born. Concerns about declining literacy rates motivated her to sign up, Chimonyo said.
"I love that the books are extremely well-written and have great grammar, as well as just they're a great visual for young learners," Chimonyo said. "It's just a treat that we're looking forward to continue having and receiving." REUTERS

Column: SCO at 25, a steadfast advocate for peace and shared development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
09:34:13 CST
10:34:13 KST

by Serik Korzhumbayev
Over the past quarter of a century, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) has transformed from a regional mechanism into one of the world's most significant platforms for dialogue and cooperation across Eurasia. Yet its importance should not be measured only by geography, population or economic weight. What matters even more is the guiding principle behind the organization.
First is the belief that security should be common rather than exclusive. For me, one of the SCO's most important contributions is its understanding of security, something that is too often interpreted through the lens of military strength, deterrence and geopolitical blocs.
Sustainable security cannot be achieved simply by increasing military capabilities. Security is also economic, social and technological. It depends on whether young people have access to education, whether businesses have opportunities to grow, whether countries are connected by modern infrastructure, and whether neighboring societies trust one another.
A country surrounded by instability cannot remain completely stable. Likewise, prosperity in one part of a region cannot be sustainable if neighboring countries remain isolated from economic development. Poverty, inequality, unemployment, weak infrastructure and technological backwardness can themselves become sources of instability. This is directly connected to another distinctive feature of the SCO.
Second is the belief that development should be shared rather than monopolized.
Countries that are economically connected have a stronger incentive to preserve stability, which is why connectivity should be seen as part of peacebuilding. Therefore, investments in development should also be understood as investments in long-term security.
The more roads, trade routes, digital links, business partnerships and personal relationships exist between societies, the greater the cost of confrontation, and the greater the value of cooperation.
Peace is not simply the absence of war. Peace is the presence of opportunity. The SCO's approach increasingly reflects this interdependence, integrating the concept of security with development.
Third is the belief that differences among states should be managed through dialogue rather than confrontation.
Another important feature that distinguishes the SCO from many other international organizations is that it was not designed as a military alliance directed against another group of states. The 21st century does not need to reproduce the bloc politics of the 20th century. The international system is already fragmented. Creating additional dividing lines would make the world more dangerous rather than more secure.
The SCO brings together countries with different political systems, economic structures, cultural traditions and development models. This diversity might appear to be a weakness from the perspective of traditional alliance politics, but it is actually one of the organization's most interesting features -- demonstrating that countries do not need to share every political position or every interpretation of international events to cooperate.
What they need is a willingness to respect each other's sovereignty, recognize legitimate national interests and continue talking even when disagreements exist. This is precisely why the Shanghai Spirit, which features mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diverse civilizations and pursuit of common development, remains relevant today. It represents an alternative political logic: cooperation without forcing uniformity.
The SCO can make its greatest contribution precisely by maintaining an open, inclusive and non-confrontational character. This does not mean that member countries will always agree, as differences are inevitable. But multilateral diplomacy is not about eliminating differences; it is about creating mechanisms that prevent differences from becoming conflicts.
An anniversary is usually an occasion to look backward. For the SCO, its 25th anniversary should above all be an occasion to look forward. The challenges ahead are enormous, as geopolitical tensions are growing, climate pressures are intensifying, technological change is accelerating, and the risk of misunderstanding between major powers remains serious.
In such circumstances, institutions capable of preserving dialogue become more valuable, not less. The SCO can play an important role in that regard. Its future relevance will not be determined simply by the number of summits it holds or declarations it adopts. It will be determined by whether people across the region can see tangible results: safer societies, stronger economies, better infrastructure, more opportunities for young people, greater access to technology and a deeper understanding between nations.
Ultimately, peace and development are not separate goals. There can be no sustainable development without peace, and there can be no lasting peace without development. This is perhaps the most important lesson of the SCO's first 25 years. That is why the organization has every reason to remain a steadfast advocate for peace, cooperation and shared development in a changing world.
Editor's note: Serik Korzhumbayev, a media veteran, is the editor-in-chief of the Delovoy Kazakhstan newspaper.
The views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the positions of Xinhua News Agency.

A Chinese cook in the Middle East serves up a very different anti-war film
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-28
01:30:10 UTC
10:30:10 KST

Jianlu Bi is a senior fellow at the Foreign Policy in Focus think tank at the Institute for Policy Studies in Washington, DC, and a research fellow at the Charhar Institute in Beijing.
This summer, Chinese anti-war film Once Upon a Time in the Middle East has dominated the mainland box office. The film implicitly answers the question: what happens when a story about international conflict is told, not through the sights of an assault rifle, but through a gentler lens?
It offers a fundamental restructuring of cinematic narrative paradigms, one that challenges decades of Hollywood inertia. For nearly a century, mainstream international anti-war cinema has been heavily anchored in the Western hero’s crucible. From The Hurt Locker to American Sniper, classic Hollywood conventions have framed global conflict through a distinct lens: military intervention, the combatant’s moral angst or the intervention of a solitary “saviour” imposing order on local chaos.
While these films often critique the horrors of war, they inadvertently reinforce a paternalistic dichotomy – reducing local populations to passive victims who form the backdrop to the agency of foreign soldiers.
Once Upon a Time in the Middle Eastdismantles this formula. Its protagonist, Xu Fu, is neither an elite mercenary nor a geopolitical agent. He is an ordinary Chinese cook earning a living abroad to pay off debt. When war erupts around his small restaurant, he neither picks up a weapon nor delivers lofty ideological speeches. Instead, he simply keeps the cooking stoves lit.
By centring a civilian whose primary act of defiance is feeding people, the film shatters the Western “saviour” archetype. It reframes anti-war drama from a spectacle of military prowess to a quiet testament to human endurance. This shift has ignited a fresh debate about global storytelling: can international cinema move past the binary of conqueror vs victim to build narrative tension around the preservation of daily life?
Trailer Chinese Movie Once Upon A Time in the Middle East 2026 United States Invasion Iraq US August
Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’s narrative is rooted in Chinese history. The protagonist’s name, Xu Fu, brings to mind the alchemist sent overseas by Emperor Qin about 2,200 years ago. Yet while the ancient Xu sailed to seek imperial immortality, the modern Xu travels simply to earn a living. He represents generations of Chinese migrants who built roads, manned kitchens and quietly endured hardships in foreign lands.
