Foreign Minister Penny Wong said there was an "unfortunate possibility" the number of missing Australians could rise.
"We are urgently working to identify how many Australians have been in the region and to confirm the welfare of any Australians who are not accounted for," Senator Wong told the ABC's RN Breakfast.
She said Australia would provide a $5 million assistance package and the government was deploying additional staff to Nepal to assist with the humanitarian response.
Australia has 20 staff in Nepal and the government is sending four officers to the region in the next 24 hours, and a second team in the next couple of days, she said.
US President Donald Trump said the US has spoken with Nepali leaders and offered to provide "anything they want".
Hundreds of people rescued, including tourists
According to the latest figures from Nepal Police, 466 people have been rescued.
That included more than 30 foreign citizens, including people from India, South Korea and the United States, according to Nepal's Tourism Board.
No Australians were among the list, but the nationality of eight foreigners rescued had not yet been confirmed.
Many of those rescued have been taken to the Tribhuvan Teaching Hospital in Kathmandu, which has become crowded with people trying to find their loved ones.
The walls are lined with lists of people's names who are being treated inside the hospital, along with photos of missing people and those who have died.
Preksha KC is volunteering there, even though her uncle is missing.
"It is really helpless, hopeless, but we are building our confidence to find people with our team and our Nepal government," she told the ABC.
Ranjana Poudel is at the hospital to try and find news of her brother-in-law who was at the border when the flood hit.
"Last time he spoke to his family it was 8:15, and he said he would enter China by 10. But after that we had no contact with him," she told the ABC.
New flood warnings issued
Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has warned a lake forming at the site where the flood occurred is now at risk of bursting, triggering fresh floods.
Similar alerts have been issued in China and Tibet.
The lake formed after the glacier collapse blocked the river on Wednesday, according to the authority, which urged rescue workers and locals in the area to stay away from riverbanks until further notice in case the lake breached.
The formation of the barrier lake was captured in aerial footage by a Chinese rescue team on Thursday, which showed brown water accumulating in a basin with no visible outlet.
"The notice states that the lake is in the process of rising and is at risk of bursting,"
According to the Chinese water resources ministry, the lake was already overflowing, yet another 3 million cubic metres of water was expected to flow into the lake over the next three days.
More rain forecast over the coming week was expected to exacerbate the threat, Chinese state media said, citing the Chinese water resources ministry.
It prompted some rescue workers in Nepal to move towards higher ground.
"We are here for rescue and don't want to be near the danger zone," Pawan Koirala said, who moved away from the riverbed with his team of 13.
Environmental anthropologist Austin Lord, a senior fellow and the Nepal lead at the Stimson Center, told The World the more water, the faster it would travel.
"The natural dam that's created around it has not yet fully been compromised, and that lake could be gaining volume and could burst again," he said.
He said the terrain was "impassable in many points" for vehicles and that the rescue and recovery effort upstream from Nepal would be "brutal and slow".
Mr Lord said given Nepal was still in its monsoon season, there was a risk of landslides.
"There's always a possibility of another surge, there's always the possibility that … there could be other landslides along the route," he told the ABC.
"If the slopes have been destabilised or undercut at the bottom, if then rain occurs and they're saturated, the whole topography becomes increasingly unstable."
Loading...
Nepal PM orders rescue operation to 'speed up'
After visiting part of the flood-affected area on Thursday, Nepal's prime minister, Balendra Shah, assembled a high-level meeting of his ministers, where he urged authorities to "speed up rescue operations", provide free health care to injured people and offer immediate aid and support to impacted families.
More than 13,000 personnel from Nepal's police, army and armed police forces are currently deployed to the disaster zone and helping with rescue efforts.
David Fisher, head of the Nepal delegation with Red Cross and Red Crescent societies in Kathmandu, told the ABC rescue teams were trying to get aid into affected areas of the Himalayan floods but many communities were completely cut off.
"The [floods have] cut the roads. The electricity is out in many places. Cell coverage is out. So it has only been accessible from the outside by helicopter," Mr Fisher told The World.
"We know, at least from those who we have been able to access, that many, many of them have lost their homes," he said.
"They've lost everything they own."
International aid organisation UNICEF said at least 17,000 children had been affected by the natural disaster, with that number likely to rise.
"Children across Rasuwa and Dhading saw their lives being literally washed away in front of their eyes in a very short span of time, with homes, classrooms, and medical facilities damaged," Alice Akunga, UNICEF representative to Nepal, said.
"Children who have survived the floods now face heightened risks of disease, malnutrition, violence and exploitation."
She said at least 18 schools had been destroyed and 20 others damaged.

Google Engineer Accused of Polymarket Insider Trading Says He Was Just Gambling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:12:39 UTC
04:12:39 KST

Michele Spagnuolo, the Google engineer arrested in May by US authorities for alleged insider trading on Polymarket, is making a new bold bet. On Wednesday, his legal team filed a motion to dismiss the charges against him. Spagnuolo isn’t outright denying that he made money using internal information from Google. Instead, his legal team says that the wagers were not financial instruments subject to regulation by the United States’ Commodities Exchange Act but rather good old-fashioned international betting that the US has no authority over.
Spagnuolo, who has been placed on leave from Google, is accused of committing commodities fraud, wire fraud, and money laundering. Using the alias “AlphaRaccoon,” he allegedly made a series of wagers on Polymarket’s flagship platform that resulted in profits totaling over $1.2 million. According to the criminal complaint, “AlphaRaccoon” correctly wagered that the singer D4vd, who gained notoriety for his suspected connection to a grisly killing, would be Google’s most-searched person of the year in 2025. (D4vd was later charged with murder; he pleaded not guilty.)
You might not expect the lawyers defending someone accused of felonies to agree with state prosecutors, but the vicious legal infighting over prediction markets is creating strange alliances. Across the United States, state attorneys general and regulators are battling against both the federal government and prediction markets over whether event contracts should be considered “swaps” and therefore have to follow the Commodities Exchange Act, or instead be categorized as gambling, which is regulated by states.
Spagnuolo’s lawyers argue that defining swaps to include wagers like who the most-searched person on Google will be each year “would fly in the face of the statute’s purpose and history” and lead to “absurd results.” They say it would make it so that any wager in the world, from a charity raffle to a local Ping-Pong match, could be classified as a financial instrument. “Spagnuolo is basically making the same argument as the states that are suing prediction markets,” says a financial services regulation expert Todd Phillips. “This is the issue that will likely go up to the Supreme Court.”
In addition to disputing the idea that prediction markets offer swaps, Spagnuolo’s legal team argues that the US government had no jurisdiction over him in the first place because he’s a non-US citizen who was wagering on a non-US platform. Although Polymarket is headquartered in New York, the company’s flagship prediction market is banned in the United States and technically is administered by an ostensibly Panama-based entity known as Adventure One QSS.
Spagnuolo was living in Zurich, Switzerland, when he allegedly made the Google-related trades on Polymarket. “The extraterritorial argument is interesting and raises the question of whether the US should be the world’s prediction markets cop,” Philipps says. Spagnuolo’s team also claims that the charges should be dismissed because the internal information he supposedly leveraged did not have any commercial value to Google. Google did not respond to requests for comment.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency tasked with regulating prediction markets, and Spagnuolo’s legal team also did not respond to requests for comment. CFTC chairman Michael Selig previously told WIRED that the agency has the ability to pursue extraterritorial jurisdiction in cases involving offshore platforms in “extreme circumstances.”
Spagnuolo was the second person publicly charged with alleged insider trading on Polymarket in the US. A month prior to Spanguolo’s arrest, Special Forces soldier Gannon Ken van Dyke was charged with allegedly making more than $400,000 from wagers on Polymarket connected to the raid on former Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro. Van Dyke’s defense team is also arguing for the charges to be dismissed because they say his activity should be classified as gambling and therefore not subject to federal commodities law.
Earlier this week, the CFTC—which filed a separate civil lawsuit against Van Dyke—repeatedly stressed in an amicus brief for the criminal case that his Polymarket events contracts were, indeed, swaps. It won’t be surprising if the CFTC does something similar in Spagnuolo’s case. By mounting this type of defense, the alleged insider traders have now inserted themselves directly into a much larger existential showdown over prediction markets.

It was a spy satellite, now NASA's new telescope is set to head into space
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope set to explore the universe
This weekend, NASA plans to launch its next flagship mission into deep space.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which started life as a spy satellite, will help find alien planets, map the universe, and possibly contribute to the collapse of a major theory in modern physics.
Ami Choi, a research astrophysicist at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, says the telescope will help make discoveries in dark energy and dark matter.
But, as previous space telescopes have done, it may find things that astronomers can't even imagine yet.
"The unknown unknowns that we'll probably discover — I think that's also very exciting," Dr Choi says.
If the launch goes to plan, the telescope will release its first images and data in about three months.
And Australia will play a role beaming back the discoveries the telescope makes.
New life for a spare spy satellite
The $US4.3 billion ($6 billion) telescope, called Roman for short, is named after astronomer Nancy Grace Roman.
Roman, dubbed the "Mother of Hubble", was the first chief of astronomy at NASA and a powerful advocate for space-based telescopes.
The telescope is a souped-up version of one of two spy satellites donated by the US National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) to NASA in 2012.
"It was a surprise to everyone when we heard that they just plonked on Goddard's doorstep," Brad Tucker, an astrophysicist at the Australian National University, says.
Both satellites had been developed for observing the Earth, before cost overruns caused the NRO's project to be cancelled.
To create Roman, NASA bolted some new instruments onto one of the satellites, including an infrared camera, and refitted it for flight into deep space.
Despite cutting costs by using a hand-me-down satellite, Roman's launch was not a certainty, with the first Trump administration proposing its cancellation in 2018 and 2019.
Benjamin Pope, an astrophysicist who was working at New York University at the time, was among hundreds of astronomers who travelled to the US capital to lobby against its cancellation.
"People came from all over the United States, just go to Congress and say: 'This matters to us, this matters to our universities, this matters to our research, this matters to the public,'" Dr Pope, now at Macquarie University, says.
The mission survived both proposed cancellations, and even another by the second Trump administration in 2025, and is now launching nine months ahead of schedule.
"We're super lucky that despite all of the drama about its funding history and development history … everyone's really excited for Roman," Dr Pope says.
What the Roman telescope is built to see
The telescope's 2.4-metre mirror is the same size as the Hubble telescope and smaller than the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), making it less powerful.
But the Roman telescope has a wider field of view than either of the other space telescopes, meaning it can capture a bigger section of the sky in each snapshot.
It's also designed to see in a different part of the light spectrum to the JWST, looking at visible and near-infrared light rather than further into the infrared.
"It looks at colours that JWST really isn't looking at," Dr Tucker says.
Once launched, the Roman telescope will head to the same part of space as JWST: Lagrange Point 2, or L2, some 1.5 million kilometres from Earth.
Galactic panoramas to find dark matter
The telescope is fitted with a 300-megapixel infrared camera which will capture large chunks of the sky in each exposure.
"We consider it to be very powerful for surveys of the sky, or mapping out very large regions of the sky in very clear detail," Dr Choi,who is working on Roman's camera, says.
These wide-angle shots are particularly useful for learning about two of the great mysteries in modern physics: dark matter and dark energy.
Dark matter makes up most of the universe's matter, while dark energy is thought to be behind the universe's accelerating expansion, but physicists don't know what either phenomenon really is.
Surveying large portions of the sky allows researchers to find things like supernovas, which can be used to measure the expansion of the universe.
Observations from different telescopes are also important, because they can cross-check each other's results.
Some other astronomical surveys are starting to suggest that current models of dark energy could be wrong.
"We're really starting to see hints that dark energy is even funnier than we previously thought," Dr Tucker says.
The Roman telescope is expected to help confirm, or refute, these findings, over its first five years of operation.
Looking for alien planets
Dr Pope, meanwhile, is excited by the telescope's other big objective: finding "exoplanets" orbiting other stars.
"Roman may discover, over the course of its lifetime, many more planets than are currently known by all other telescopes and methods," Dr Pope says.
Roman's second instrument, its coronagraph, is designed to block out light from stars, letting the telescope see fainter objects near those stars.
While it won't quite be powerful enough to see small exoplanets like the Earth, Dr Pope says it will deliver unprecedented information on larger exoplanets — more like Jupiter in our solar system — including enough data to study their atmospheres.
"Before the end of my career, I want us to be participating in discovering habitable worlds and understanding what they look like," Dr Pope says.
"Roman is the biggest stepping stone towards that."
West Australian antenna collecting the data
Once the telescope is in position, it will beam back some 1.4 terabytes of data to Earth each day.
One of the three places receiving this data is in Western Australia, at the newly-built European Space Agency antenna run by the CSIRO in New Norcia, 130km north-east of Perth.
CSIRO site manager Suzy Jackson says the Roman telescope will transmit multiple times more data than other deep space satellites the station communicates with.
"We've basically had to upgrade our comms links on the ground in order to support that, which is quite hilarious," she says.
The station has to be operated with extreme precision, with parts of the 35-metre antenna being positioned to an accuracy of 0.5 millimetres.
"We've got 700 tonnes of antenna and we've got to point that to an accuracy of hair-splitting in order just to hit the target at all," Ms Jackson says.
"Everything's got to be absolutely perfect."
When will the Roman telescope release its first pictures?
The telescope is scheduled to launch from NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida at 7:26am US Eastern time (9:26pm AEST) this Sunday, August 30.
Then, the telescope will take three months to travel to its deep space destination and go through commissioning tests and checks.
If the launch and tests go to plan, Roman's first images will be publicly released three months after launch, and the telescope will begin its scientific observations.
All of Roman's scientific data will be available for anyone to download, immediately after it's collected.
"It's when you enable tonnes of different minds to look through data and do analysis and brainstorm — that's when you get all this interesting new information," Dr Choi says.
Dr Pope says the telescope's "open skies" policy is exciting.
"We're all going to be trying to drink from this fire hose of data," he predicts.
"This is going to spur a lot of excitement, conflict, drama, technology — everything."

Careful with those Accusations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:59:04 UTC
03:59:04 KST

Careful with those Accusations
Academia is in turmoil regarding partially or wholly AI-written research. AI-written work is being submitted to journals, but it isn’t clear how much. Publisher, journal, university, and department policies are emerging and fluctuating. Technology develops, rendering recently enacted policies ambiguous, vague, or subject to unintended loopholes.
With everything in flux, it’s impossible for norms to develop.
There is no general sense of whether and what kind and what degree of AI use by authors is acceptable. Different policies across different institutions means that what may be problematic AI use in one place is acceptable AI use in another, and vice versa.
Into this chaos steps forward the vigilantes. The vigilantes have always been there, but now they are newly armed and emboldened. In the everchanging and never ending race between the technology of deployment and the technology of detection, the latter seems to have a temporary lead in the form of Pangram. You can feed a text into Pangram and it will tell you its analysis of whether it is AI generated, and if so, what percentage of it is AI generated.
Pangram claims to have a remarkably high detection and low false-positive rates, and cites studies by third parties to support these claims. Yet I have seen plenty of posts by friends and colleagues across social media showing false positives with some of their own work. So user beware.
That said, even if Pangram’s claims about its accuracy are correct, it won’t always be helpful to simply know that a text is “AI generated.” This because there are two further problems.
The first problem is ambiguity about what “N% AI generated” means. If someone asks Claude to write them a novel article about a philosophical problem, not even giving it a thesis to work with but asking it to come up with one itself, and that’s the extent of the human’s contribution, the resultant paper will get a “100% AI generated” evaluation. And if someone spends a year researching, writing, workshopping, and revising a paper, and then asks an AI to improve the writing style throughout the paper, the resultant paper will get a “100% AI generated” evaluation, too. Despite their same scores, though, these seem like cases that it might be plausible to treat quite differently. And of course, there are countless variations of AI-use between these extremes.
The issue remains even for “0% AI generated” findings, for such a score might be given to both an article that was written entirely by a human who never used any AI tools, and an article written entirely by an AI after minimal prompting by a human, but then rewritten by the human in their own words and style.
The second problem concerns the variation in policies across academic publishers and journals. Different kinds of AI use are allowed or prohibited in different venues. Learning that Pangram reports a published article as, say, “50% AI generated”, even if that figure is in some sense correct, cannot tell us whether the AI use it’s detecting was illicit, except if the article is published somewhere that prohibits any and all AI use. Not only does that percentage not tell us how the AI was used, but it doesn’t tell us whether the AI use violated any of the journal’s or publisher’s policies.
Now it is still the case, today, that most philosophers disapprove of other philosophers using AI to write their articles. Whether you agree or not, many philosophers view the use of AI to write for you as wrong—as a form of plagiarism or cheating, or a misunderstanding of what it is to do philosophy. In short, “AI generated” is, to most ears in our discipline, a kind of condemnation.
What this means is that when someone feeds an article into Pangram and publicly reports that it was “100% AI generated”, they are accusing the named author(s) of professional misconduct.
That is a serious accusation! It can be quite damaging. Given how human psychology works (and how internet searches work), even if the author is shown to not have acted wrongly, negative connotations may linger, damaging the author’s professional prospects for years to come.
Given the possible damage, and given the two problems described above, it seems we have strong reasons, at least for now, to refrain from publicly posting the “scores” of articles fed into AI detection services like Pangram.
What’s an alternative? Well, you could initially privately contact the author, the editor, or the publisher with your concerns.
* * *
As some readers will have figured out, the foregoing was motivated by a recent actual case in which one philosopher posted on social media that another philosopher’s recently published article was, according to Pangram, 100% AI generated, despite the article lacking an acknowledgment of AI use. This led to an investigation by the publisher (Open Library of Humanities), which ended up clearing the author of any wrongdoing. The publisher wrote:
The investigation found no issues with the content of the article that would suggest any academic malpractice was committed, nor does the OLH have any reason to believe that generative AI was used to the extent that the complainant suggested, or with the intent to commit academic malpractice… In line with the OLH’s ‘Artificial Intelligence (AI) Policy’ on providing an ‘AI Declaration Statement’, the author did not meet the criteria set out within the policy to provide a public declaration statement, namely: ‘the use of generative AI that forms the basis of a specific research purpose’, ‘the use of generative AI that forms the basis of a controlled simulation that produces outputs, such as synthetic data to supplement partial datasets, which informs the article’s argument(s)’, or ‘the use of generative AI for specific demonstrative purposes, with generated output(s) quoted and cited clearly with the prompts used, the model version and the URL of the service as part of its citation or caption’…
[W]e have concluded that there are no verifiable issues found that provide or support accusations of AI misuse or malpractice.
You can learn more about this case here. Note: I ask that readers not use or mention the name of the author or the title of the article in that case in the comments here. The article was published in Political Philosophy, so if need be you can call it the PP case.
By the way, the philosopher who had posted on social media about the article’s Pangram score has now kindly removed his original post about it.
>[Edited to add:] I thought this would be clear from the post but in light of some of the comments (not all of which have been approved) I guess it wasn’t, so I’ll make it explicit: vigilantism in the comments regarding the PP case is not welcome, and any further comments relitigating it or speculating about the nature and extent of the AI use in that case will not be approved.<
* * *
Relatedly, a friend recently wrote in with a tip for referees concerned about refereeing AI-written work: start with the references.
They write:
Usually, before reading a paper, I read the references to get a sense of the context of the paper. I immediately noticed a reference to me that was fabricated: I have no paper with that title and have never published on that topic in the journal it was supposedly in. When I put the fabricated reference into Google AI and then Chatgpt (free versions), both responded by saying it was a paper in [journal name redacted]… Only after I responded, “this paper does not exist!” did they both reply with their usual, “sorry, I made a mistake,” etc.
I then checked the rest of the references in the paper and found 3 other errors: 2 relatively minor and another fabrication.
Other suggestions welcome. Use them responsibly.

Why Meta's 'big tobacco moment' in US might not flow to Australia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:52:21 UTC
03:52:21 KST

No guarantee Australian teens will benefit from Meta addiction settlement
Meta's landmark court settlement is being hailed by some as social media's "big tobacco moment", but there is no guarantee Australians will benefit from the safety measures the tech giant has agreed to.
The $2 trillion company, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, has just settled a suit with 29 US states.
It agreed to pay a record fine of $23.6 billion over 10 years — the largest payout of its kind for a social media company.
The settlement also marks the first time the company has been forced to change key features of its main apps, Facebook and Instagram, in the US.
Meta agreed to new default settings for under-18 users, including:
- Two-hour time limits across Facebook and Instagram combined.
- Night mode (12am-6am) and school mode (8am-3pm) settings to limit notifications and app use.
- Hidden likes.
- Blocking "extreme" beauty filters.
Teens in the US will also have the choice to switch to a chronological feed and ditch the algorithm designed to keep them scrolling longer.
The agreement came within the first week of a two-month trial alleging Meta's platforms were intentionally designed to addict young users.
"We've seen a number of different lawsuits that have gone against Meta in the last number of months," Lisa Given, professor of information sciences at RMIT, said.
"So I think they saw the writing on the wall."
The news has been welcomed by some Australian parents.
"The reckoning is happening before our eyes after 15 years of … I guess you would call it a free-for-all," Dany Elachi said.
Mr Elachi, from the Heads Up Alliance, a parent group focused on children's online safety, was sceptical Meta would follow through on everything it promised, but hopeful Australian kids would ultimately benefit.
"Meta has been forced into a position where they've had to make undertakings to make their platforms safer," he said.
"We just hope that at some point they will just have to throw their hands up."
Meta's move to settle 'quite smart'
Experts were less certain the effects would reach Australian shores.
"There's no requirement under this court case for things to change in Australia," Johanna Weaver, executive director of the Tech Policy Design Institute, said.
"Traditionally they roll out region by region and it doesn't mean that Australia will necessarily be top of the list."
While she agreed the settlement was groundbreaking, Professor Weaver said it was still a path Meta helped design for itself.
"There is no finding against Meta in this, there is no acceptance of liability," she said.
"And so it's actually quite a smart move [on] Meta's part to settle."
Professor Given said the changes Meta made to its platforms were likely changes the company was "comfortable" making.
But she was more optimistic the changes would ultimately be made global.
"Partly because they want to avoid court cases in future," she said.
"If they only apply this within the United States, then cases could crop up in Australia and other places."
Wherever Meta makes changes that apply only to teens, their efficacy will depend on whether the company can determine which of its users are under 18.
Professor Given said Australia's teen social media ban demonstrated it was still not able to do that in most cases.
"We've seen many kids that are still on the platforms — over 80 per cent of kids [are] still accessing social media content."
Meta is yet to face any fines for non-compliance with the policy, which has been touted by the Australian government for its role sparking similar change in 20 other jurisdictions.
Mr Elachi said the effect of combined international pressure should not be ignored.
"What we did in Australia a couple of years ago in passing legislation to create a minimum age has had reverberations around the world," he said.
"I believe all these things that are happening in tandem are all contributing to Meta and other social media companies having to listen to the demands of parents."

What do we know about China's new ambassador to Australia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:50:33 UTC
03:50:33 KST

analysis
Wolf warrior, intellectual, sock puppet? What do we know about China's new ambassador to Australia?
China's new ambassador-designate to Australia has barely got his feet under the handsome desk in his embassy office, but he has already generated plenty of chatter.
As Beijing's power swells, its emissaries and envoys inevitably draw more scrutiny and curiosity.
And it's no different for career diplomat Liu Jinsong, who has already been labelled a hardliner and a "wolf warrior" by some China watchers in Australia.
That's largely because when you search for Liu on the internet, one of the first things that pops up is an image that seems to portray him as the embodiment of autocratic Chinese disdain: aloof, standing with his hands in his pockets, looking down at a senior Japanese official who almost seems to be bowing.
The picture has a complex backstory.
Last year, the China-Japan relationship was plunged into crisis when Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told parliament that an attack on Taiwan by Beijing could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan.
When Tokyo sent senior foreign affairs official Masaaki Kanai to Beijing to try to defuse the situation, it was Liu — as Director-General for Asian Affairs at China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MFA) — who was tasked with conveying Beijing's fury.
It's not clear from the video that Kanai was actually bowing. When you watch it, it looks more like the Japanese official is leaning in closely to listen to a translator.
But the image of Liu, hands shoved nonchalantly in his pockets and looking rather superciliously at Kanai's bowed head, was splashed across Japanese media.
Tokyo complained that Beijing had blindsided them by allowing media in to film the talks' aftermath, while Chinese state media tried to use the video to crow that Japan had been humiliated.
But it's not certain what — if anything — this brief episode tells us about Liu and how he's likely to operate here in Australia.
Liu certainly read the riot act to his Japanese counterpart in the meeting and demanded (without success) that Takaichi withdraw her remark.
But analysts and officials who the ABC spoke to about Liu emphasised that any Chinese official in his position would have done exactly the same thing — because that was what he was instructed to do.
As one former senior official puts it: "This tells us plenty about the way China wanted to present the meeting, and the message it wanted to send to Japan, but it tells us very little about Liu himself."
"To some degree, every ambassador [in the world] is a sock puppet, but particularly in the Chinese system,"
Sam Chetwin George, a senior fellow at the Asia Society Center on US-China Relations, puts it more delicately, telling the ABC that China's Foreign Ministry "is not an apex policy-making part of the bureaucracy".
"It is largely a policy-taker, charged with implementing priorities set higher up in Beijing," he says.
"Diplomacy generally, and Chinese diplomacy in particular, is highly choreographed so Liu's principal role will be to steward the relationship in the direction set by Beijing, rather than leave his own personal imprint on it — though all diplomats of course have their own personal approach and style."
Still, Liu has also held several senior positions in the Foreign Ministry, and Mr George says it's worth scrutinising them closely for what they might reveal about how China wants to approach the relationship.
"In the last several years Liu has held two important posts during a period of shocks and profound transformations in geopolitics," he says.
"One was running MFA's internal long-range strategy department during the first US-China trade war, and the outbreak of COVID, and the other was running MFA's Asia Department as the Biden administration was strengthening America's 'Indo-Pacific' alliance system," he tells the ABC.
In this job, he says one of Liu's principal missions was to persuade Asian governments not to allow this architecture to harden into an "anti-China bloc".
"In other words, he is experienced in dissuading Asian nations from aligning more closely with America," he says.
Liu's record also shows that he is "not afraid of sharp language", he says — which might be a sign of what's to come when Australia and China next inevitably find themselves at loggerheads.
"In 2021, Liu referred to the Indo-Pacific strategy, AUKUS, and the Quad as a 'poison curtain' that would damage regional peace," Mr George said.
"The next year he borrowed a Bangladeshi proverb to describe America as a rooster strutting supreme on its own dung heap, but destined for humiliation.
"These remarks of course echoed Beijing's carefully considered rhetorical strategy, but illustrate that Liu will issue statements of this nature and communicate punishments insofar as Australia transgresses on China's defined interests."
For the moment, though, Liu seems keen to avoid that sort of language, with the ambassador-designate keen to project an energetic, confident and positive aura on arrival in Australia.
His opening statement contained the usual warnings about how both countries should "respect each other's core interests and major concerns".
But the ambassador-designate spent much more time dwelling on how he wanted to ensure everyday citizens felt the benefits of the relationship.
"Relations between countries ultimately rest on bonds between their peoples," he wrote.
Liu even mentioned he took the bus down to Canberra from Sydney after flying into Australia, saying he "enjoyed chatting with ordinary Australians along the way, which made the journey all the more enjoyable".
Stunt or not, that's not the sort of thing you could imagine some of his more stiff and dour predecessors doing.
There was also the distinct whiff of confidence in the statement, with Liu keen to suggest — as Chinese officials sometimes do — that China's rise is inevitable and unavoidable, and that Australia would be better served getting on board.
"Time awaits no-one, and neither does history," he wrote.
"Once our course has been set, we must pull hard on the oars and press forward — without hesitation, without deviation, and without turning back."
As one diplomatic source observed, rather wryly: "He really rocketed out of the blocks, didn't he?"
In fact, so hasty was his entry that Liu and his embassy staffers ran roughshod over diplomatic protocol.
There was some hurrumphing in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) about the fact Liu was calling himself "ambassador" — and advertising his welcome meetings with community groups — well before he'd actually presented his credentials to the governor-general.
A not-so-subtle note was sent out to all diplomatic missions the next day reminding "ambassadors-designate" to "avoid media engagement (and) commentary" that "creates the impression" they'd already started in the role.
The official English-language version of his statement, sent out by the Chinese embassy a day later, dutifully corrected it to "ambassador-designate".
But others have been less fixated on the titles Liu adopted — or his mode of transport to Canberra — and more interested in what those first photos of his arrival might tell us.
Senior analyst Geoff Wade from the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) pointed out that one of the photos posted by the Chinese embassy showed the incoming ambassador meeting with two prominent members of United Front groups in Australia tasked with championing Beijing's messages, and its push to take control of Taiwan.
This "immediate public display of affection with United Front members", he wrote, "was a clear signal as to the assertive stance Liu will take".
He argued that "a major element of Liu's tenure" would be mobilising diaspora groups to serve "the interests of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)", including its efforts to "incorporate Taiwan".
"This is certainly not a new agenda, but the actions of the ambassador suggest that this program will be accelerated."
And Sam Chetwin George says Beijing's overarching objective — which Liu will no doubt pursue — will still be to weaken Australia's alignment with the US and ultimately to erode the strength of the US-Australia alliance.
"The second Trump administration has given him a lot of ammunition to make this argument more persuasively," he says.
"America is now in an open trade war with Canada — its treaty ally and Five Eyes partner — and in recent days also scaled back annual military exercises with another ally, South Korea, for fear of offending Kim Jong Un.
"Within Australia, the arguments of voices like Paul Keating and Hugh White — who argue that America is unreliable and that Taiwan is not core to Australia's national security — are gaining more traction than before.
"Liu and his colleagues will attempt to amplify such arguments.
"China will attempt to maintain that stability while sowing doubt about American reliability and dissuading Australia from full commitment to any US-led war in the region," he says.
Wolf warrior or not, that will be Liu's task — and he'll likely pursue it with plenty of energy.

Albanese is seeking the icing on the international cake
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:48:55 UTC
03:48:55 KST

analysis
Albanese about to hit campaign trail for United Nations Security Council seat
Like many of his predecessors, Anthony Albanese has grown to enjoy the international diplomatic round that goes with the prime minister's job.
These days it's quite a thing, with an extensive "summit season" that dominates the latter months of the year.
Summit season includes the international climate conference (COP), ASEAN, APEC and the G20 — a string of meetings where Mr Albanese can rub shoulders with dozens of world leaders.
Ahead of the summits, he will be at the United Nations during leaders' week in September.
That is an excellent opportunity for a prime minister with lobbying on his mind.
Mr Albanese, who will address the General Assembly for the second year running, will launch Australia's bid for one of the non-permanent places on the UN Security Council in 2029–30.
If Australia can secure a seat, it would be icing on the international cake for the Albanese government.
The council period would fall in a Labor third term which, given its huge majority and the chaos on the conservative side, appears a fair bet as things stand.
Foreign Minister Penny Wong says:
"At a time when the world is more contested and more uncertain, a seat on the Security Council would give Australia a stronger voice in the decisions that affect us and our region.
"As an active middle power, we have a practical contribution to make to international peace and security, standing up for the rules and working with others to deliver outcomes."
Labor places much more faith in the UN than the conservatives do, so obtaining that seat would be a high priority for Senator Wong and Mr Albanese.
Australia has had five stints on the Security Council: 1946–47, 1956–57, 1973–74, 1985–86 and 2013–14. Norman Makin, Australia's ambassador to the United States and a former Labor minister, was president at the council's first session in 1946.
The last time Australia had a seat turned out to be particularly significant, after the downing of the Malaysia Airlines MH17 flight over Ukraine by pro-Russian forces killed 38 Australian citizens and residents. Then-foreign minister Julie Bishop carried Australia's reaction in the council.
Bids for the non-permanent seats can have long lead times, and it was actually Ms Bishop who, in September 2015 under the Turnbull government, announced the current one.
The Liberals had not always been so keen on pursuing a spot. In 2012, while in opposition, Tony Abbott lambasted the Labor government for the cost.
But Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is giving in-principle support to the current bid.
There is no doubt such campaigns can be expensive, especially if contested. They can also distort foreign aid, with some money spent effectively to buy votes.
So far, however, there is no contest.
Two spots are available for the Western European and Others group — of which Australia is part — and the only other nomination is Finland, which Australia and Luxembourg beat for the 2013–14 places. The government believes a late new runner is unlikely, but it is not complacent.
The UN election is in June 2028, just after the federal poll's due date. Even if the spot is uncontested, a country must be elected by a two-thirds majority of those voting at the General Assembly (about 129 votes if all 193 member states are present and voting).
Leaders' week should be an easy run for Mr Albanese. By contrast, the diplomacy around the UN climate summit is more complicated, requiring a good deal of dexterity.
The government wanted to host the COP, in partnership with Pacific countries, but found itself in an arm-wrestle with a very determined Türkiye. That led to a less-than-satisfactory co-hosting compromise. But Energy Minister Chris Bowen is the "president of the negotiations".
This year's COP has become more challenging for Australia than might have been expected when Labor proposed, ahead of the 2022 election, to bid for a COP.
Domestically, as the cost-of-living crisis has gripped the nation, climate change has slipped down the list of people's concerns.
Internationally, this will be one of the less notable COPs — more focused on nitty-gritty issues than on making major strides. Also, it comes when it is clear the world is not going to meet earlier ambitious goals.
Loading
Ritchie Merzian, chief executive of the industry body Clean Energy Investor Group, foresees the November COP as "workmanlike" but "symbolically" important.
It comes at a time when the multilateral system is being undermined. There is also pushback on environmental standards, with companies stepping back from earlier commitments. So it will be a "rallying cry of support around processes and the ultimate objective," Mr Merzian says.
Among the specific issues will be the perennial one of money — in this case, finance for small islands' battle with climate change.
Australia's progress in meeting its own targets is mixed. There are two main ones: a reduction of 43 per cent below 2005 emissions levels by 2030, and having 82 per cent of its electricity coming from renewables in 2030.
Grattan Institute senior fellow Tony Wood says Australia will come close to meeting the first. But "despite Chris Bowen's heavy lifting", it is unlikely to meet the second.
With the economics of large wind farms becoming difficult, and other investment problems, the government is stepping on the accelerator wherever possible to promote the renewable rollout.
Mr Albanese has sought to insist, in the government's specifications for data centres, that all proposals must bring an accompanying new renewable energy source to provide the power.
But pushback from Queensland and the Northern Territory at Wednesday's National Cabinet led Mr Albanese to provide some flexibility.
"In Queensland, you have public ownership of power generation, transmission, and distribution. So, if there is surplus, then that, of course, could be available," he told a news conference.
The COP is preceded by a "pre-COP" in Fiji in early October that includes a special leaders' event in Tuvalu, a tiny nation seriously threatened by rising sea levels that has been dubbed "a country without a future".
But hopes of attracting a good turnout of leaders were overoptimistic.
Even under this government, Australia remains on the defensive in the Pacific on climate issues — with countries always wanting their big neighbour to do more.
Mr Albanese flagged he will be at pre-COP when he told parliament recently the Thai prime minister would be there.
Given both Australia's hosting responsibilities and the government's concerted effort, for strategic reasons, to promote special relationships with Pacific countries, staying away would be a diplomatic misstep.
Michelle Grattan is a professorial fellow at the University of Canberra and chief political correspondent at The Conversation, where this article first appeared.

David vs Bunnings: Mitre 10 franchisee wins crucial legal costs case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:37:25 UTC
03:37:25 KST

Mitre 10 franchisee wins crucial legal costs case against hardware giant Bunnings
A Mitre 10 franchisee has won a crucial legal costs fight against Bunnings, allowing him to take on a high-stakes case to try to stop the hardware giant from opening up next door to his Queensland store.
David Woodman's story was detailed by the ABC's Four Corners program last year, with the family-owned retailer airing concerns about competition in the hardware sector.
Mr Woodman is trying to use the Competition and Consumer Act to stop Bunnings from opening a site in the town of Jimboomba, which he argues would put him out of business.
He had applied to the Federal Court to be protected from paying Bunnings' legal costs if he lost, under laws designed to help smaller businesses take on corporate titans.
Justice Robert Bronwich has now ruled in Mr Woodman's favour.
"I am delighted for the client," his lawyer Michael Daniel told the ABC.
Mr Daniel estimates Bunnings could easily spend $6 million fighting the case, a sum Mr Woodman could not risk paying.
"If we didn't get this order, the chances are that David wouldn't be able to pursue the case," Mr Daniel said.
"This decision improves that risk and increases access to justice."
What is a no adverse costs order?
Typically, when a civil action is brought, the entity lodging the case faces the prospect of paying the legal fees of the party they lodged against, known as an adverse costs order, if they end up losing.
The laws Mr Woodman used — known as a no adverse costs order (NACO) — were introduced for business owners in 2019.
Mr Daniel thinks today's ruling is the first time NACO has been granted for an anti-competitive conduct case.
"I was hoping we'd get the result, but I was apprehensive we'd get it," he said.
"The client had spent a lot of money just getting to this stage."
Bunnings, which is owned by the giant retail, mining and industrial conglomerate Wesfarmers, had already brought in a high-profile barrister, Garry Rich SC, to argue against the NACO application.
The barrister recently won a bombshell case against another high-profile retailer, Coles, on behalf of the competition regulator, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC).
Only today, Wesfarmers posted its annual results, showing a statutory net profit after tax of $2.87 billion, up 8.3 per cent from the previous year.
"Bunnings has the resources to fight at every point and do so with very expensive experts and lawyers," Mr Daniel argued.
"I expect them to keep going, quite frankly."
What does Bunnings say?
Mr Woodman's family has been in the hardware business for 90 years.
He bought the store in Jimboomba with his brother and father in 2018 under a franchise agreement with Metcash, the second-largest hardware retailer in Australia after Bunnings.
Bunnings purchased the vacant lot next door a year later, in 2019, and was later approved for a warehouse eight times larger than Mitre 10 Jimboomba.
Mr Woodman's case argues this will put him out of business, saying:
As a result of Bunnings's conduct, Woodman abandoned plans to expand the size and product range of Mitre 10 Jimboomba, because once Bunnings Warehouse opens at the Jimboomba site, it is commercially likely that Mitre 10 Jimboomba will become non-viable within the short to medium term and therefore would have to close.
Mr Woodman is seeking damages for losses and is ultimately seeking an injunction to stop Bunnings from opening its store.
There are already several Bunnings stores in the surrounding region. However, Bunnings argues the Jimboomba site is needed and will enhance choice and jobs for locals.
"We note the Court's decision on costs and will continue to respond to the proceedings through the appropriate legal process," the company said in a statement.
"We believe opening a Bunnings store in Jimboomba will bring more choice and competition to the local community, while providing local employment opportunities."
In an interview with ABC's The Business, Wesfarmers boss Rob Scott reiterated that "competition is great".
"It offers better choice and value for consumers," he said.
"So we will compete very competitively against all competitors, and ultimately customers are the ones that decide.
"Bunnings is still very interested in growing its network."
In his ruling, Justice Bronwich noted the still significant challenge ahead for Mr Woodman to win his case against Bunnings.
"The case brought by Woodman is novel, as it freely acknowledges," he noted.
"The discretion to make the NACO is appropriate in all the circumstances.
"That does not entail underestimating the challenges that Woodman faces in bringing this proceeding.
"But in my view, a case such as this is precisely what the NACO regime was intended to facilitate."
Mr Woodman's lawyer said he thinks the case could drag on for years.

The US has withdrawn its attacks on Canadian culture and its French language, leaving the door open to resume trade talks, Canada’s chief negotiator said on Thursday.
“Canada welcomes that the U.S. is now withdrawing its positions on discoverability and labelling and is confirming that measures to promote French language and Canadian culture will not be subject to future U.S. trade actions,” Dominic LeBlanc posted on X.
“We look forward to further constructive U.S. clarifications on their other positions which would create the possibility of a mutually beneficial trade deal that respects Canadian sovereignty.”
It appeared the two countries were close to a deal which would have staved off new 50% US tariffs on CAN$27 billion (US$29.5 billion), but Canada balked last Friday and Prime Minister Mark Carney abruptly ordered a pullout of trade talks after the US made a few last-minute demands that Canada considered an attack on its sovereignty.
The US enacted the tariff on about 700 items and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney countered with a promised dollar-for-dollar trade tariff on US imports to take effect Sept. 8.
But while LeBlanc hinted that negotiations could be rekindled, his American counterpart Jamieson Greer said there were no current “open channels’ between the two nations.
Canada has said its targets for tariffs is fluid, depending on advice from Canadian businesses. For example, it changed the proposed tariff on seafood.
“Based on feedback, we have made select adjustments to protect against broader economic harms,” Finance Canada said in a social media post, including removing seafood and fish products from our list of counter tariffs, while maintaining dollar for dollar and rate for rate responses to U.S. products.

Finland Prepares Major Air Defense Support for Ukraine Ahead of Winter Russian Attacks
Finland is preparing to significantly strengthen Ukraine’s air defense capabilities as Kyiv braces for another winter of Russian attacks, Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in an interview with We—Ukraine on August 26.
Speaking to Ukrainian media, Stubb said protecting Ukraine’s airspace should remain a key priority for Kyiv’s international partners, particularly as Russia continues to threaten the country’s energy infrastructure.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Finnish president said he had already discussed additional air defense support with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Nationals' deputy Chester says Joyce departure 'sad for him, sad for party'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Nationals' deputy Darren Chester on Barnaby Joyce and the rise of One Nation
Darren Chester has spent 18 years in parliament as the National Party's member for Gippsland in Victoria.
In that time, he has served as a minister under both the Turnbull and Morrison Coalition governments, twice watched bushfires sweep through his electorate, collapsed in parliament due to fatigue and at one point even took a break from his own party.
Today he's the National's deputy leader, facing a looming threat from Pauline Hanson's One Nation, although it doesn't appear to be something the MP is too concerned about.
"In terms of my own future and in terms of One Nation, I don't even worry about what they're doing in Gippsland," he told Annabel Crabb on ABC iview's Kitchen Cabinet.
'Sad for our party'
But it's difficult to avoid the elephant in the room. Barnaby Joyce, a former leader of the Nationals, has left the party to join One Nation.
Mr Chester doesn't believe the New England MP's actions have made it harder for voters to distinguish the Nationals from One Nation and said there's no suggestion other National Party members would follow Mr Joyce.
"That's a decision he made for reasons that he has never fully explained, really,"
Mr Chester called the move "self-indulgent" and said it was sad that Mr Joyce had undermined his own legacy.
"The idea that a leader — someone who had been the deputy prime minister — would leave the party and join another party just because they didn't get the job they wanted in opposition is quite extraordinary."
The job in question was a position in the shadow ministry, according to Mr Chester.
At the time of his decision to leave the Nationals, Mr Joyce said his relationship with the leadership of the party "had broken down" and he had been relegated to the "ejection" seat on the backbench.
In a recent episode of Australian Story, speaking on Mr Joyce's move from the Nationals, his wife Vikki Campion asked: "How long do you have to be loyal to a party that mistreats you?"
Mr Chester said Mr Joyce's defection is not only "sad for our party" but also "sad for him".
"Our party had made him the Member of Parliament that he was; given him those opportunities," he said.
'Loose coalition of independents'
According to Mr Chester, the National Party is like a "a loose coalition of independents" who are "very independently minded" and "hard to lead".
"People in the [party] room expect to be treated as equals and get to have their say on behalf of their community," he said.
"There are issues which reflect the differences in the people we represent, and we are specialists in rural and regional Australia.
"They're the only seats we contest so there will be issues that impact rural and regional Australia disproportionately, and quite rightly, the Nats will have a stronger view than any other party with [those] issues."
Mr Chester said communicating the concerns of regional Australia — particularly those in industry — was becoming increasingly difficult.
"A lot of people in metropolitan areas now don't have a point of reference to a regional community,"
"They don't have a cousin who lives on a farm, they don't visit a farm, so they don't understand how farms work.
"The lack of understanding is a real problem for us."
Getting climate policy wrong
There has been a shift in climate policy within the Coalition since the early days of Net Zero, when the Morrison Coalition government pledged net zero greenhouse emissions by 2050.
Mr Chester initially supported Net Zero but has since changed his position, aligning himself with National Party leader Matt Canavan, who has long been one of its loudest critics.
He said his initial support for Net Zero was due to his belief at the time that Australia's trading position would otherwise be jeopardised.
"A lot has changed since that time and I have no hesitation in saying that Matt was right and I got it wrong," he said.
Mr Chester says he and Senator Canavan are working "really well" together.
Mr Chester is now arguing for nuclear power in Australia, advocating for a power station to be located in the place of the coal-fired power stations currently in Gippsland's Latrobe Valley.
He said it would come with enormous benefits, including the ability to link into existing transmission corridors while avoiding farmland.
Latrobe Valley residents are divided at the prospect of a nuclear power station in the region. Some cite safety and waste disposal as an issue, but others argue it would provide a boost to the local economy.
Despite his backflip on Net Zero, Mr Chester said he is not anti-renewables and believes it's about finding the "right energy solution for our country".
"We're going to have nuclear-powered submarines. We've had a reactor at Lucas Heights for 60-odd years. And we've got a moratorium in place based on some … Simpsons' episode about three-eyed fish?
"If your point of reference is a Simpsons' episode, you've kind of lost your credibility in [the] broader energy debate," he said, referring to the time Labor MPs shared a meme mocking the Coalition's nuclear plan.
'Waking up in the middle of the night'
Mr Chester's electorate has seen challenging times over his term in parliament, perhaps one of the toughest being the bushfires of Black Summer.
By February 2020, the bushfires had been burning for several months, incinerating millions of hectares along the east coast, including in Gippsland.
Mr Chester said this was partly behind his widely reported collapse in parliament at the time.
"It was during the Black Summer bushfires. You had 30-odd days in a row doing the recovery work. I was fatigued — I know that now," he said.
At the same time, there were rumblings taking place in the party's backrooms.
"Barnaby [Joyce] was hunting [then National Party leader and deputy prime minister Michael] McCormack relentlessly. I was waking up in the middle of the night, your mind was just staying active."
Mr Chester said he was "frustrated" by Mr Joyce's actions.
"There was a natural disaster of quite epic proportions, [and] we were again being distracted by a leadership conversation, which we should not have been having."
"I wasn't aware I wasn't getting enough rest until my body just basically shut down for a few seconds and gave me a wake-up call."

Most movies take months to film. This Australian director did it in six days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

One email to Sharknado royalty landed director his first feature film
A single email was all it took for Anthony Frith to secure his first feature film with The Asylum, the infamous B-movie studio responsible for unleashing Sharknado and hundreds of other 'mockbusters' upon the world.
The aspiring Adelaide filmmaker had just welcomed his first child, and his CV mostly consisted of comedic skits he posted to YouTube which went nowhere and cutting commercial videos for his parents' business.
So Frith reached out to the high-ups at The Asylum.
One email exchange and a Zoom call later and Frith found himself appointed director of the new Asylum movie and the first to be filmed in Australia: The Land That Time Forgot.
He was also bestowed with the fodder for his own film — Mockbuster — which documents the process.
It was a dream come true.
But after travelling to The Asylum's LA headquarters, the stars in Frith's eyes were quickly knocked out when he was informed that there was almost no budget, a mere outline of a story and that it would all have to be shot in Australia in six days.
Frith always had a soft spot for B-movies; not the kind you would rush to the cinema to catch but the ones on streaming services with bad acting, terrible stories and even worse effects.
"What I kind of like about bad movies is that sort of earnest naivety that goes into making them," Frith tells ABC News.
"I think people discredit bad movies and specifically Asylum films as shameless cash grabs, which to a point they are, but they are made by people who are passionate who put their time and effort into making them.
"There's something kind of special about that."
What is The Asylum?
The Asylum is far from the first studio to pump out mockbusters — low-budget, low-quality spins on already popular movies or stories in the public domain. The genre has roots in everything from 70s Blaxploitation classics to CGI animations that can almost pass for Pixar (if you really squint).
But The Asylum turned the subgenre into an art form of its own. Originally founded in the late 90s by David Michael Latt, David Rimawi and Sherri Strain as a basic distribution company, the trio quickly realised they couldn't compete with the big studios.
So they pivoted to a different business model: pump out as many movies as they could, for as little money as possible, in order to always make profit or at least break even.
But Frith wasn't prepared for just how committed they were to their short filming windows, which they lovingly dub 'the six-day special'.
"I thought it was 10 or 12 days because that's what I read on Wikipedia," Frith laughs.
"What actually happened was during COVID in LA, you had to test on the first day of shooting and the seventh day of shooting. So they thought if they shot in six days, they wouldn't have to pay for the second test. So they just ran with it, and never stopped."
Despite everyone at The Asylum having full faith in Frith, he landed in Australia with a massive task: find a local cast and crew who would work for less, scout dozens of locations and then hope a script comes together in time for a six-day shoot.
"It was a stressful, crazy time. There were moments where I was like, 'This is the stupidest thing I've ever done in my life. Why do I do this to myself?'" Frith says.
"But then I was also contractually obligated to deliver the movie AND the documentary. I'm glad I did it in retrospect, like, you know, hindsight's 20-20."
Dinos everywhere
It's nailbiting to watch Frith stumble through costuming mishaps, arguments between the cast and crew and a missing producer (The Asylum sends a can-do LA implant over at the last second), but it's just as exciting to see Frith move mountains to pull the whole thing off.
Frith is in awe of the work and dedication his cast and crew pulled out.
"We never had overtime. We had to move scenes to the following days and stuff but we never went over time, which was insane to me," he says.
"One of my favourite scenes in The Land That Time Forgot, one where we have someone tied up on the tree. It's got tension and it kind of works. We shot that in like 15 minutes because the light was fading," he says.
"It's like those moments where everything kind of coalesces in a nice way and just works. Everyone might think I'm an idiot once they see it but that's okay. I'm proud of it."
And while they might have been a few million dollars shy of a regular feature, there was still enough in the budget for a small wrap party.
"We had like a carton of beer in the Surf Lifesavers club after. I think one of the actors, Dave Margetts, bought some doughnuts to share with everyone. It was nice," Frith says.
Once the Australian crew had wrapped, all that was left to do was send the film back to The Asylum for their trademark special effects, in this case ravaging dinosaurs.
The Land That Time Forgot has the bittersweet honour of being one of the last films under supervision of legendary special effects artist Glenn Campbell, who died in late 2024.
"He worked on the original Tron, the original Star Trek motion picture, all these incredible films that he kind of pioneered a lot of those sort of things that they still use today," Frith says.
"There's still super talented people there, but he left a big hole to fill. So, then they started just using generative AI because it was like it could keep up with Glenn's speed and talents."
While Frith understands the rationale, especially after seeing how The Asylum business operates, he still feels something will be lost for future mockbuster lovers.
"I think what's fun about bad movies is the human touch. The imperfections come from a person and they're unique to that person and that film," he says.
"Whereas if you're using generative AI, it all inevitably feels the same or looks the same aesthetically."
Send the email
A year after The Land That Time Forgot's premiere and as Mockbuster hits Australian cinemas, Frith still can't believe what he experienced.
"I've got copies of my movie on DVD in my lounge room, which is crazy to me that I've made something that's being sold on DVD. It's such a dream. It's something you dream about when you're a teen, and you're wanting to be a filmmaker," Frith says.
And while The Asylum has been knocking on his door to direct another mockbuster, Frith has some other dreams that need tending to.
"I kind of fell into documentary a bit, and fell in love with it. You can just like meet real people who are funny, doing interesting things, I really love that," he says.
But the director would 100 per cent push any prospective filmmaker to send their own email to The Asylum.
"Say what you want about The Asylum, I think the fact that they give someone a shot to make a film is really important. It's something that's dying and inaccessible," he says.
"The fact that you even get to make a film is kind of important in itself, because you learn so much. Sure, not a lot of people might watch it, but you can say you've directed this feature film.
"That's all that matters."

North American aliyah hits record month as over 1,100 olim arrive, with 4,000 expected in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
18:29:54 UTC
03:29:54 KST

More than 1,100 North Americans have immigrated to Israel this month through Nefesh B’Nefesh, marking a new monthly aliyah (immigration to Israel) record for the organization, Nefesh B’Nefesh said on Thursday.
“It’s record-breaking for us,” Nefesh B’Nefesh’s Vice President of Diaspora Partnerships Marc Rosenberg told The Jerusalem Post at Ben-Gurion Airport that day, as some 150 more North American olim (immigrants) arrived in the country.
“It’s quite a summer,” he said. “Over 2,300 people are arriving. It’s really been a very busy summer.”
Founded in 2002, Nefesh B’Nefesh facilitates aliyah from North America in partnership with Israel’s Aliyah and Integration Ministry, the Jewish Agency for Israel, Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael and Jewish National Fund-USA. The organization recently marked the arrival of its 100,000th oleh.
According to Nefesh B’Nefesh, more than 2,200 North Americans are expected to make aliyah over the summer, including olim arriving on nearly 100 group flights or completing the process from within Israel.
Approximately 2,700 North Americans have made aliyah since the beginning of 2026, and the organization estimates that more than 4,000 will do so by the end of the year, making 2026 one of its strongest years.
Among the new olim were seven families from the Persian Jewish community of Great Neck, New York, who arrived at Ben-Gurion Airport earlier this month.
Rosenberg said one factor driving the wave of aliyah was parents’ desire to raise their children in Israel.
“They want to be a part of the project that built Israel,” he said. “They see a big quality of life here, and they admire what young people in Israel are doing. And they’re saying they want to be a part of it.”
Aliyah on the rise
Nefesh B’Nefesh has seen “a significant increase in interest in aliyah,” Rosenberg said, with numbers rising between three and five percent annually in recent years.
Among them are a growing number of singles under 30, many of whom are required to serve in the military. Others are set to study at Israeli universities. Families making aliyah are also getting younger.
“The average age of families last year, two years ago, used to be around 32. It’s 29 this summer,” Rosenberg said. “So we see some younger families that are coming.”
Nefesh B’Nefesh said this summer’s olim include approximately 1,100 singles, 480 families and 250 retirees, ranging in age from five months to 98 years old.
Some 700 school-aged children also made aliyah this summer, including 80 who will begin first grade next month.
“As we recently celebrated our 100,000th Oleh, it is particularly inspiring to see so many young people choosing to make Israel their home, to build their careers and families here, put down roots and invest their futures in this country,” Nefesh B’Nefesh co-founder and executive director Rabbi Yehoshua Fass said.
One of those arriving Thursday was Marlene, who landed with her husband, Michael, and their baby.
Marlene told the Post that, for her, the timing was right.
“We got married last year, so it’s something that I’ve been trying to make happen,” she said, adding that Michael, who had made aliyah a few years earlier, “just made it easy for me.”
“This is always where I wanted to be, wanted to raise my children, have my future,” she said.
Marlene, from Brooklyn’s Syrian Jewish community, said she was the last of eight families from the community who had made aliyah over the past week, and that the trend appeared to be spreading.
“The trend started years and years ago. It was one family, then another family, and then over the years, more and more families were getting it into their heads,” she said. “This summer was a really big deal that eight of us made it happen at the same time. And I think there’s already a group in talks to do it next summer.”
Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer: 'Inspiring' to see young people choose Israel
Aliyah and Integration Minister Ofir Sofer said it was “inspiring to see so many young people and families choosing to build their futures in Israel,” adding that government programs were intended to help new olim integrate into Israeli communities and the workforce.
Jewish Agency chairman Maj.-Gen. (res.) Doron Almog similarly described the month’s 1,100 olim as families and young people who had chosen “to build their lives here and be part of the future of the State of Israel.”
Chava, from Richmond, Virginia, also said it was “the time” to make aliyah and that the move was what was “best for our family.”
“Our kids are the right age, and also I’m approaching middle age, and it just seems like the right time,” she said. “Just everything lined up.”
“We were kind of done with the US and all of the craziness that’s happening there. But at the same time, we were just drawn to the Holy Land. We need to live as our authentic Jewish selves.”
Another new oleh, Gedalia, who has worked in the rabbinate in the US for several years, said he had wanted to move for a long time and was now joining several of his children who already live in Israel.
“Another rav came and listened to a shiur (lesson) of mine, and he told me it was the best shiur he had heard,” Gedalia, who was making aliyah from Silver Spring, Maryland, recalled.
“He was going all up and down the East Coast, and he said it was fantastic. And I said, ‘I need to go somewhere people will really appreciate this skill.’”
Rivka and Rella, a mother and daughter from New York whose family also made aliyah on Thursday, voiced their elation at becoming Israelis.
“We love it here, and this is where we feel like we’re home,” Rivka told the Post.
“Why wait?” Rella asked. “You know, we could have done it two years from now, but take the risk! Do it!”
Jerusalem, Tel Aviv-Yafo, Modi’in, Ra’anana and Beit Shemesh are among the most popular destinations for this summer’s North American olim, according to Nefesh B’Nefesh. Some 650, however, are moving to communities in Israel’s North and South, bolstering peripheral communities.

Labor Day 2026 Deals Got Me a Complete Starter Tool Kit for Under $375

03:25:30 KST

Most people know that Labor Day is one of the best times of the year to buy tools (get it? Labor?), but if you’re a newly minted homeowner or DIY-er, the landscape can be intimidating. When I bought my first home, I owned only two screwdrivers, a pair of pliers, and a hammer; I had no clue what I was in for.
Now that I’ve been a homeowner for 17 years, I agree with WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson that unless you’re a professional tradesperson or really love large projects, you don’t need a garage full of specialty tools. Just the basics will do: a drill, a saw, a set of manual screwdrivers, and a stud finder, for example.
Luckily, early Labor Day deals are pretty decent this year. In fact, after examining all the major sales, I was able to find a rather encyclopedic house-repair kit for any new homeowner or DIY-er for under $375 (minus tax and shipping) with deals from Home Depot, Lowe’s, and Walmart. Any of these would also be great to stash away for a holiday gift.
Here’s what I chose:
Power-Tool Workhorses: Ryobi 4-Tool Kit for $199
Look, you’re not going to take Ryobi tools to a jobsite or use them to build a house from scratch (a former WIRED editor once deemed them “the Kia of tools”), but if you’re just using them for basic, casual home use, they’ll do the job. Ryobi’s 18V ONE+ batteries (this set comes with one) are fully backward compatible with all Ryobi tools ever made, and this set has a three-year warranty. I live in a DeWalt household, so I don’t have a lot of firsthand experience with Ryobi, but my brother, a contractor, says the brand is great for the average DIY homeowner and offers a much broader range of tools than competitor Bauer from Harbor Freight.
This set packs a ½-inch drill/driver, an impact driver (which WIRED reviewer Scott Gilbertson said had a profound 'I can't believe I didn't own one sooner' impact on him, though his is Milwaukee), a circular saw, and an LED light. The impact driver packs 1,800 pounds of torque, which is pretty decent for a consumer-level tool. If you need a sander, there's also another kit with a sander plus drill/driver and circular saw, which may be worth a look if this set sells out.
The Hand-Tool Essentials: Workpro 408-Piece Set for $144
I don't have this exact set, but I do have remnants of a similar one. Again, you're not going to bring these to a construction site, but this kit is a knockout deal for everything you get—pliers, screwdrivers, Allen keys, wrenches, sockets, bits, tape measure, knife, hammer, wire stripper … there's even a metal box in which to store everything. A lot of the “pieces” are doodads like screwdriver heads and drywall anchors, but it still contains pretty much any non-power tool you might need for light home repairs and even basic car maintenance. (There's no level, but you can always use an app on your phone for that.) However, note that this is a flash deal, so it's likely only live for a limited time.
Wall-Hanging Must-Have: Franklin Sensors Stud Finder for $22
No household repair kit is complete without a stud finder. (And if you're a dad, it will give you years of built-in dad jokes.) In fact, you can't—or, at least, shouldn't—hang anything even slightly heavy on your wall without one. I have a Franklin Sensors stud finder, though not this exact model, and it's done well to help my family hang pictures, shelves, mirrors, and pretty much everything else for the past decade or so. This is the best deal I could find, though it's not technically on sale. However, Lowe’s is having a sale on plenty of other tools, including outdoor furniture, appliances, and grills.
