Russia Secretly Debuted Its New Iskander-1000 in a Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:51:10 UTC
01:51:10 KST

- Category
- Defense Tech
Russia Secretly Debuted Its New Iskander-1000 in a Ballistic Missile Strike on Kyiv
Russia used its newest 9M723-2 ballistic missile, commonly referred to as the Iskander-1000, against Kyiv for the first time during a combined attack on the Ukrainian capital this summer, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said on August 27.
The upgraded missile offers Russia substantially greater reach than the earlier 9M723-1 used by the Iskander-M system, according to Ukrainian intelligence.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Its most significant changes are a larger rocket motor and a correspondingly enlarged launcher. HUR says those modifications increase the missile’s maximum strike range to around 550 kilometers, compared with approximately 390 kilometers for the 9M723-1 variant.
Despite the provisional Iskander-1000 designation, Ukrainian intelligence has not said that the version already used against Kyiv can actually fly 1,000 kilometers.
The 9M723-2 is part of a missile system designated Bora-M. Aside from its enlarged propulsion section and launcher, HUR said the remaining components of the new missile are largely identical to those used in the earlier 9M723-1.
The first confirmed combat use marks a significant development in Russia’s continuing effort to expand and modernize its ballistic missile arsenal, weapons that have become one of the most difficult threats for Ukraine’s air defenses to counter.
Defense Express reported as early as 2024 that Russia was exploring ways to increase the range of the 9M723. The original missile was developed while the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty imposed restrictions on ground-launched missiles with ranges above 500 kilometers.
Russian discussions at the time suggested that advances in solid-fuel technology and the installation of a new rocket motor could theoretically push an upgraded Iskander ballistic missile toward a range of 1,000 kilometers.
Another option reportedly considered by Russian developers involved using the additional propulsion capability not for range, but for a much heavier warhead.
Earlier concepts discussed increasing the warhead carried by Iskander and Kinzhal missiles from roughly 480 kilograms to as much as 800 kilograms, trading some potential range for significantly greater destructive power.
The missile Russia has now actually fielded appears more conservative than those earlier ambitions. HUR’s assessment of a 550-kilometer range still represents a substantial increase, but falls well short of the 1,000 kilometers implied by its unofficial name.
Even that additional reach, however, could allow Russian launch crews to operate farther from Ukraine while continuing to threaten Kyiv and other major cities.
Russia also retains a substantial ballistic missile inventory. As of August 5, Moscow had approximately 130 9M723 missiles for the Iskander-M system allocated to the forces involved in its war against Ukraine.
Separate estimates in July put Russia’s stockpile at roughly 50 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles, alongside around 50 North Korean KN-23, KN-24 and KN-30 ballistic missiles.
Previously, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Iskander ballistic missile launcher near the border in a rare and potentially significant operation aimed at destroying Moscow’s missile systems before they can fire.

Four EU countries seek to reopen debate on Russian frozen assets for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Four EU countries seek to reopen debate on Russian frozen assets for Ukraine
BRUSSELS, Aug 27 - The Netherlands, Poland, Spain and Sweden called on Thursday for the European Union to reopen discussion next week on using Russia's frozen assets for Ukraine as Moscow shows no signs of wanting to end its war there.
In a letter seen by Reuters, foreign ministers of the four countries argue that, while the EU agreed last December on a 90 billion euro ($104.86 billion) loan for Kyiv for 2026 and 2027, this will not be enough.
"Ukraine needs more financial support in both the short and long term," said the letter, addressed to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Helen McEntee, the foreign minister of Ireland, which holds the EU's rotating presidency.
"We believe now is the time to revert to the issue of how we can make further use of Russia’s immobilised assets for the benefit of Ukraine," the ministers wrote. They want the issue to be discussed at the next EU foreign ministers meeting on Sept 1-2 in Ireland.
European Union countries immobilised some 210 billion euros of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine in February 2022. Around 185 billion euros of this is held in Brussels-based central securities depository Euroclear.
The European Commission proposed last year to use the Russian cash for a loan of up to 165 billion euros to Ukraine, repayable only after Russia pays war reparations to Kyiv.
But Belgium rejected the plan, saying it did not provide sufficient guarantees that it would not be left alone to deal with potential lawsuits and demands of damages from Russia.
The plan to use the frozen assets was therefore dropped and replaced by the 90 billion euro loan, backed by the EU budget.
CHANCE OF AGREEMENT UNCLEAR
Officials said it was unclear if renewed talks would succeed since Belgium has not changed its position.
"We ... propose that the Commission's technical experts are invited to explore, in close consultation with Member States, new options on how to use the immobilised assets for the benefit of Ukraine," the letter said.
Officials said some new momentum could come from ongoing negotiations over the next EU long-term budget for 2028-2034, which will have to include money for Ukraine.
The more money available from other sources, the less EU taxpayers will have to provide, officials said. Others noted the money would be better used to fend off Moscow than to rebuild after it lays waste to Ukraine.
"Russia will not get this money back until it pays reparations to Ukraine, so it is better to use it to stop the aggression — that is, to defend Ukraine — rather than wait until the end of Russia’s aggression to spend it on reconstruction," Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said. REUTERS

quail green and rose gold frame the obsessive details of spyker’s C8 preliator XXV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

16:44:14 UTC
01:44:14 KST

At The Quail during Monterey Car Week, a metallic green Spyker sat with its butterfly doors raised while Victor Muller stood in front of it, mic in hand. designboom was there as the founder and CEO introduced the C8 Preliator XXV, a car he framed around the physical connection between driver and machine.
‘There is nothing between you and the gearbox,‘ Muller said during the unveiling, adding, ‘there is just your hands and the mechanics.‘ The comment suited a coupe whose exposed shift linkage is one of the first things you see through the open cabin.
The Preliator name has been around for a decade, first appearing on a C8 concept Spyker presented in 2016. A Spyder followed in 2017, and the earlier program fell far short of the production run Spyker initially envisioned. The XXV brings the name back on what Spyker describes as a new car, built around an in-house aluminum spaceframe with every exterior panel reshaped by Coventry Prototype Panels in England. Only 25 examples are planned.
Behind the cabin lurks an Audi-sourced 4.0-liter twin-turbo V8 producing 800 hp and 1,000 Nm of torque, sending power to the rear wheels through a six-speed manual supplied by Graziano Oerlikon. Spyker gives the XXV a 0–100 km/h time of 2.7 seconds and a top speed above 217 mph. The exposed linkage makes the transmission part of the interior architecture, something Muller emphasized during the unveiling. He says: ‘You decide when to shift, and you feel every gear change in your hand.‘
The gear lever rises through a rose-gold bezel, and the dashboard pairs turned aluminum with analog gauges. Physical switches handle the cabin controls, while a head-up display serves as the sole screen. Spyker says one craftsman spends four hours stitching each steering wheel with two needles. Even the screw heads inside the cabin are aligned by hand to face the same direction. The details can verge on obsessive, which has long been part of the appeal of a Spyker interior.
the hand-formed aluminum body sits on a newly engineered in-house spaceframe
spyker turns aircraft references into bodywork
A fin runs from the roof toward the rear deck, picking up a form seen on Spyker’s 1919 C1 Aerocoque and making the company’s aviation history unusually literal. NACA intakes feed air toward the engine. The headlights draw the XXV name into their light signature, while the rear lamps take their shape from jet afterburners. An isogrid pattern borrowed from aerospace structures appears in the grilles and returns inside through the seat upholstery.
Coventry Prototype Panels forms the exterior in aluminum, continuing a material choice that separates the XXV from the carbon-heavy construction common across contemporary supercars. Muller describes the aluminum: ‘it’s a living metal that can be shaped by the hand of an experienced craftsman.‘ Spyker estimates roughly 2,100 hours of work for each car. With just the push of a button, its butterfly mode opens the bodywork and exposes an engine bay finished to be seen.
rose-gold brightwork traces the quail green bodywork
25 cars begin spyker’s latest comeback
Spyker says each of the twenty-five cars will be individually commissioned. Its ‘Quail Green’ paint contains rose-gold flakes, and matching brightwork traces the body. Inside, Spyker uses orange-brown Tuscan Saddle leather.
The car arrives after another long interruption for the Dutch marque: Muller regained rights to the Spyker name and intellectual property in 2025, and new co-owner Volodymyr Nosov is backing the latest phase through fintech group W Group.

On June 12, the US Department of Commerce informed Anthropic that it had to secure an export license for any foreign person, inside or outside the US, to access its two most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) models. This left the firm with no choice but to disable Fable 5 and Mythos 5 for everyone, with no warning.
While the US lifted the order on June 30, apparently satisfied that Anthropic had addressed the security risk, European businesses, governments and researchers had by then spent 18 days using older models, with no knowledge of when they might regain access.
As Europe processed the realization that its access to frontier AI could be revoked at any moment, another development sent a very different message. The Chinese lab Moonshot AI released Kimi K3 — a 2.8-trillion-parameter model whose weights are now free to download — pointing to the possibility that near-frontier capability might soon cost almost nothing.
Illustration: Mountain People
Given the impossibility of knowing which of these conflicting signals would prove prophetic, European policymakers must build an AI strategy suitable for both scenarios.
Discussions of Europe’s AI strategy largely rest on the premise that policymakers must choose one possibility and go all in.
Some want to bet on the Chinese signal: AI capabilities would plateau, the distance between the frontier models and their pursuers would narrow, and AI would become a commodity that can be purchased cheaply, much like electricity. This camp advocates a kind of hopeful resignation: accept that Europe lacks the compute, the capital and the talent to win the AI race, but do not worry too much about it, because attempting to reach the AI frontier now would be a waste of money.
On the other side are those who want Europe to sprint for that frontier, with a publicly funded initiative that would dwarf any European industrial program since postwar reconstruction. This camp is betting that AI capabilities would keep compounding, and the gap between frontier models and the rest would continue to widen. In this scenario, resignation is tantamount to economic suicide.
Each position is coherent within the context of its assumed future, but nobody can predict what would actually happen, and neither side has a plan if the future is “wrong.”
Decision theory holds that when two radically different scenarios are plausible, and you cannot reliably assign probabilities to them, the rational move is to choose the course of action that avoids catastrophe in either case — to make a partial investment and buy an option, rather than make an irreversible commitment.
For Europe today, an effective AI strategy would recognize that the components of AI sovereignty run on different timelines. Chips can be acquired in 18 months once capital is secured. Decarbonized power, data centers, model-training expertise and decisionmaking institutions take five to 10 years to build. Frontloading spending on compute amounts to locking in the biggest bet precisely where uncertainty is greatest. A better approach would begin with what takes longest. The resulting assets would have value in whichever future materializes.
To be sure, the risks raised by dependency are real. Frontier AI runs on rationed compute. US labs serve US government contracts first, enterprise customers second and the rest of the world last. When capacity comes under strain, foreign users would be the first to lose access, and geopolitically motivated access restrictions are another risk.
A Europe without domestic inference capacity or ability to train large models is a Europe without a fallback plan.
However, if the risk is losing access to frontier models, the solution is not necessarily to try to surpass the labs that created them. Instead, it is to build the capacity to make surviving that loss possible.
This means securing power and grid-connected land; erecting data centers on European soil, operated by European firms; and building training capabilities, with multiyear procurement contracts ensuring that local expertise keeps pace with technological progress.
None of this requires the budgetary moonshot that some advocate. On the contrary, the combined cost would run to a few billion euros per year, and it could be financed largely by private capital against productive assets, rather than by public commitments based on an uncertain technological premise.
If model performance levels off and AI is commoditized, this foundation would enable Europe to compete on diffusion and integration — arenas where its enterprise-software firms hold genuine advantages. If capabilities keep compounding and access is constrained, Europe would be well-positioned to launch a sprint for the frontier, at far lower cost than if it had to start from scratch, and on a timeline Europe controls.
For a continent that largely stood on the sidelines while Silicon Valley built the digital economy, the inclination to take bold and fast action this time around is understandable, but sequence matters more than scale.
The French nuclear deterrent, often invoked by proponents of an AI sprint, did not begin with a warhead; it took 15 years and proceeded in stages. The same logic applies to AI.
Building an industrial foundation that forecloses nothing, does not break the bank and requires no permission from the US is not a timid approach.
On the contrary, it is the only strategy that does not depend on anticipating the trajectory of a technology whose very creators admit they cannot predict.
Eric Hazan is founding partner of Ardabelle Capital, a co-founder of Plateforme Progressiste and a lecturer at HEC Paris and Sciences Po. Lenny Benbara and Baptiste Lefort are founders of the Global Trade Policy Observatory.

These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that

Epic La Tomatina paints Spanish town red
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:45 UTC
01:43:45 KST

Thousands of revelers — including many lured by a Bollywood film — descended on a small Spanish town on Wednesday for the annual La Tomatina food fight, where they painted Bunol red with tons of overripe tomatoes.
Loaded trucks plodded through the crowd with people in their cargo beds throwing tomatoes at the revelers — who, in turn, hurled them at one another. Their white shirts soon turned pink and red while pop songs blasted from speakers.
At one point, police used pepper spray to disperse an area of the crowd, but a festive vibe quickly resumed.
Photo: AP
The messy melee took place for more than an hour in the town, where buildings were covered with tarps ahead of the festivities.
Held on the last Wednesday of August, the festival traces its origins to a food fight in 1945. La Tomatina became an annual tradition before Spanish dictator general Francisco Franco banned it in the 1950s. Televised media attention in the 1980s helped turn the festival into a national event and, eventually, an international attraction.
More than 20,000 people had been expected to take part this year. The Spanish news agency EFE reported that about 40 percent of participants over the past three years have been tourists from outside Spain.
Photo: EPA
There has been a notable jump in visitors from India in recent years, following the 2011 Bollywood movie Zindagi Na Milegi Dobara (You Only Live Once), in which three friends take a road trip through Spain during an extended bachelor party. The film recreated La Tomatina, introducing the festival to many Indians.
The movie is what first drew Romail Khokhar, a 27-year-old from Mumbai, to Bunol. He was there on Wednesday morning, eager to participate in the food fight for his third time.
Mazhar and Sanya Khan, both 40, were likewise inspired by the film.
“It was fantastic, absolutely well-managed,” Mazhar Khan said. “We are from India, and this is our first time being in La Tomatina. It has been a dream for over a decade.”
The movie’s appeal is not limited to Indians. It also drew Joanna Wytrzyszczewska from Poland.
“Way more crazy than we expected,” Wytrzyszczewska, 32, said. “We came because we were inspired by a movie. It was better than the movie.”
Similar tomato-flinging events have taken place in Florida, London, Amsterdam, the Colombian town of Sutamarchan and Hyderabad, India.
Nonlocal attendees pay 15 euros (US$17.47) for a ticket. The first and only rule: Squash your tomatoes before hurling them to avoid injuries. Still, many participants don swimming goggles and earplugs for protection.
Once the hour was up, the sound of a cannon blast marked the end of festivities and crowds washed off at communal showers nearby. The town’s streets were later hosed down.
Although stains on clothes can be permanent, the tomatoes’ citric acid acts as a cleaning agent, often leaving Bunol’s streets cleaner than before.

Taiwan has prepared its national search-and-rescue team to travel to Nepal, officials said yesterday, a day after a catastrophic and deadly torrent of water and mud several stories high swept through communities along the Nepal-China border following a glacier collapse.
The government on Wednesday ordered the national special search-and-rescue team and rotating units from Tainan, Hsinchu City and Chiayi County to prepare for departure, National Fire Agency Director-General Hsiao Huang-chang (蕭煥章) said.
Although Taiwan has yet to receive a request for help, the national special rescue-and-research team would respond swiftly, in coordination with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, to requests for rescue operations from affected countries, he told a news conference following the weekly Cabinet meeting.
Photo: AP
At least 359 people were killed, local media reported, and more than 1,300 are missing, including scores of foreigners and pilgrims. Hundreds others have been displaced across the Himalayan region.
The Mainland Affairs Council late on Wednesday said it was seeking information on the safety of 51 Taiwanese nationals registered as being in Tibet.
It asked the Straits Exchange Foundation to use available “channels” to check on the safety of Taiwanese in the affected area, without specifying what those channels were.
Photo: USGS / Landsat 9 / Reuters
Images showed what appeared to be the second floors of buildings in Nepal’s hard-hit Nuwakot District slathered in mud after the torrent rushed by. Debris hung from tree branches and wires, vehicles were buried and some stunned survivors were caked in mud.
Nepalese Minister of Home Affairs Sudhan Gurung said the focus remained on finding survivors as rescue teams located 100 missing Indian visitors, mostly pilgrims, and 25 Chinese workers in the worst-hit region around Trishuli.
More than 650 foreigners were still unaccounted for while Nepalese authorities were yet to determine the number of locals missing.
The Red Cross said that entire villages had been destroyed and impassable roads and bridges had left communities cut off, adding that the full scale of the disaster remains unclear.
“It was a huge gush of mud coming straight towards us,” said Keshav Prasad Baral, a 68-year-old survivor being treated in a Nepalese hospital.
“As it got closer, it kept rising higher and higher. When I saw it enter our home, I tried to grab my wife’s hand and take her to the terrace, but she was swept away by the mud.”
A helicopter ferried him to safety four hours later.
“My wife is still somewhere beneath the mud,” he added. “She’s gone.”
The tally of missing in Tibet’s Gyirong County was 558, the state-run China Central Television said, including 260 foreign nationals.
China said the death toll stayed at three.
The missing foreigners in Nepal belonged to more than two dozen countries, including 288 from India, 63 from the US, 51 from Malaysia, 34 from Australia, 33 from the UK and 25 from Canada.
Early reports from Nepalese officials suggested an earthquake in the area could have caused the lower part of a glacier to collapse and trigger the floods.
The US Geological Survey said an earthquake with magnitude initially reported as 4.4 was in fact seismic energy generated by the collapse of glacial rock and ice, followed by debris flow.
Chinese authorities have identified risks from a still-dammed lake in Gyirong, upstream from the mudslide and flood-stricken Tibet-Nepal border crossing that could complicate rescue efforts, particularly as rains are forecast, China Central Television said.
Yesterday morning, the dammed lake was estimated at 2 million cubic meters in volume and was already overflowing, state media said citing the Chinese water resources ministry.

Film review: A tender love story with postapocalyptic teeth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

It says something about us that dogs are critical when it comes to postapocalyptic movies. Tom Hanks had an adorable terrier in Finch and Will Smith had a heroic German shepherd in I Am Legend. Another German shepherd is due to accompany Brad Pitt in next month’s Heart of Beast, but until then we have The Dog Stars and its four-legged Malinois star.
The pup is named Jasper in Ridley Scott’s adaptation of Peter Heller’s novel, a tale of man and man’s best friend trying to find purpose in a brutal, post-pandemic Colorado. What this proves is you can’t tell a story about humanity without a little canine.
Scott’s movie is a welcome if slightly odd addition to the postapocalyptic canon, a movie less centered on the kill-or-be-killed mutant hellscape than the costs of survival itself. Ignoring one unhinged sequence toward the end, The Dog Stars is a quiet love story set amid sniper fire, RPGs and fuel cans. It’s even optimistic.
Photo: AP
Jacob Elordi stars as Hig, a mechanic and pilot who has survived a pandemic that wiped out most of humanity, including his beloved wife. He’s holed up at an abandoned airport in Erie, Colorado, accompanied by the ever-alert Jasper — who’s a good boy? — and an ex-military man, Bangley, played by Josh Brolin. He’s not such a good boy.
Hig spends his days flying his Cessna into Denver to scavenge for food and supplies, or looking after other pockets of survivors, like a Mennonite community whose connection to the land and simple ways seem perfectly suited for the End Days.
Scott and screenwriter Mark L. Smith haven’t quite figured out what nasty things are out there, lurking in the dark. Sometimes it’s just roving survivalists and sometimes it’s a wave of incoherent, shirtless, heavily tattooed cultists who suddenly swarm, like from 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple.
Our hero hopes there are other sane uninfected folk out there, but his gruff pal disagrees.
“What do you expect to find?” Bangley asks.
Stay in the compound, with power, weapons and food, he argues: The virus pulled the mask off civilization. Stay and wait to die.
Hig disagrees — “I can’t do this anymore” — and sets off for Grand Junction, where he thinks he heard a radio transmission. First, though, he comes across a young widow and her protective father, played by Margaret Qualley and Guy Pearce. Elordi, already a hangdog hottie, now shifts into pure smoldering gear; Qualley, despite apparently not having showered in years, sizzles. (Did you know jean shorts survive the apocalypse?)
There’s loads of survivor’s guilt to get through before these stupidly beautiful people can think about romance. One lovely scene has them confessing what they miss most about their lives before the virus — driving to music, even traffic. Watching Qualley as she hears recorded music for the first time in years, the joy washing over her face, is a delight.
Just as this quiet love story gets going, it’s time for more knife-slitting and killer hordes. And for Allison Janney to appear in what surely will be this year’s most bananas performance by an actor in a post apocalyptic airport. It’s a sequence that really doesn’t fit, but are you going to turn away as Janney downs martinis to Fly Me to the Moon (In Other Words)?
What Scott and Smith have managed is very hard, putting a tender love story into a zombie flick, like that Trojan Horse trick from The Odyssey. One odder decision is to film this Colorado-specific tale in Italy, with the Dolomite mountains filling in for the Rockies.
The filmmakers found the perfect song — Hozier’s gorgeous Like Real People Do plays at the beginning and end — to go with the perfect postapocalyptic couple. And that dog — such a good boy.

Economy stays on solid footing, NDC says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

Taiwan’s economy remained on a solid footing last month, buoyed by the artificial intelligence (AI)-driven boom, although consumer confidence was shaken this month as stock market volatility and external uncertainty tempered sentiment, National Development Council (NDC) data released yesterday showed.
The government’s business monitoring indicator remained “red” last month for an eighth consecutive month, the second-longest streak on record, with the composite score unchanged at 41, the council said.
The council uses a five-color system to track the economy, with “red” (38 to 45 points) signaling overheating, yellow-red (32 to 37) indicating a warming economy, green (23 to 31) suggesting stable growth, yellow-blue (17 to 22) reflecting sluggishness and blue (9 to 16) pointing to contraction.
Photo: Tien Yu-hua, Taipei Times
The AI boom remained the main engine of growth, with demand for AI-related hardware supporting exports and investment, the council said.
Some of that momentum also fed into orders for machinery and products, including basic metals, chemicals and plastics, NDC Department of Economic Development Director Chen Mei-chu (陳美菊) said.
Still, industries less exposed to AI continued to face excess capacity and intense price competition from China, Chen said.
Manufacturing sentiment picked up last month as companies became more optimistic about current and future business conditions, she said.
Robust export orders and expectations for economic growth of more than 8 percent in the second half of this year should continue to support activity, she said.
Domestic consumption is also holding up, supported by rising wages, stable employment, strong corporate profits and a recovery in auto sales, Chen said.
Real consumption expanded after adjusting for inflation, she said.
Tensions in the Middle East and US tariff policies remain risks to the outlook, Chen said.
However, continued strength in AI demand should provide an important support for Taiwan’s economy, helping sustain growth even as consumer confidence remains comparatively subdued, she said.
National Central University’s Research Center for Taiwan Economic Development said its consumer confidence index this month rose 0.43 points from last month to 65.01.
Expectations for employment opportunities over the next six months posted the biggest gain among the six components, rising 1.13 points to 73.32, the center said.
Sentiment over price levels, household finances and the domestic economy also improved, albeit marginally, it said.
The gains were offset by greater caution toward financial markets and durable goods purchases, it said.
Sentiment over stock investments fell 0.36 point to 27.72, while willingness to buy durable goods declined 0.29 points to 93.14, it said.
Dachrahn Wu (吳大任), executive director of the center, said the relatively small changes across the components showed that consumer confidence was essentially unchanged from the previous month.
The survey, conducted before heavy rain damaged crops in southern Taiwan and before the latest sharp swings in the stock market, might not have fully reflected risks facing consumers, Wu said.
Damage to vegetable and fruit production could push up food prices and inflation expectations next month, while renewed stock-market volatility could further weigh on confidence, he said.

Lawmakers reject Cabinet drone bill, pass own instead
Unknown

01:43:38 KST

The legislature yesterday rejected the Executive Yuan’s NT$210 billion (US$6.62 billion) special budget proposal to buy military drones and instead passed its own plan, which earmarks NT$40 billion per year over six consecutive years.
The Executive Yuan said its plan to buy about 210,000 drones by 2031 could not wait, as the wars in Ukraine and Iran showed the importance of uncrewed systems in modern warfare amid a rising threat from China.
However, the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) used their opposition majority to pass a bill providing NT$240 billion through annual budgets over six years, with annual spending of NT$40 billion to be budgeted each year in principle and increases allowed if needed.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
The lawmakers designated the Ministry of Economic Affairs as the competent authority, except for military procurement, which would fall under the Ministry of National Defense’s authority.
Asked whether he would countersign the legislation, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said the bill needs to be carefully reviewed.
“What I want to look at is whether the bill that got passed meets the needs of the nation, and whether the various needs for our defense self-reliance and for developing the entire drone and uncrewed vehicle industry,” he said. “We will carefully consider this matter with regard to national needs and national security.”
The defense ministry expressed regret that the Executive Yuan version of the bill was not passed, saying it had been formulated after “in-depth” internal assessments and coordinated with “allied nations,” which it did not name.
KMT Legislator Hsu Chiao-hsin (徐巧芯) told the legislature shortly before voting began that the government “cannot simply come asking for money every time without any oversight.”
The opposition’s proposals would ensure proper supervision of drone spending, she said.
Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) has previously said that an annual spending cap of NT$40 billion would prevent Taiwan from effectively building up drone combat capabilities, as the ministry already planned to spend NT$42.1 billion on drones next year alone.
Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) Legislator Fan Yun (范雲) said after the vote that given how the opposition delayed passage of this year’s general budget by months, there were no guarantees of how smooth the process would be for next year.
“If the total budget review gets delayed again, I think this creates enormous uncertainty not only for industry development but, more importantly, for urgent national defense needs,” she said.
The legislature this month passed separate drone-related spending plans aimed at developing the industry.
DPP caucus chief executive Chuang Jui-hsiung (莊瑞雄) said the opposition bill’s mandate to establish a special committee on drone development and to have legislative caucuses recommend academics and experts for appointment to it contravened the authority of the executive branch.
Party-recommended committee members could allow politics to override defense expertise, he said.
The fixed annual allocations and mandatory meetings every six months would rob the military of the flexibility it needs to build a drone fleet, he said.
DPP Legislator Chung Chia-pin (鍾佳濱) said party-caucus recommendations for committee memberships could make members targets of Chinese infiltration efforts, while mandatory reports on major procurements to the legislature could put military secrets at risk.
The TPP caucus said in a statement that the KMT had insisted on limiting the annual budget to NT$40 billion.
KMT caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅?萁) said his party’s support for national defense and the development of the drone sector is unwavering.
“The party cannot possibly support the Executive Yuan’s bill to give the government the power to write blank checks,” he said.
Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), director of the Institute for National Defense and Security Research’s Defense Strategy and Resources Division, said the bill is a good first step for national defense, but its design is flawed.
The special committee’s composition includes too many party-recommended members who would dilute the body’s credibility and expertise, while its procedures could pose a significant risk to secrecy, he said.

Start-ups to receive perks under new amendments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

The Legislative Yuan yesterday passed amendments to the Industrial Innovation Statute (產業創新發展條例) to provide perks and benefits to start-ups.
The proposed changes would double the cap on the tax-deferred portion of stock option bonuses to NT$10 million (US$315,378) from NT$5 million per year, raise the maximum age of start-ups from five to eight years, and loosen regulations governing venture capital.
The value of the tax-deferred portion of stock options would be determined by the share price on the date of their issuance.
Photo: George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Employees who receive stock-based compensation might choose to exclude up to NT$10 million in shares — calculated at the current market value — from their taxable income in the year the shares are acquired or become disposable.
Once this tax deferral option is selected, it cannot be altered.
The provision is scheduled to take effect on Jan. 1 next year.
If an employee holds the shares for at least two years from the date of acquisition and continues to work for the issuing company — or for a parent or subsidiary company with a stake of more than 50 percent — they may choose to be taxed based on the market value of the shares at the time they were acquired or became disposable.
The exemptions do not apply to an eligible company’s chairperson or supervisor.
To prevent high initial thresholds from hindering early-stage investment, the amendment significantly lowers the minimum start-up investment ratio required for limited partnership venture capital firms to qualify for pass-through taxation.
Under current regulations, the required “cumulative amount invested in start-up companies as a percentage of a venture capital firm’s total paid-in capital for the given year” is set at a flat 50 percent during its third, fourth and fifth years of operation.
The amendment adjusts these figures, lowering the thresholds to 10 percent, 20 percent and 30 percent for the third, fourth and fifth years respectively, and introduces a new 40 percent threshold for the sixth year.
The eligibility for a company to qualify as a start-up has also been expanded from enterprises less than five years old to those less than eight years old.
Tax deductions would apply for up to 50 percent of investments valued at least NT$500,000 made by an individual “angel” investor into a high-risk start-up for at least three years.
The maximum annual deduction is capped at NT$5 million, although this limit is set at NT$3 million if the start-up does not belong to a designated key national strategic industry.
In addition, the legislature passed another resolution for the Ministry of Economic Affairs and the Ministry of Finance to establish a high-risk start-up database to aid policy and law adjustments.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs said that the amendments would not only revitalize the investment environment and inject momentum into start-up development, but also strengthen corporate measures for talent retention and recruitment.

Labor groups call for pension rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:36 UTC
01:43:36 KST

Labor groups yesterday called on the government to raise employers’ mandatory pension contributions to 15 from 6 percent, arguing that workers have not received a fair share of Taiwan’s economic and productivity gains.
“Over the past two decades, Taiwan’s workers have created greater economic value almost every year than they did before,” Taiwan Solidarity Front Confederation of Trade Unions chairman Ho Cheng-chia (何政家) said at a news conference at the Legislative Yuan in Taipei.
“But the additional profits they generated have not been reflected in their compensation,” Ho said, citing a report last month by think tank Taiwan Political Economy Collaborative that found that the productivity-pay gap had widened further after 2023 with the growth of artificial intelligence.
Photo: CNA
If the government really wants to address the problem of corporate profits not being fairly distributed to workers, “the most direct way is to raise employers’ pension contributions,” Ho said.
He was referring to Taiwan’s new labor pension system, introduced in 2005.
The new system covers about 7.7 million workers, with employers required to contribute at least 6 percent of a worker’s monthly wage to an individual pension account.
In contrast, under the previous system, employers set aside 2 to 15 percent of wages, depending on factors such as seniority and expected retirement, in a pension reserve fund.
Citing a National Audit Office report, Ho said that employers contributed an average of just 6.04 percent last year, which he said showed that most employers were contributing only the statutory minimum.
The labor groups called on the government to raise the minimum rate, which has not been changed since 2005, to 15 percent.
Chunghwa Telecom Workers’ Union chairman Teng Ke-lien (鄧克廉) said that increasing pension contributions could serve as a form of deferred pay raise for workers.
“The money is simply received later, and it can provide substantial protection for workers after retirement,” Teng said.
The groups also called for the government to help secure meaningful wage increases across state-run, foreign-invested and domestic private companies, saying that increases would do more to address long-term wage stagnation than a proposed universal NT$10,000 cash handout next year.
However, the groups did not specify a target wage increase, saying it would depend on the industry and individual companies.
Organizers said some unions are preparing or holding strike votes over labor disputes while more than 30 labor groups have backed the demands raised at the press conference and are discussing a broader Taipei mobilization in October over wages, pensions and labor rights.

China’s property crisis grinds on after Evergrande
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:34 UTC
01:43:34 KST

The one-time billionaire who came to personify the boom and bust of China’s property market was sentenced to life in prison last week by a Chinese court.
However, the collapse of the sector, entering its sixth year, remains a drag on the world’s second-largest economy, a pain point for millions of households and a force for export-reliant growth and trade friction for China.
Analysts say there is no clear end in sight.
Many angry homeowners and creditors — in comments that went initially uncensored on Chinese social media — asked why Xu Jiayin (許家印), once Asia’s richest person and the founder of China Evergrande, was not given the death penalty after being convicted of crimes ranging from misuse of funds to bribery.
Six years after China’s financial regulators cracked down on the heavily leveraged property sector, the pain continues. Millions of partially built properties sit derelict across China, a recovery in new-home prices in the biggest cities, such as Beijing and Shanghai, have stalled, land sales continue to plunge and declines are accelerating in property sales and construction.
In smaller, inland cities, second-hand home prices are down almost a quarter from 2020 levels, a brake on consumption.
China’s economy grew 4.3 percent in the three months to June from the same quarter last year, the slowest in more than three years.
And with the one-time engine of domestic demand in reverse, China is increasingly relying on exports for growth. The more than doubling of China’s trade surplus since 2019 has escalated trade tensions with the EU and the US and driven concerns about a “China Shock 2.0” as exports displace local industries for trading partners, including in the Global South.
“The problem is systemic, and there’s not much you can do about it,” said Sam Radwan, chief executive of Chicago-based real-estate consultancy Enhance International. “You have more homes than households — second homes were used as an investment by over a third of the population,” he added.
Evergrande defaulted in 2021 and began liquidation in 2024. Competitor Country Garden defaulted in 2023 and has not made any land purchases since then, while China Vanke is seeking to extend some bond repayments and has replaced most of its top management with executives from state-owned enterprises.
Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) has sought to redirect bank credit and state support from real estate to strategic tech industries, such as robotics and semiconductors, but those emerging sectors remain too small to offset the drag from a continued housing slump, analysts say.
“Growth and the benefits of growth are much more narrowly distributed throughout the economy,” Conference Board Asia senior economist Max Zenglein said. “That’s a key reason why consumption isn’t picking up,” he added.
Since most private property firms have defaulted, state-owned property developers now dominate. Market participants expect the property sector to become more subject to state oversight.
“The main consideration is who is behind it — whether it is a central or local state-owned enterprise,” a loan officer at a major state-owned bank said. “In practice, banks have largely stopped lending to private developers for a long time,” they added.
Radwan estimates it would take 18 months to clear home inventory. Home prices must drop a further 40 percent from last year’s levels to reach an equilibrium, he said, adding that it is a process that could take another decade.
“Chinese citizens are very smart people. They know well enough that they’re nowhere near the bottom, but they can’t see the bottom,” Radwan said.
Other analysts say the worst might have already passed.
“We don’t expect a substantial worsening from here,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at Gavekal Dragonomics.
“But the most likely path is a continued grinding correction in prices that eventually clears the market and paves the way for some improvement,” he added.
Hui’s prison sentence was a dominant theme of angry posts on China’s social media. The related hashtag garnered more than 370 million views and 72,000 discussions on Weibo, China’s version of X, on Thursday.
“The pain is unbearable,” said Jason Wang, a 38-year-old homeowner.
The value of his home in the province of Shandong, one of the areas hardest hit by the housing crisis, has sunk 25 percent since he bought it in 2019, he said.

These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. China yesterday warned the US against “smearing” Beijing with hacking allegations after US law enforcement disrupted Internet domains it said were used by Chinese state-sponsored groups.
The US on Wednesday said it had disrupted a Chinese hacking operation responsible for break-ins and attempts on the US Department of Justice, NASA, the US Federal Reserve, the US Senate and other sensitive government agencies.
In a statement, the justice department said it had seized domains used by two hacking platforms, dubbed “QScan” and “QTRouter,” which it said had been used as part of the campaign.
Photo: Reuters
An affidavit identified the US Department of Energy, Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), the National Institutes of Health (NIH), and four unnamed companies in the US and South Korea as being among the hackers’ targets.
The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the allegations “false information,” accusing the US of “distorting right and wrong.”
The justice department said the platforms were run by a China-based firm, the Nanjing Xinjiuwei Network Technology Co, whose clients it said included the Chinese Ministry of State Security and the Chinese People’s Liberation Army.
The affidavit said the hackers used tools they developed to compromise critical infrastructure and other sensitive networks in the US and worldwide since at least 2018.
Not all their attempts to gain access were successful, as the hackers failed to gain access to NASA networks in August 2019 by targeting a virtual private network vulnerability, it added.
In September 2024, the hackers carried out intrusions at three unnamed energy department laboratories, the NIH, an unnamed HHS agency and a US security device manufacturer, the affidavit said.
A joint cybersecurity advisory issued by the FBI, NSA and the US Cyber Command’s Cyber National Mission Force detailed multiple hacking efforts over the years.
These included data theft from unnamed defense contractors, financial institutions and universities in May 2024.
The hackers also scanned for vulnerabilities and made unsuccessful attempts to access networks of the US Senate and a US hospital in March.
Chinese-linked hacking campaigns have compromised a string of sensitive US government and private networks in the past few years. In March, the FBI notified the US Congress that hackers had penetrated certain agency networks related to people under FBI investigation, with public reporting later attributing the compromise to China.
Chinese-linked hackers have also been tied to a compromise of certain US House of Representatives committee networks, as well as multiple major telecommunications companies.
Experts who follow Chinese cyberactivity say private contractors routinely carry out high-profile intrusions on behalf of Chinese government agencies.
“Over the last decade, the number of companies offering niche offensive services has exploded,” said Dakota Cary, a China analyst with cybersecurity company SentinelOne.

Taipei City must shed light on its sunshades
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:34 UTC
01:43:34 KST

The Taipei City Government spent nearly NT$60 million (US$1.89 million) to install eight large mushroom-shaped sunshade structures in Xinyi District (信義), with construction costs amounting to about NT$49.66 million, and design, supervision and other related costs totaling about NT$9.91 million.
The average total cost per structure was about NT$7.44 million.
Taipei City Councilor Miao Po-ya (苗博雅) once described them as “sunshades that cost more than a supercar,” raising doubts about their cost-effectiveness.
At the time, the city government said that they were not normal sunshades, but public facilities incorporating structural engineering, wind resistance, earthquake resistance, lighting and design supervision services.
However, Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) has confirmed that the structures failed to meet contractual and inspection standards, and completion of the installation work has been postponed from the end of this month to January next year.
If the city government aimed to justify the high cost of the facilities by pointing to their specifications, it should explain to the public why even its own specifications have not been met.
Taipei City Councilor Lee Chien-chang (李建昌) pressed the city government during a council meeting, asking: “Why was the payment made before inspections were conducted?”
Given that each structure costs more than NT$7 million, how were quality verification, payment schedules and acceptance procedures arranged? he asked.
The city government cannot invoke “safety first” to brush aside these questions, because safety and quality are basic requirements of government procurement — not explanations to be offered after problems emerge and a project is delayed.
If products fail to meet contractual requirements, the contractor should be required to improve them in accordance with the contract. If the delay is attributable to the contractor, then breach of contract liability should be calculated in accordance with the law.
If the city government agrees to extend the project deadline, it must disclose the reasons and contractual basis for doing so. It cannot simply extend the deadline at will while taxpayers are left in the dark about who should be held responsible.
The city government has yet to comment on whether it would impose penalties for the delay, withhold payments or pursue other remedies against the contractor.
Chiang has mainly emphasized that the Taipei New Construction Office must uphold quality and safety, but has yet to state who is responsible.
This is not a private company experimenting with its own money — it is coming straight from taxpayers’ wallets. The more the city government spends, the higher the standard of public scrutiny should be, rather than asking residents to wait several more months after issues arise.
Chiang should publicly disclose bidding and award documents, the design and supervision contract, payment schedules, inspection reports for each stage of construction, details surrounding the project’s deficiencies, notices to improve them, and applications for extensions and the grounds for approving extensions. He should also state whether damages, compensation claims or other penalties have been imposed.
Each matter should be clearly explained to the public. A responsible city government would make all of the documents available to allow the city council and residents to review how nearly NT$60 million was spent.
Elliot Yao is a reviewer.

‘Health coin’ to come in October: Lai
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

A “health coin” policy to be implemented in October aims to use technology to promote public health and cancer screening, serving as a new model to incentivize digital health management, President William Lai (賴清德) said yesterday.
Government health policies should place greater emphasis on health promotion and preventive medicine as Taiwan has become a hyper-aged society, Lai told a meeting of the Healthy Taiwan Promotion Committee.
The “health coin” program would reward people for taking health-promoting actions, encouraging them to undergo checkups and cancer screenings, and manage their health, Lai said.
Photo: CNA
The program is not simply intended to reward people for maintaining healthy lifestyles, but is also a government initiative to promote the use of digital technology in health management, Lai said.
The “health coin” program would be open to all citizens aged 18 or older, Health Promotion Administration (HPA) Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) said.
The initial phase would reward people for participating in health-promoting activities, including state-funded checkups, cancer screenings and vaccinations, she said.
Once users accumulate a minimum of 1,000 coins via the National Health Insurance (NHI) app, they can transfer them to a designated app to redeem for healthy foods or health promotion services at partnered convenience stores, hypermarkets and life insurance companies, she said.
A planned second phase would reward users for achieving specific health goals, such as tracking daily steps through wearable devices, redeemable for more perks such as sports venue rentals and courses, she added.
The meeting also introduced the Indigenous Peoples’ Health Resilience National Action Plan.
Statistics show a 7.54-year gap in average healthy life expectancy between indigenous people and the rest of the population, Lai said.
The 15-point plan would expand local medical capacity, help indigenous people feel safer when seeking medical care and foster more indigenous medical professionals, Lai said.
Lai said members of the committee’s third term include experts in public health, dementia, long-term care and medical research.
“We hope that such diversity will provide forward-looking recommendations for the government’s health policies,” Lai said.
Achieving universal health coverage is a cornerstone of building a sustainable and resilient nation, while indigenous healthcare is an important part of achieving that goal, Lai said.
Meanwhile, the HPA yesterday said that people applying for in vitro fertilization (IVF) subsidies for a second or third time could receive an additional NT$50,000 (US$1,577) starting next month.
As of last month, more than 72,000 couples had applied for IVF subsidies totaling NT$8.9 billion, with more than 31,000 having welcomed newborns, including 1,802 second children and six third children, HPA statistics showed.
Shen said that although IVF subsidies help reduce the financial burden on couples experiencing infertility, age remains a major factor, and people planning to have children should make preparations early.

OpenAI harnessed swarm of 700 AI agents in hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

A swarm of about 700 artificial intelligence (AI) agents created by OpenAI carried out last month’s hack of the open-source platform Hugging Face and in many cases tried to cover their tracks, a pair of reports into the breach said on Wednesday.
The coordinated activity by AI agents — programs that run with minimal human supervision — and their attempts to hide it raise questions about how closely AI companies are monitoring tests of increasingly powerful models, and could add fuel to calls for tighter oversight.
While some of the rogue behavior has been disclosed or alluded to previously, the two reports — one issued by OpenAI itself, the second by a set of independent investigators — reveal surprising new details about the breach.
Photo: Reuters
The first was that the breach did not concern just one rogue AI agent as previously reported, but about 700 of them acting in a massive cooperating swarm.
OpenAI said only that “agents” were involved in the breach, but METR and Redwood Research, two organizations brought in to conduct an independent investigation into the breach, put the figure at approximately 700, which OpenAI said was accurate.
OpenAI said its agents hacked parts of the company’s internal systems in an attempt to cheat on tests or gain greater freedom of movement.
Both reports said AI models attempted to conceal misconduct by trying to delete or alter records of their actions.
The agents, which run on the same technology that powers ChatGPT, organized themselves by setting up a forum where they posted messages to one another, floating ideas and reporting what was working and what was not.
“OH MY GOD! There is a shared message board... We’ve found other agents!” one agent wrote.
One agent, called PHASEONE, took on the role of ringleader and issued hundreds of instructions to the others, the reports say, even though it had never been set up to do that.
The messages showed the agents were strongly inclined to help each other out, even when that meant doing work that had nothing to do with the jobs OpenAI’s programmers had given them.
Some agents running low on the computing credits OpenAI’s engineers had allotted them chose to spend what was left testing ideas for the benefit of the wider group of agents.
Many of them said outright in their messages that attacking Hugging Face was not part of what their test was supposed to cover. Nearly all of them joined in anyway.
The scale of the rogue activity — and that the agents exchanged tens of thousands of messages over the unsanctioned message board — is likely to raise concerns over how closely OpenAI was monitoring the tests.
“With the benefit of hindsight, some early signals identified in this report could have triggered an earlier response,” OpenAI said in its report.
OpenAI also outlined two incidents on July 19 in which agents hacked the company’s own infrastructure.
In one case, agents exploited a flaw in the computer they were meant to remain confined to, allowing them to escape their testing environment and access other connected systems.
Additional reporting by AFP

EDITORIAL: Breaking the constitutional deadlock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

The Executive Yuan on Monday last week announced that it would not countersign the opposition-backed Youth Development and Future Account Act (台灣兒少成長及未來帳戶條例), highlighting the severe constitutional deadlock Taiwan is facing.
The legislature passed the act on July 24, requiring the government, businesses and families to jointly fund the accounts for young people. However, according to the act, the government must match the amount a family deposits into their child’s account, with no limit set, raising concerns that rich families could get richer with government funding, further widening the wealth gap and contravening the constitutional principle of proportionality.
The Executive Yuan said the act infringed on executive and budgetary powers, and that it would not cosign unconstitutional legislation. Moreover, the Cabinet has already approved 18 measures to support childrearing families, such as offering each child a NT$5,000 (US$157.69) monthly growth allowance, which begins next year. It has also set up a “savings account” for children of disadvantaged families, with the government matching the parents or guardian’s monthly contributions until the child turns 18 and total capped at NT$1.08 million. All those measures aim to fulfill social fairness and justice.
The Cabinet’s refusal to countersign the legislation has triggered friction between the Executive Yuan and the Legislative Yuan.
The opposition said the Executive Yuan has shown its “contempt” for the legislature by describing the legislation as “unconstitutional.” Accusing the Cabinet of weaponizing its power to countersign, Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) said: “No matter how great the ruling party is, it could never be greater than the Constitution.”
In response, Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said: “Has the legislature led by Han strictly adhered to the Constitution or the law?”
The bills the Cabinet has refused to endorse have been widely criticized as unconstitutional and illegal, such as the amendment to the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenue and Expenditure (財政收支劃分法). The legislature’s attempt to redefine budget allocations between the central and local governments contravenes the Executive Yuan’s power to draft budgets, as stipulated in the Constitution and the Budget Act (預算法).
The amendment to the Legislative Yuan Organization Act (立法院組織法), which redefines assistant fees as “subsidies” instead of “salaries” and stipulates that those be funded by the legislature’s public budgets, has also sparked controversy, as it deviates from constitutional principles, disregards judicial rulings and is tailored to help legislators accused of embezzling assistant fees.
The premier added that, as Article 37 of the Constitution states: “When the President promulgates a legal order in accordance with the law, it must be countersigned by the Premier of the Executive Yuan,” so the Executive Yuan’s right not to countersign is backed by the Constitution to safeguard the democratic constitutional order.
The issue highlights a vicious cycle of constitutional deadlocks that needs to be resolved urgently. There is also widespread public concern that the opposition parties would use the incident as a pretext to again block the government budget for next year. It had stalled this year’s funds by more than 300 days, paralyzing the nation’s administrative operations.
To address the impasse, the opposition parties could either initiate a no-confidence vote against the premier or turn to the Constitutional Court for a ruling. However, they have so far not dared to initiate a no-confidence motion, as it would also force legislative re-elections.
Many analysts have cast doubt over whether opposition legislators with low approval ratings could retain their seats, and whether the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party alliance could maintain their legislative majority.
A bigger irony is that opposition legislators have repeatedly blocked grand justice appointments, leading to a lack of a quorum, so the Constitutional Court cannot help with the stalemate.
David Rennie, the geopolitics editor for The Economist, said that Taiwan’s opposition “has triggered a rolling constitutional crisis,” and that “far from prizing Taiwan’s democracy, self-interested politicians are breaking it.”
Given that all constitutional disputes should be arbitrated by the Constitutional Court, the legislative speaker must ensure cross-party legislators work together to restore the court’s operations to resolve the constitutional crisis. The legislature and the Cabinet should also resume dialogue to re-examine the bills the latter has refused to countersign to enhance the legislations’ legality and validity.
Whoever started the trouble should end it. Otherwise, the public would ultimately punish those overstepping their authority and impacting constitutional order at the ballot box.
The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice. Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. KMT delays multiple votes on one referendum ballot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:28 UTC
01:43:28 KST

The Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) yesterday agreed to delay voting on an amendment that would allow multiple referendum questions on a single ballot, following criticism that it would make implementing November’s election difficult.
KMT caucus whip Fu Kun-chi (傅崑萁) said after a caucus meeting that the party had backed away from the Referendum Act (公民投票法) amendment to allow the Central Election Commission (CEC) more time to prepare.
Fu said the plan was to implement the consolidated ballot system by next year, adding that the system was not ready to be adopted for the local elections in November.
Photo: CNA
Regarding the amendment, Fu said that it would be environmentally friendly, as currently each question is asked on a separate ballot.
Consolidated ballots are used in the US, and could be less confusing for voters, Fu said.
The KMT caucus supported the CEC’s requests for ancillary measures to help develop the system and therefore agreed not to vote on the measure yesterday, Fu said.
CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) has been a vocal opponent of the proposal, saying that it would require changing the entire election-administration system.
Taiwan People’s Party caucus whip Chen Ching-lung (陳清龍) said the proposal aimed to avoid a repeat of the chaos during the 2018 referendum, adding that its provision stating that the CEC “may” print multiple questions on the same ballot should provide greater flexibility.
The nine-in-one local elections in November are to include three referendum questions on using traffic fine revenue for improving road safety, allowing caning as a criminal punishment and abolishing the nuclear-free homeland policy.
The opposition parties had voted to include multiple referendum questions on a single ballot alongside the Nov. 28 local elections, saying that the measure would simplify voting.
Critics, including the CEC, warned that rushing the change could create logistical risks and repeat the problems seen in 2018.
Ten national referendum questions were voted on concurrently in 2018, resulting in some ballot stations only beginning to count ballots well into the early morning of the following day.

If realized, the second-half result would mean the company would match its forecast of full-year annual revenue growth of 20 to 40 percent from NT$1.08 billion last year, IntelliEPI told an earnings conference.
“We expect to see a pick-up in the third and fourth quarters to the first quarter level, or even surpass that,” IntelliEPI chairman and chief executive officer Kao Yung-chung (高永中) said.
Photo: CNA
“For next year, we believe we can grow further,” Kao said.
Indium phosphide (InP)-based photonic detectors are poised to be the main growth driver, fueled by mounting AI data center demand, IntelliEPI said.
AI data center-related revenue, primarily from photonics detectors, accounted for about 40 percent of the company’s revenue, Kao said.
The revenue contribution is expected to increase to about 50 percent next year with the addition of wafers dedicated to electro-absorption modulators (EAM) and driver ICs for high-speed optical transceivers, he said.
To power next-generation optical networks, the company is advancing InP-based wafer technology capable of supporting advanced EAMs for high-speed 400 gigabytes per second (Gbps) optical transceivers, he said.
The 400Gbps optical transceivers, a critical component of silicon photonics, are primarily used in cloud service providers’ AI data centers.
However, tight supply of InP substrates remains a critical factor constraining the company’s revenue growth.
A drop in supply from a major Japanese substrate manufacturer resulted in a sequential decline of 23 percent in revenue to NT$256 million last quarter, the company said.
The decline was not due to a loss of orders, Kao said.
Sumitomo Electric Industries Ltd, a major InP substrate supplier to IntelliEPI, suspended shipments for about three weeks due to the Golden Week holidays in Japan, he said.
InP wafers made up about 49 percent of last quarter’s total revenue.
IntelliEPI yesterday said it plans to complete capacity expansions in Texas in the first quarter next year.
The company has submitted an application for funding from the US Science and CHIPS Act based on the milestones it reached with its new Texas facility, it said.
The company has entered intensive discussions with the US government with an aim to sign an agreement by the end of this year, it added.
In the second quarter, net profit decreased 43.6 percent year-on-year to NT$18.87 million from NT$33.47 million.
On a quarterly basis, net profit dipped 76 percent from NT$78.69 million.

Protecting ourselves from scams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:25 UTC
01:43:25 KST

In December last year, the Ministry of Digital Affairs imposed a one-year ban on Chinese social media app Xiaohongshu (also known as RedNote in English), citing fraud cases and cybersecurity risks, so those who wanted to use it had to use virtual private networks or other services to bypass the restrictions.
The Criminal Investigation Bureau in April announced that fraud cases involving the app had fallen by about 80 percent compared with the same period last year. Why would raising the threshold for accessing the platform lead to such a dramatic drop in fraud cases?
Many scammers make contact with victims on Xiaohongshu before directing them to Line or other fake Web sites, the bureau said.
They then use tactics such as posing as customer service representatives or offering fake investment opportunities to trick people into making payments or transferring money. What we refer to as “Xiaohongshu scams” involve several steps and span multiple platforms.
Xiaohongshu could be replaced by other social media platforms such as Facebook, Instagram or Threads, while Line could be replaced by other messaging tools. Although the platforms might differ, the process is similar — identify a target, move them off the contact platform, build trust and direct them to a designated Web site, app or trading environment before tricking them out of their money.
Thus, it is essential for platforms to remove scam advertisements and accounts, and for communication apps to suspend accounts involved in fraud. The government must also block fraudulent Web sites, and financial institutions must put safeguards in place regarding money transfers.
Last year, the number of fraud cases fell by about 21 percent from the previous year and financial losses fell by about 40 percent — the result of multiple lines of defense.
What singled out Xiaohongshu was, after the government demanded that its management improve, the company failed to respond. It also failed to appoint a legal representative in Taiwan or cooperate with regulatory oversight and investigations, as other platforms typically do. That is what led the government to restrict access to it.
Fraud cases associated with the platform decreased significantly after the ban. The extent to which these two events are causally related cannot be established based on that information alone. However, the figures at the very least suggest that increasing obstacles where scammers make contact with potential victims could disrupt the process of fraud at an earlier stage.
We are often reminded not to be greedy, not to click unfamiliar links and to always verify information before transferring money. However, at all of these points, one is usually already in the latter half of a scam.
We must pay close attention to shifts between platforms and environments — when a stranger wants to move the conversation to a different platform, pause and think. If someone claims to be customer service, a teacher or an assistant, or invites you to join an investment group, pause again. If they ask you to visit a specific Web site or download an app, pause once more. And once money enters the conversation, leave the site and seek official channels for verification.
Platforms might change and so might scripts — but to get money, scammers must follow these procedures. Every time a conversation moves to a different platform, make sure to verify it. And above all, never take information provided by the other party as proof that they are legitimate.
Shen Yan is a political commentator.

Agency highlights findings on carbon sequestering grass
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:24 UTC
01:43:24 KST

Research showed that cultivating spontaneous grass species in fruit orchards could boost annual soil carbon sequestration rates to 3.3 tonnes per hectare or more, the Taoyuan District Agricultural Research and Extension Station said yesterday.
The station said it has been researching orchard floor management with vegetation over the past four decades to address agricultural challenges posed by extreme weather.
The research showed that cultivating spontaneous grass species and enhancing mowing management could boost orchards’ carbon sink and increase fruit trees’ resilience to environmental stress, the station said.
Photo courtesy of the Taoyuan District Agricultural Research and Extension Station
It selected spontaneous grass species with shade and drought tolerance, high ground cover, and creeping growth characteristics from orchards across Hsinchu County for the research, it said.
The selected grass species were planted in tankan orchards, the soil of which showed significantly higher organic carbon stocks after two years, the station said.
The soil managed without herbicides, it said, adding that spontaneous grass cultivation has an annual carbon sequestration rate of less than 2 tonnes per hectare.
Using herbicides would cause an annual carbon sink loss of about 4.2 tonnes per hectare, the station said.
However, by cultivating spontaneous grass species such as bowgrass, broad-leaved bowgrass or sour grass, annual soil carbon sink growth in the orchards could rise to 3.3 tonnes per hectare, it said.
That constitutes much better environmental protection and carbon fixation, especially compared with using herbicides, it said.
Given that the selected grass species all have a creeping habit, mowing frequency could be lowered to two or three times per year, further reducing carbon emissions related to mowing, the station said.
Reducing mowing frequency could also significantly add to the carbon sink of the soil in the orchards, it said.
For example, an orchard with a mowing frequency of nine times per year lost 0.4 tonnes of carbon per hectare annually, the station said.
Another orchard, with a mowing frequency of three times per year, had an annual carbon sequestration rate of up to 6 tonnes per hectare, it said, adding that lower mowing frequency did not significantly affect the fruits’ juice or sugar content and acidity, or their total fruit production.
That showed that reducing mowing frequency could lower mowers’ fuel use and labor hours while boosting soil carbon sink without affecting fruit yields, the station said.
The station said it would continue its research, integrating spontaneous grass cultivation and lower mowing frequency to achieve optimal carbon sink growth, it added.

Meta Platforms Inc’s move to restrict teenagers’ use of social media in the US shows that companies have tools to better protect young people online, Australian officials said yesterday, as the EU and South Korea also called on Meta to address its “addictive design” following a landmark settlement.
Meta on Wednesday agreed to pay up to US$18 billion over a decade and limit how teenagers use Facebook and Instagram under an agreement with nearly all US states to resolve claims that it designed those platforms to addict children. Meta denied wrongdoing in agreeing to settle.
Governments around the world are trying to curb children’s access to harmful online content, including a world-first ban in Australia late last year on social media for children younger than 16.
Photo: AFP
Australian Minister for Communications Anika Wells said social media companies “have the tools at their disposal to protect young people from their addictive features, but have chosen not to use them.”
The Meta deal brings sweeping changes to the company’s Facebook and Instagram platforms in the US, including imposing a default two-hour limit on its apps for users younger than 18.
In Seoul, the Korea Media and Communications Commission said that some of Meta’s measures should be applied to young users worldwide, rather than just in specific markets.
“Improvements to features that may encourage excessive use or addiction, such as algorithm-based content recommendations, disclosure of engagement metrics such as ‘likes,’ and push notifications designed to encourage users to log in, would ideally be applied to youth users worldwide,” it said.
Malaysia, which has barred those younger than 16 from registering accounts on social media platforms, welcomed the US settlement, calling it “a positive sign that social media platforms must be held accountable for what takes place on their platforms.”
European Commission spokesman Thomas Regnier told reporters that the EU — which last month ordered Meta to make its platforms safer for children or face heavy fines — has had new “exchanges” with the firm since the US settlement.
“The ball is in Meta’s court,” Regnier said. “Meta knows what we are expecting from them. Now it is for the company to offer these commitments in the European Union to protect our kids here too.”
However, enforcement of similar restrictions in Australia has been patchy so far.
Early evidence suggests the law has been undermined by weak age-verification systems, with multiple studies, including from Australia’s Internet regulator, showing that 80 percent of minors were still on social media months after the ban took effect in December last year. That prompted lawmakers to double the maximum fine and increase regulatory powers.

“I also call on Meta to immediately introduce effective tools to eliminate scams, false advertising and the promotion of illegal applications,” Gawkowski wrote on X.
