World’s soils deteriorating: UN report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:21 UTC
01:43:21 KST

More than half of the world’s soils are in poor condition, threatening global food supplies and biodiversity, while proven measures to improve soil health are not being implemented, a UN report released yesterday said.
“Globally, we must shift from a mindset of soil exploitation to one of soil stewardship,” the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said.
Soils “support 95 percent of our food production, host 59 percent of global biodiversity and serve as the planet’s second-largest carbon sink after the oceans,” the report’s authors said.
Photo: AFP
Yet “soil degradation continues to accelerate at an alarming rate.”
The report found that in 52.5 percent of regions and subregions soil management was poor or very poor. In one-third, it was fair, while in only 14 percent was it good or very good.
It is the second major report by the FAO, after a pioneering effort in 2015, assessing soil health across the planet. The first study found that most of the world’s soils were in fair, poor or very poor condition.
Since then, the world’s population has grown by 800 million people, while 80 million hectares of additional land, nearly the combined area of France and Germany, had been turned over to major crops, the FAO said.
By far the greatest threat to soil is from erosion, the experts said, with soil washed or blown away because of unsustainable practices.
Other threats include loss of the organic matter in soil (known as soil organic carbon), nutrient mismanagement, depleted soil biodiversity, salt buildup, pollution and urban expansion. Climate change threatens to make most of the problems worse, while soil degradation itself can contribute to climate change.
Improving soil health could also improve resilience and help fight global warming.
The authors said that most techniques for protecting and restoring soils were already well known before 2015, but they were still not being widely implemented.
Soil management improved in just 10 percent of assessed areas and deteriorating in 58 percent of them, they said.
One major technique for reducing soil degradation is reducing or abandoning tillage, such as ploughing. While as old as agriculture itself, tillage destroys organic life in the soil and, by breaking it up, leaves it prone to erosion.
Other methods for protecting and improving soil include planting cover crops, such as legumes and brassicas.
They are grown on fallow fields to lock soils in place and improve their nutrient content, and agroforestry, in which trees are integrated into farming practices.
Better use of natural and artificial fertilizers, which can themselves be a source of pollution, is also a key strategy.
The FAO said it was not a lack of knowledge, but limited access to resources and high upfront costs that were preventing farmers from implementing better soil management and called for greater financial incentives, more localized data and the use of indigenous knowledge, among other suggestions.
The report was published with diplomats and experts from around the world gathered for the COP17 summit on desertification in the Mongolian capital of Ulaanbaatar, where they hoped to agree a global deal to combat drought. COP16, held in Riyadh two years ago, failed to reach an agreement.

Nvidia Corp on Wednesday gave a bullish sales outlook for fiscal 2028, easing concerns that artificial intelligence (AI) spending is poised to lose momentum.
“We expect to grow revenue by approximately 70 percent in fiscal 2028,” Nvidia chief financial officer Colette Kress said during a post-earnings conference call.
Analysts have projected a rise of about 45 percent for that year, data compiled by Bloomberg showed.
Photo: Reuters
Moreover, Nvidia would be growing even faster if it had access to more supplies, Kress said.
“Incredibly, we are seeing demand acceleration even at our scale,” she said. “Customers’ forecasts point to our growth doubling next year.”
The upbeat outlook offered relief to investors concerned about a bubble in the AI economy.
In Nvidia’s second-quarter earnings report, chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) said demand is only accelerating.
He also touted the rollout of the company’s latest chip line, Vera Rubin.
“The AI infrastructure build-out is at full steam,” he said. “Vera Rubin, now in full production, was built to power exactly this moment.”
Revenue this quarter is expected to be US$108 billion, plus or minus 2 percent, the company said.
Analysts had estimated US$105.2 billion on average.
Gross margin would be about 74 percent in the quarter, the firm said.
The company warned that margins would narrow in the coming months while Nvidia copes with a surge in memory costs.
It expects the measure to bottom out in the fiscal fourth quarter — a period that runs through January next year — at 71 to 72 percent.
As Nvidia increases its own prices, the range should settle down to 72 to 73 percent in fiscal 2028, Kress said.
The broader message was that there has been no letup in demand from customers.
After years of runaway growth, some investors had become concerned about a potential bubble. Nvidia’s myriad investment pacts with companies in the AI economy also sparked fears that circular deals would leave the industry on shakier ground.
“We would love more supply,” Kress said in an interview. “It’s really about how much more could you do?”
In the second quarter, which ended on July 26, sales more than doubled from a year earlier to US$96.2 billion.
Profit was US$2.22 per share, excluding some items.
Analysts had projected revenue of US$92.5 billion and earnings per share of US$2.09.
Nvidia’s all-important data center division had revenue of US$89 billion, compared with an average estimate of US$85.8 billion.
A group known as hyperscalers, which includes Amazon.com Inc and Alphabet Inc’s Google, accounted for much of those sales.
Nvidia has spent much of the past year lining up investment deals with major AI companies, including developers of software and the infrastructure that supports it.
Those agreements — and the promised financial backing — have, in theory, put Nvidia on the hook for tens of billions of dollars of liabilities.
The company has said such deals would accelerate the adoption of AI, something that would create even more demand for its products.
However, critics have voiced concern that circular financing would foster artificial demand.
Kress described the deals as a part of Nvidia’s efforts to increase supply.
The biggest portion of its spending commitments took the form of long-term purchase agreements with vendors, she said.
“The majority of what we have been helping folks with in terms of commitments is one very important thing called supply,” Kress said.

Wait. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s war chief, holding a puppy?
Yes, and it’s no accident. In a collision of dog lovers, sports and ongoing war with Russia, the Ukrainian president was seen on video Tuesday as never before — cuddling and cooing over a floppy, 3-month-old American pit bull terrier, handed to him by US former boxer Terence Crawford.
The cute and fluffy scene in Zelenskyy’s office in Kyiv was the latest volley in a deadly serious battle of visuals that runs in parallel to Ukraine’s fight against Russia’s brutal four-year invasion.
Photo: Ukrainian Presidential Press Office via AP
Crawford, a longtime supporter of Ukraine and a devotee of the American pit bull terrier, came forward and handed a reddish-yellow puppy to Zelenskyy.
And for a few minutes in Kyiv, cultures, death and geopolitics yielded to the power of sweetness and puppy love, as well as the symbolism of resilience and protection.
SERIOUS BACKDROP
It’s a truism of the political world: If you want a friend, get a dog. Zelenskyy, weighed down by war and scandal, seemed to have found both in the light-eyed puppy that melted into his chest.
The president smiled and cooed something into the dog’s fur. He cradled her as he was told the pup’s name is Freya — after Zelenskyy’s pet project, Freyja, Ukraine’s proposed missile defense system with European allies.
He was further informed that Freya’s grandfather survived the devastating Russian siege of Bucha in 2022. Zelenskyy cuddled the pup close as they posed for photos. She appeared to relax, letting two white-tipped paws dangle from Zelenskyy’s arms.
“The president said he would accept” Freya, said Vadym Danylchenko, adviser to the minister of youth and sports in Ukraine, who helped organize the visit.
Politically and culturally, it might have been problematic to refuse. Animals have become a symbol of the nation’s forbearance during the four-year war. One mural in a Kyiv park immortalizes a Jack Russell terrier named Patrone who is renowned for assisting mine-clearing teams in the northern Chernihiv district and became a mascot for Ukraine’s emergency services. Zelenskyy awarded him a state medal. UNICEF recognized the pup as the first “Goodwill AmbassaDOG.”
Another mural depicts volunteer fighter Oleksii Movchan, holding a gray-and-white cat. He and three fellow soldiers rescued 11 civilians and the cat in the eastern Donetsk region shortly before being killed by Russian shelling in 2022.
Stories abound of others going to great lengths to rescue Ukraine’s animals during the Russian invasion, including one Ukrainian woman who worked to save hundreds from the war by shipping some to safer western Ukraine and others overseas.
THE POLITICS OF NATIONS
Then there’s the fraught matter of American support for Ukraine. Zelenskyy was famously dressed down by US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance last year in the Oval Office, though the leaders have appeared to have mended fences since then. But in Zelenskyy’s office on Tuesday, an American sports hero was handing him an American dog breed. Zelenskyy embraced the love.
Freya is the granddaughter of Athos — a dog who survived the Russian brutality in Bucha and was found on the street where Ukrainian forces destroyed a large Russian convoy, Danylchenko said.
Through rescuers, Athos made his way to Crawford’s friend Francisco Lopez, a professional breeder and longtime Ukraine supporter in America. Athos’ daughter had been left behind in Ukraine. Lopez flew an unrelated male dog to Ukraine to mate with Athos’ daughter. She gave birth to Freya.
The puppy’s name has a particular resonance in Ukraine. European nations are developing the antiballistic missile defense system with Ukraine amid shortages, particularly of American-made Patriot interceptors. Patriot interceptors are in shorter supply as the US and Israeli war against Iran continues to rage, and Trump last month appeared to back away from a recent commitment to give Ukraine a license to produce them.
“Terence really wanted to give the president this particular female puppy,” said Danylchenko, who said he wasn’t initially supportive of giving the president a gift laden with such responsibility.
“They named her Freya. Obviously, from the perspective of our country’s future, this was important,” he added. “This little girl is a symbol of the fact that her grandfather survived and was a direct witness to the events in Bucha. So it was very symbolic for them.”

Visiting a hilltop creative sanctuary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:04 UTC
01:43:04 KST

From Banqiao city center, the 30-minute cab ride south runs parallel to the Tamsui River, past the Bitan Suspension Bridge before gradually pivoting and winding southeast.
The road snakes steeply upwards along Zhangchun Rd and into Meitan Village (美潭里) located in the hills of Xindian District (新店區), New Taipei City.
Of course one can’t help but think: Why here? Why is this isolated and neglected site suitable for Tsai Ming-liang (蔡明亮), one of Asian cinema’s great directors, to open an art center?
Photo: Shane O’Reilly
As it turns out, both Tsai and his longtime collaborator, actor Lee Kang-sheng (李康生), retreated to this region for health reasons around 2014, finding refuge and respite in a quieter, more natural setting.
Barring the inhabited homes on either side, the atelier is centrally located within a row of dilapidated buildings, ruins really, their hollowed-out shells stained and crawling with vegetation.
The location is strangely evocative, even eerie, and complements the sheer, brutalist aesthetic of the Tsai Ming Liang Art Space (蔡明亮藝術空間), all sharp angles and straight lines.
It’s easy to draw parallels between Tsai’s cinematic style, often referred to as “Slow Cinema”, and this laid-back environment that perhaps encapsulates or even mirrors his creative pace.
Upon entering, you’re immediately greeted with a coffee shop counter and a handwritten chalkboard menu of beverage options. There’s also an ever-changing menu of Nanyang-style small plates cooked by Tsai himself.
Behind the coffee station, sturdy shelving supports all of Tsai’s awards, including those both he and Lee won in 2013 for Stray Dogs (郊遊).
Speaking of Lee, the two have known each other since 1989 when Tsai gave him a small role in the made-for-TV film All the Corners of the World (海角天涯).
They remain one of cinema’s great enduring partnerships and are now co-owners of this artistic hilltop endeavor.
A compact staircase leads to a second-floor lounge, flooded with light from a bank of windows overlooking various nooks and crannies, accompanied by an assortment of vintage stools and sofa seats.
The sparse walls are pockmarked with rows of circular holes, remnants of the tools that held the original framework as the concrete was poured, which add a simple but fun contemporary pattern to the surroundings.
Otherwise, the only decoration, beyond the fixed track lighting above, is Tsai’s framed oil paintings, mostly large vertical portraits, a therapeutic hobby of his developed during the COVID pandemic.
People are peppered throughout, murmuring softly. Many are reclining with coffee in hand, relaxing or flicking through one of the many art books strategically placed always within arm’s reach.
At a large mahogany desk, someone is quietly tapping away on a laptop. Nearby are tasteful, handcrafted side tables whittled from old tree trunks alongside neatly arranged stacks of large film reel canisters.
An Escher-esque circular route leads downward to connecting gallery rooms or around to an entranceway into the cozy comforts of a 12-seat cinema projecting Tsai’s short films on loop.
A third level reveals glossy-tiled flooring and several interconnected rooms of merchandise, miscellaneous items and a broad selection of large-format movie posters for sale.
Visitors might be surprised to see Tsai himself pottering around, a cheerful, unassuming presence and personification of this isolated hub miles away from the hurried traffic and oven humidity of the city center.
From a seat in an alcove by the wall of windows, watch the outside world of wild, untethered verdancy, with the shadowy blues and neon greens of Tsai Ming-liang’s cinematic universe behind.

Five companies, seven people suspected of illegal waste disposal in Kaohsiung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:03 UTC
01:43:03 KST

Five companies and seven people suspected of illegal dumping have been indicted, with more than 1,700m3 of business waste found at illegal disposal sites in Kaohsiung, the Environmental Management Administration said yesterday.
The agency identified a case of illegal cross-regional waste transportation and disposal in cooperation with the Kaohsiung District Prosecutors’ Office, the National Police Agency’s Seventh Special Police Corps and the Investigation Bureau’s Kaohsiung Office.
The prosecutors’ office filed an indictment last month, the agency said.
Photo courtesy of authorities
In February last year, the Seventh Special Police Corps received a report from a member of the public that business waste was being transported from other administrative areas to unauthorized waste storage and transfer sites in Kaohsiung’s Siaogang District (小港), it said.
The waste was disguised as locally generated waste and transferred to incinerators in the city, the administration said.
A task force was set up to trace the flow of illegally disposed waste and launch a cross-regional investigation, it said.
Law enforcement personnel conducted 19 administrative inspections and constant monitoring, as well as using big-data analysis and field investigations to track waste-hauling vehicles and waste flows, the administration said.
They also cross-referenced waste manifests, operating records and vehicle GPS tracking data, it said.
The task force’s investigation showed that waste-removal company vehicles transported waste from northern and central Taiwan to unauthorized temporary waste storage sites in southern Taiwan, the administration said.
In January, the prosecutors’ office directed simultaneous searches in northern and southern Taiwan and conducted searches at the storage sites in the city’s Siaogang and Lujhu (路竹) districts, it said.
About 1,738m3 of business waste yet to be transferred to incinerators were found at these sites, the administration said.
The task force identified nine waste-removal companies allegedly involved in the illegal dumping operation in violation of articles of the Waste Disposal Act (廢棄物清理法), it said.
The companies are based in Changhua, Yunlin and Hualien counties, as well as Kaohsiung and New Taipei City, it said, adding that it has asked local governments to impose administrative penalties as required by law.
Operators allegedly involved in the case would also be under criminal investigation in accordance with the act’s articles, the agency said.
The prosecutors’ investigation concluded with an indictment brought against seven suspects, truck drivers and five companies suspected of involving in criminal violations, it said.
The agency called on waste-removal operators to accurately report waste flows and GPS tracking data and to refrain from establishing unauthorized waste disposal or transfer sites.
It also called on the public to call the 0800-066-666 public nuisance hotline to report any suspicious waste-hauling vehicles or suspected illegal dumping and storage of waste.

Traffic deaths declined in first six months: ministry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:03 UTC
01:43:03 KST

The number of people who died within 30 days after being in a traffic accident was 1,333 in the first six months of this year, down 15 percent from the same period in 2023 and the first time that the Ministry of Transportation and Communications met a target it set three years ago.
The enforcement plan of the Road Traffic Safety Basic Act (道路交通安全基本法), enacted in 2023, stipulates that the ministry should decrease traffic deaths by 5 percent every year.
“We are not happy with the results as we still have a long way to go before fulfilling the zero-death vision,” Department of Railways, Highways and Road Safety Director-General Wu Tung-ling (吳東凌) said.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Motorcycle-related fatalities decreased by 214 from the same period in 2023, a 21.4 percent decline, data collected by the ministry from January to June showed.
Deaths among elderly people fell by 30, or 4.8 percent, while pedestrian fatalities decreased by 16, or 9.2 percent, the data showed.
Deaths caused by drunk driving dropped by 77, or 58.8 percent, while fatalities involving children and teenagers declined by 28, or 59.6 percent, it showed.
The most significant decrease was in motorcycle-related deaths, which only recorded a single-digit percentage decline in the previous years, Wu said.
He attributed the decline to the public’s increasing road safety awareness, as well as the collective efforts of local and central governments.
Deputy Minister of Transportation and Communications Chen Yen-po (陳彥伯) said Taiwan has more than 14.9 million registered scooters nationwide, with each household having an average of about two scooters.
Motorcycles bring mobility and convenience, but motorcycle riders face a greater risk of being killed or sustaining injuries if they collide with other vehicles, he said.
Although there was a significant improvement in the number of motorcycle-related deaths, it nevertheless accounted for 58 percent of traffic fatalities in the first six months, Chen said.
More than 55 percent of those killed in motorcycle-related accidents were aged 55 or older, with nervousness and absent-mindedness as the main causes of deaths, Chen said, adding that 27 percent of motorcycle-related accidents occurred because of single-vehicle crashes.
“All these statistics show that speed control is a crucial factor in enhancing road safety,” he said.
The latest road safety campaign will focus on educating motorcycle riders about the importance of speed management, he added.
The ministry and Kaohsiung Medical University Chung-Ho Hospital also produced a video illustrating the impact of speed on the human body.
“Through the video, we hope to show motorcyclists that speed management does not mean that they only watch the operating speed on the dashboard. They need to be vigilant about road conditions and traffic, and adjust the gas and hit the brake accordingly,” Chen said.
Chen Chao-wen (陳昭文), director of the Department of Trauma and Critical Care Surgery at the hospital, said he has treated many patients with severe injuries following accidents.
“Data show that a collision at 30kph is roughly equivalent to falling from the height of a one-story building, while at 90kph, the impact is comparable to a vertical fall from a building more than 10 stories high. That split-second burst of acceleration can lead to torn internal organs, shattered bones and, all too often, irreversible tragedy,” he said.

Iran’s regime will fall through a mix of operations, economic pressure, and protests by its own people, recently retired Mossad chief David Barnea said in his first speech since stepping down on June 1.
In a speech to the Jerusalem Municipality, where he received an award on behalf of the Mossad, Barnea supported the Trump administration’s latest economic pressure moves against the Islamic Republic.
He said that it was clear these were needed, but that they would be insufficient alone and would require the use of force as well, although he did not specify whether that force would require another round of massive airstrikes or whether a covert sabotage campaign would be sufficient.
“The decision to place the most severe sanctions on Iran was a correct and praiseworthy decision. But the sanctions are just another stage. There will be no choice, in my view, other than to escalate the economic actions, the policies, and the operations against the regime until it falls, and it will fall,” said Barnea.
According to Barnea, US President Donald Trump and much of the world – regardless of their complaints about gas prices – now understand deeper than ever the multiheaded threat which Tehran presents to all of them: whether through nuclear weapons, ballistic missiles, or proxy terror.
Barnea: World knows Iran is not just Israel's problem since Operation Roaring Lion
“Until Operation Roaring Lion, we felt that Iran was a problem for the State of Israel. Today, the whole world knows clearly that the Iranian saga is not solely our problem,” said Barnea.
Regarding Hezbollah and Hamas, he said that both terror groups were far weaker than before October 7, 2023, leaving Israel militarily more secure than it was three years ago.
Specifically, with Hezbollah, he hinted that Mossad’s sleeper operations had harmed the terror group psychologically, while also giving credit to the IDF, which has carried out two massive invasions of Lebanon since 2024.
Addressing Hamas, he said that the organization is no longer anything close to resembling the national military that it constituted in 2023, when it had 24 highly organized and coordinated battalions.
Barnea did not comment on previous criticism of Netanyahu, Israel's diplomatic standing
Barnea did not address the low point Israel has hit on the diplomatic plane or criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, his and the Mossad’s plans to topple the regime in early 2026.
The former Mossad chief also called on Israel as a people to be more tolerant of one another and to be more patient with hearing out different views from different sides of society.
On August 3, it was announced that Barnea would join US-based defense company Ondas’ senior executive leadership team as its new global president and chairman, and support the company’s global expansion, strategic technology development, government and defense relationships, and the business and technological integration.
Ondas defines itself as “a leading provider of autonomous systems and next-generation defense and security technologies.”

Young Japanese break the rules by practicing ‘guilty consumption’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

If you sit down to eat in Japan these days, you might be faced with some interesting choices.
Would you like more cheese with that — perhaps a comically large amount? Or maybe a bowl of uber-fatty ramen, the one that is explicitly labeled as containing “extra lard?” If you cannot choose between two main dishes, why not have both!
It is part of a trend known as “guilty consumption,” as firms bet on calorie, fat and sugar-dense foods to attract consumers.
It is not that people are constantly stuffing their faces: It describes a deliberate indulgence, a controlled micro-splurge, the active decision to take those extra few hundred calories in the conscious knowledge that it is bad for you, but you deserve it.
The portions can be ludicrous and leave no room for subtlety, and they are designed to be displayed on Instagram. The trend is also sometimes referred to as “immoral foods,” with one estimate finding that the market has grown to surpass that of health foods and supplements.
The phrase has entered the zeitgeist since being adopted by Suntory Beverage & Food Ltd’s new cola Nope, which launched earlier this year with a massive marketing blitz and became the firm’s fastest-selling new release in years. While most soft drinks these days try to advertise their healthiness or at least play down how bad they might be for you, Nope actively revels in it, labeling itself “the guilty taste that keeps you coming back for more.” It is higher in calories than Coca-Cola, with vivid branding that intentionally plays up acts of rebellion — as if consuming calories when society wants you to be healthy is somehow fighting back against the system.
And its success, shipping 55 million bottles in 50 days, has others wondering how they can cash in on guilty consumption. A survey from market researcher Macromill Inc found that one in five people say they make such purchases weekly, with the main excuse being the need for a break.
Consciously or not, the language used for such justifications is the same Japanese word used for the Christian “letters of indulgence” sold in 16th-century Europe — which similarly sought to turn guilt into something that could be managed and justified with a transaction, a practice that helped lead to the Reformation. This is the key to understanding the trend: The idea of a treat is nothing new, but here is the admission that what you are doing is wrong — and a permission structure for a generation that counts calories and Japanese yen.
Younger Japanese are the first generation in decades to arrive in the workforce finding inflation in everything from daily food to housing costs. It is no surprise that they report having less money to spend on hobbies and fun, with those in their 20s saying that figure is down to an average of just ￥16,596 (US$104) per month, down 20 percent since 2022.
Like their peers elsewhere, many Japanese youth are also more disciplined: The number of 24-hour gyms soared during COVID-19, rising nearly five-fold last year compared to before the pandemic, and activities such as Hyrox, the intense and competitive indoor workout, are gaining in popularity.
The trend is even reflected in Japan’s closely watched consumer price index basket. For the first time, this year it added protein powder, displacing aojiru, a once-notoriously bitter-tasting vegetable drink favored by older generations.
There is even a nascent cola war, as Asahi Group Holdings Ltd takes the other side of the bet to Suntory. It has launched its version of the Greek-developed Green Cola, with the slogan “No sugar, no calories, no guilt.” Which drink wins out might give insight into where shoppers are going; my money is on the one that explicitly feels like a little wrongdoing.
It is not just that every age group needs to blow off some steam. The form vice takes is changing: Younger Japanese are less interested in traditional habits such as smoking and drinking, meaning wrongdoing must be repackaged into smaller, cheaper and more controllable doses. The key to guilty consumption is to make what is, in fact, a modest expenditure feel extravagant.
There is money to be had in selling the right to break the rules, if only just briefly. In an age of portion control and tight budgets, a little excess goes a long way.
Gearoid Reidy is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering Japan and the Koreas. He previously led the breaking news team in North Asia, and was the Tokyo deputy bureau chief. The importance of a name change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

In the rush to summer vacation, some readers might have missed the launch of the renamed Diet members group supporting Taiwan. Indeed, the decision by Japan’s largest pro-Taiwan parliamentary organization to rename itself received only modest media attention. Yet historians might eventually view it as one of the most revealing symbolic acts in the evolution of post-World War II Taiwan-Japan relations.
For the longest time, the group, founded in 1973, was called the Nikka Giin Kondankai (Japan-ROC Diet Members’ Consultative Council). However, after more than five decades, the organization on June 11 adopted a new name — the Japan-Taiwan Diet Members’ Consultative Council, or Nihon Taiwan Yuko Giin Renmei.
The change replaced the term nikka (Japan-ROC) with nittai (Japan-Taiwan) and, in doing so, it acknowledged a political reality that had been developing for decades. The organization was no longer defining itself through the language of the Republic of China (ROC). It was viewing its role through Taiwan itself.
The change was announced at a general meeting and reception at the Imperial Hotel under the leadership of Chairman Furuya Keiji, who was one of the key endorsers of Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae as a candidate for the party presidency.
Both are known as strong supporters of Taiwan and share the view of the late Japanese prime minister Shinzo Abe that Taiwan’s security is Japan’s security. Furuya is seen as the elder brother of Takaichi, and his relationship with the Abe family goes back to the time when he served as a secretary to Abe’s father, Shintaro Abe, who was also strongly pro-Taiwan.
At first glance, this might seem like a minor semantic adjustment. It was anything but. The story begins in 1972, when then-Japanese prime minister Tanaka Kakuei normalized relations with the People’s Republic of China (PRC). In exchange for diplomatic recognition of Beijing, Japan terminated formal diplomatic relations with the ROC.
The diplomatic rupture raised an immediate question: What would happen to the extensive political, economic and personal networks that had connected Taiwan and Japan since the 1950s?
On March 14, 1973, six months after diplomatic relations ended, pro-Taiwan members of the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) established the Nikkakon. The organization was led by Nadao Hirokichi, one of post-WWII Japan’s most influential conservative politicians. The organization initially attracted 152 Diet members, comprising 99 members of the House of Representatives and 53 members of the House of Councilors.
This was much more than a friendship society. The organization became a vital, alternative diplomatic channel.
Japanese parliamentarians visited Taiwan, maintained personal relationships with political leaders, facilitated exchanges, promoted economic cooperation and ensured that communication continued despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations.
Parliamentary diplomacy filled a vacuum that traditional diplomacy could no longer occupy and still does today.
The organization itself evolved as Japanese politics changed. The fragmentation of the LDP during the 1990s led to the creation of a separate pro-Taiwan group within the New Frontier Party, itself mostly born from those who had left the LDP. In February 1997, the two organizations merged to form the modern, bipartisan Nikkakon. This transformation was significant, because support for Taiwan was no longer confined to one faction within one political party. It had become a broader parliamentary movement.
Membership eventually grew to more than 300 legislators, making it the largest parliamentary friendship organization in Japan. Yet the most fascinating aspect of this history might be the changing meaning of a single character.
The term 華 (ka) in 日華 (nikka) reflected the political vocabulary of the Cold War. It referred to the ROC, the government that had retreated to Taiwan after militarily losing the Chinese Civil War. In the 1950s and 1960s, that terminology made perfect sense. The ROC officially claimed to represent all of China, and many of its supporters in Japan continued to think in those terms.
However, Taiwan changed. Martial law ended in 1987. Opposition parties became legal. Democratic reforms accelerated. Direct presidential elections began in 1996. Peaceful transfers of power became routine. Taiwan gradually transformed itself from an authoritarian government-in-exile into one of Asia’s most vibrant democracies.
Japan also changed. A younger generation of Japanese politicians had no memory of the Chinese Civil War. For them, Taiwan was not an unresolved question of Chinese representation. It was a democratic partner, an economic partner and, increasingly, a strategic partner.
Security considerations accelerated this transition. The PRC becoming a hegemon and rejecting a peaceful solution to issues in the Taiwan Strait and the region has led Japan and the world to reevaluate their relations with China and Taiwan.
Taiwan sits less than 100km from Japan’s westernmost islands. The security of Taiwan and the security of Japan can no longer be viewed as separate issues. Japanese policymakers increasingly recognize that any crisis in the Taiwan Strait would have direct implications for Japan’s territorial defense, sea lanes, supply chains and alliance obligations with the US.
Economic realities have further reinforced the trend. Semiconductors, advanced manufacturing, tourism, trade, disaster relief, education, local government exchanges and civil society cooperation have all deepened the relationship between Taiwan and Japan.
The most recent name change therefore represents more than a rebranding exercise. It acknowledged that the historical framework established in 1973 no longer accurately described the relationship.
For more than half a century, that parliamentary organization helped preserve and deepen one of East Asia’s most unusual international relationships. Taiwan and Japan built an extraordinarily close partnership despite the absence of formal diplomatic relations. The organization’s new name recognizes a simple truth.
Importantly, the general meeting in June was extremely well attended, and included a video message from President William Lai (賴清德), greetings from Representative to Japan Lee Yi-yang (李逸洋), as well as speeches and remarks from other participants.
The parliamentary league has also decided to launch nine project teams, three of which are new, including disaster resilience, economic exchange and contents cooperation. If the past 50 years has been any indication, the future of Taiwan-Japan relations appears to be very bright.

The government would consider raising its average annual electricity demand growth forecast through 2035 above the 2.5 percent it projected in June based on a high-demand scenario, Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin (龔明鑫) said yesterday.

Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
The government initially projected average annual electricity demand growth of 1.7 percent from last year to 2034, before raising the forecast in June to 2.5 percent from this year through 2035.
Power demand forecasts take into account economic growth, actual electricity consumption and energy-saving efforts according to demand scenarios, Kung said.
Ensuring stable power supply remains Taiwan Power Co’s (Taipower, 台電) top priority, he said.
On Taipower’s recent proposals to supply electricity to large AI data centers through direct lines, Kung said the key is data center site selection and local grid conditions.
North of Hsinchu, grid conditions are tight and new large-scale AI data centers could face restrictions and require assessments, while central and southern Taiwan are less likely to face those constraints, he said.

The fire resulted from an equipment malfunction, but the exact cause remains under investigation, he said.

Photo: Huang Shu-li, Taipei Times
The conditions showed that China was not allowing the produce to enter based on science-based inspections, but was instead using the issue to highlight the “magnanimity” of the Chinese government as the Mid-Autumn Festival approaches, the MAC said.
Cross-strait produce trade remains highly unstable and could be unilaterally cut off by Beijing at any time, the MAC said.

China deploys record number of ships near Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:42:55 UTC
01:42:55 KST

China deployed a record number of coast guard, scientific research and other ships near Taiwan’s waters last month, the Coast Guard Administration (CGA) said, as Beijing dials up pressure on Taipei.
The coast guard warned of an increasingly severe situation, as analysts say the increased activity is part of China’s bid to map the region for submarine warfare.
The number of Chinese ships detected around Taiwan proper soared to a record 244 last month — an average of nearly eight every day, official data showed.
Photo: Coast Guard Administration via AFP
That compares with 55 ships detected in June and 30 in May, and 58 in July last year.
In the first 21 days of this month, 152 vessels were detected.
About 60 percent were coast guard ships, with research vessels and other government boats making up the rest.
The figures do not include Chinese warships, which China’s military deploys around Taiwan on a near-daily basis.
China has long dispatched coast guard and research ships around the Asia-Pacific region, particularly in the hotly contested South China Sea.
China uses the ships to assert authority over the waters, government officials and analysts say, describing them as “gray zone” tactics: actions that fall short of an act of war.
The number of Chinese ships detected around Taiwan and several of its outlying islands since May is 1,247, CGA figures showed.
“When we say the situation is becoming increasingly severe, we mean that the number of their government vessels in the waters surrounding Taiwan has increased, and there was a marked increase in July,” a senior CGA official said, speaking on the condition of anonymity as they were not authorized to speak to the media.
The Chinese Communist Party “has never ruled Taiwan for even a single day” and “without sovereignty over land, it has no right to claim economic zones at sea,” the official said.
While Taiwan faces the constant threat of a Chinese invasion, China’s increasing maritime presence has also fueled concerns about a potential quarantine or blockade to prevent ships carrying energy or other critical supplies from entering or leaving its ports.
China operates more than “120 oceanographic research vessels,” the CGA said previously.
The CGA is tracking about 41 ships that operate in Taiwan’s waters.
They include the Tong Ji (同濟號), which circled Taiwan in May, tracking the edge of Taiwan proper’s restricted waters and refusing the CGA’s orders to leave.
Its activities likely involved “oceanographic sampling and seabed survey operations,” which could contribute to China’s “antisubmarine warfare databases,” the CGA said.
That was followed in June by China’s first law enforcement patrol in waters east of Taiwan.
Earlier this month, China also announced “traffic control measures” for the Taiwan Strait as Typhoon Dolphin swept toward the region.
Ryan Martinson, an expert on China’s maritime strategy at the US Naval War College, said Chinese research ships are owned and operated by civilian research institutes, but the data collected are shared with the military.
“That kind of data/knowledge is highly useful for Chinese naval forces, which will operate in these waters in the event of a conflict,” Martinson said in an e-mail, noting that he was speaking in a personal capacity. “It is especially important for anti-submarine warfare and submarine warfare.”
In the past couple of months, Martinson said he had observed a “very large increase” in the number of Chinese research vessels operating around Taiwan, especially to the east of Taiwan proper.
“This is not a new ‘play’ in its ‘playbook.’ Rather, the novel aspect is that the scale of these operations around Taiwan is unprecedented,” he said.
Chinese research vessels have been seen “operating in conjunction” with China Coast Guard ships around Taiwan, the CGA official said.
This month, China’s Xiang Yang Hong 03 (向陽紅33) research vessel was observed operating within Taiwan and Japan’s exclusive economic zones, moving over deep sea trenches and telecoms cables, said Jason Wang (王柏仁), chief operating officer of ingeniSPACE, which analyzes satellite imagery and ship signals data.
The research vessel was escorted by a China Coast Guard vessel and a fishing boat that is part of China’s maritime militia, Wang said.
“This is the first time we have seen maritime militia escort a research vessel in Taiwan’s waters,” he said.
China’s objective was to gather “fresh hydrographic data of the Ryukyu Trench and East Taiwan Trench to conduct anti-submarine warfare” and “deny US and other allied vessels from doing the same,” Wang said.
“All of these developments are connected, I believe,” Martinson said. “They represent a clear escalation in Beijing’s efforts to exercise jurisdiction over the waters surrounding Taiwan, putting pressure on the country’s leadership and undermining its sovereignty and sovereign rights.”

Tim Curry, the English actor best known for his star turn as Dr Frank-N-Furter in the cult classic musical film The Rocky Horror Picture Show, has died at the age of 80, media reported on Wednesday. Curry, who had struggled with his health for more than a decade after a debilitating stroke, died at his home in Los Angeles, TMZ said, citing unnamed sources. The actor, who launched his career in London’s West End theater district, first played the gender-bending mad scientist in Rocky Horror before reprising the role in the 1975 film, which is still a staple of midnight cinema showings more than 50 years later. Former prime minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob was yesterday charged with failing to declare his assets, making him the nation’s third leader to face criminal charges after leaving office. The charge sheet lists large amounts of cash in Malaysian and foreign currencies, as well as gold and silver. If convicted, he faces up to five years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to 100,000 ringgit (US$24,795).

Animal cafes investigated
The government plans to probe popular animal cafes, where visitors can interact with anything from cats to capybaras, following concerns about hygiene and the creatures’ welfare, authorities said yesterday. The nation has hundreds of the cafes where campaigners say animals are sometimes kept in cramped spaces, and that their popularity encourages the capture and illegal trade of rare wildlife. A fact-finding survey is to begin as early as next month to determine the number of establishments and what animals they keep, a Ministry of the Environment official said. The ministry would examine whether they comply with laws, including whether animals have enough space and how often cleaning takes place, said the official, who asked not to be named. “We may then do on-site inspections if we find facilities that appear to be breaching rules” stipulated by the animal welfare law, he said. The decision to launch the survey followed recommendations by members of an expert panel about animal welfare.

Now they look like a million dollars.
Photo: EPA
Muchova and Mensik won the title on Wednesday in their first time playing together, beating Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli 6-3, 1-6 (10-6).
The Czech duo, wearing the same pink tops and maroon bottoms that they decided to wear on Monday, pulled out match tiebreakers in both matches on the second night of the two-day event, fueled by Mensik’s powerful serve combined with some good hands near the net.
He put away the final with an ace to earn US$1 million for him and Muchova to share.
Photo: AP
“I think at the end, really the matching outfit made the difference for us,” Muchova said.
They were a point from losing in the semi-finals, erasing two match points and running off the final four to edge Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev 5-4 (8/6), 3-5 (11-9).
Quite a performance, considering that Mensik said he had never played in a mixed doubles event.
“My first mixed doubles, 100 percent win rate,” he said.
Bencic and Cobolli rallied to end the run of spouses Elina Svitolina and Gael Monfils in the first semi-final with a 4-5 (9/7), 4-1 (10-5) victory.
They appeared headed toward a matchup with Andreeva and Rublev, who were smiling and pumping their fists after opening the lead in the match tiebreaker. Muchova flung her racket to the court in disgust after missing a volley that gave the Russians a 7-5 lead.
However, the Wimbledon women’s runner-up never lost belief, thanks in part to her hard-serving partner, who turns 21 next week.
When Mensik first asked Muchova to play, she told him to improve his ranking. When the US Open mixed doubles tournament was revamped last year, the ability to directly qualify was based on the combined singles rankings of the two players.
Mensik did his part by reaching the semi-finals of the French Open.
“I put a little pressure on him, but in a fun way. It worked,” Muchova said. “I’m happy we managed and we got in, that we are here now.”
The final was the only match of the tournament that resembled a regular match, with standard sets to six games and a tiebreaker at 6-all. Through the first three rounds, sets were to four games, with a tiebreaker at 4-all.
Bencic and Cobolli knocked Serena Williams and Carlos Alcaraz out of the tournament on Tuesday in the quarter-finals.
Then they dropped a set for the first time in the tournament in the semis, but began to dominate midway through the second set, winning the final 11 points to force the match tiebreaker.
However, they could not win their second one in the final.
“This year is already the second final. I never expected in my life to play a Grand Slam,” said Cobolli, this year’s French Open runner-up. “This is mixed, but still something that you never forget.”
The biggest challenge for the winners might have been the outfit selection. Mensik apparently was not familiar with the word “maroon.”
Now he knows and loves it.
“My favorite color right now is pink and maroon, that’s for sure,” he said.
It was the second year of the new format in mixed doubles, with the event shortened and moved to the week before the singles main draw begins, with the US Tennis Association hoping that would get top singles players to compete.
Plenty of top names did compete, but much of the star power, including Williams and Alcaraz, went out early. Aryna Sabalenka and Novak Djokovic lost their opening match, as did Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime, and Jessica Pegula and Taylor Fritz.

The 41-year-old from Switzerland is no longer ranked high enough to qualify directly for the tournament and it appeared his chances of playing were over when the US Tennis Association awarded its last wild-card spot to Patrick Kypson, an American who is ranked No. 115.
However, the association said that Kypson had withdrawn with an injury and it gave his place to Wawrinka.
“I’m incredibly excited to accept the wild card for the 2026 US Open and look forward to competing in front of the fans in New York once again,” Wawrinka said in a statement.

Japan’s ‘polka dot queen’ Yayoi Kusama aged 97
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:42:53 UTC
01:42:53 KST

Japan’s Yayoi Kusama, one of the world’s most celebrated contemporary artists, has died aged 97, her company said yesterday, triggering tributes from around the world.
The “polka dot queen” channeled hallucinations and battles with mental health into vibrant art featuring her trademark dots, nets and infinity motifs over a career spanning decades and continents.
“Throughout an extraordinary lifetime devoted entirely to artistic creation, Kusama pursued an internationally acclaimed career as a pioneering avant-garde artist whose creative practice encompassed visual art, performance, fiction and poetry,” a statement said, announcing her death on Aug. 14.
Photo: Reuters
“She continued to paint until her final days, never setting aside her brush, and continued exploration of forever love and eternal soul,” it added.
Born in 1929 to a wealthy and conservative family, Kusama began producing her unique signature art aged 10.
“One day, after seeing a tablecloth with a red flower pattern on a desk, I saw the same red flower pattern all over the ceiling, windows and pillars. It filled the room and covered my body,” she wrote in her autobiography.
After studying art in Japan, Kusama moved to the US in the late 1950s, and — helped by Georgia O’Keeffe — made a splash in New York’s avant-garde scene.
Despite facing discrimination as a Japanese woman, she won fame for bold, big paintings and provocative 1960s “happenings” featuring body painting and polka dots.
She also launched a fashion line, established a “Church of Self-Obliteration” and styled herself the “High Priestess of Polka Dots” to officiate at a gay wedding.
Returning to Japan in the 1970s, Kusama checked herself into a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo, where she lived — and worked — for the rest of her life.
Instantly recognizable in her bright red wig and bold spotted outfits, her fame enjoyed a renaissance from the 1980s.
Her infinity rooms, pumpkin sculptures — including one on Japan’s “art island” Naoshima — and immersive installations still attract crowds and have sold for millions of dollars.
“It’s a great quality to be weird and to express yourself no matter what,” said Velislava Nuneva, a 21-year-old college student from Bulgaria.
Outside the Yayoi Kusama Museum in Tokyo, Nuneva said she was inspired by how the artist succeeded in the male-dominated art world of New York.
Yasuko Minami, 58, called Kusama “someone who projected her inner soul in her works like an explosion.”
“She expressed herself honestly,” Minami said.
Students Hibiki Karasawa, 20, and Hinata Sakamoto, 19, have visited Naoshima Island and seen Kusama’s yellow polka-dot pumpkin in its setting by the sea.
“I feel her work was something that even those who may not be familiar with art can appreciate, with the vibrant designs and bold use of color, or turning something like a pumpkin into a work of art,” Karasawa said. “She conveyed her world view in a very unique way.”
“I love the way she uses colors,” Sakamoto said. “Vivid yellow and red. You see it and immediately you know it’s Kusama san’s work.”

Underground Tainan Railway Station could open by mid-October, bureau says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:42:53 UTC
01:42:53 KST

The new underground Tainan Railway Station could be operational by mid-October if it passes inspection next month, the Railway Bureau said yesterday.
The project has finished a series of key preparations and entered its final stage, bureau Director-General Yang Chen-chun (楊正君) said.
The station passed its accessibility inspection last month and its fire safety inspection this month, and has obtained the required completion certification for special-purpose buildings, he said.
Photo: Wu Liang-yi, Taipei Times
Integrated testing and trial operations along the entire line have also been completed, he added.
The Ministry of Transportation and Communications is expected to conduct a final inspection next month, he said, adding that it could be opened as early as mid-October.
The Railway Bureau’s Southern Region Engineering Branch said the Tainan Urban District Railway Underground Project spans 8.23km.
In addition to converting Tainan Station into an underground facility, the project adds two new underground commuter stations: Linsen (林森) and South Tainan (南臺南).
Once the project is completed, it is expected to eliminate nine railroad crossings, eight underpasses, four overpasses and two railway bridge crossings, removing 23 railway-road intersections and reducing the barrier posed by the railway to urban traffic and space, the office said.
To maintain railway operations during construction, the project is being carried out in two phases.
After the first phase, the ground-level railway tracks would be dismantled, followed by the second phase of construction and landscaping work at ground level, the office said.
Linsen Station is scheduled to open in 2029, followed by South Tainan Station in 2030, it added.
The main station’s signage and wayfinding system would be available in four languages — Chinese, English, Japanese and Korean — the first railway station in Taiwan to have this feature.
About 85 percent of the rail materials used in the project are domestically produced, the office said.
The station would feature a third-rail power supply, a ballastless track and high-performance vibration-isolation materials to improve ride stability and comfort, it said.
The tunnels would have a centralized control and ventilation system to provide real-time monitoring of passenger traffic and equipment operations, the office said.
A Taiwan Railway boxed lunch shop and convenience stores would also be opened at the Tainan Railway Station when it begins operations, it added.
Yang said Tainan Station is a heritage station that carries a century of railway history, and the underground railway project has managed to preserve the historic station during the new construction.
The project would create a new gateway to the city that combines cultural heritage with modern convenience, he said.

How a Chinese film shot in dialect is finding a global audience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

The buzziest film in China this year was shot almost entirely in a southern Chinese dialect that most Chinese viewers need subtitles to understand.
Yet Dear You has become China’s second-highest-grossing film of the year. Now it is heading overseas, part of a broader wave of Chinese cultural exports.
Dear You was shot mostly in Teochew, a dialect spoken in Guangdong’s Shantou region. Set among the Teochew immigrant community in Bangkok, it tells the story of people who left China in search of work to support their families. Made on a low budget, it features a cast of mostly unknown actors.
Photo: AP
The film provides a glimpse into the centuries-long history of Chinese migration to Southeast Asia. It has succeeded in making this little-discussed history visible to a wider audience, threading the fine needle of passing official censorship requirements, experts say, while telling a compelling story.
As of this month, the movie had grossed about 269 million yuan (US$40 million) at the Chinese box office. It was released in Thailand early this month after being shown in Singapore, Malaysia and Australia. It will be released in the US next month.
SOFT POWER
The film’s popularity comes as Chinese culture and consumer brands have been gaining global cachet — from collectible Labubu dolls to “Chinamaxxing,” a social media trend of embracing aspects of the Chinese lifestyle.
The Chinese government began promoting the film as it became a hit and prepared for its international release.
The Chinese consul in Sydney said at a June screening of the film that it “reflects the Chinese nation’s virtues of diligence, kindness, courage and unity.”
The movie aligns with Beijing’s broader goal of “telling China’s stories well,” highlighting themes of friendship, tradition and family, including motherhood and kinship, said Belinda He, an assistant professor of East Asian cinema and media studies at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.
China’s ambassador to Thailand presented the film at a special screening in July and again at a red carpet event this month.
“We’re grateful to Guangdong for making such a wonderful film,” Chinese ambassador Zhang Jianwei (張建衛) said at the red carpet event, which was attended by officials from Guangdong’s Information Office. “Stories about ordinary people and simple, genuine emotions can be even more moving. This film is an excellent vehicle for telling China’s story well.”
CHINESE MIGRATION TO SOUTHEAST ASIA
The film first resonated in Malaysia and Singapore because it showcases a history that’s rarely featured in mainstream films.
Chinese migration to Southeast Asia dates back centuries, with many migrants coming from the Guangdong and Fujian provinces in southern China. Many worked as laborers in building projects in an era of Western colonial rule across much of Asia.
The film starts with a young man trying to find his grandfather, Deng Musheng, in hopes of getting a loan to repay his debts. In the family lore, there was supposedly a wealthy grandfather in Thailand, who left his young wife and children behind in China and never came back.
Using an address on an old remittance letter his grandfather had sent, he meets people who became part of his grandfather’s life in Bangkok, uncovering the mystery of why his grandfather never returned.
The film’s director, Lan Hongchun, wrote in a column for the People’s Daily, a state media outlet, that he grew up hearing stories from his grandmother about people she knew migrating to Bangkok, and wanted to tell these stories in film.
THAI CHINESE VIEWERS
The plot revolves around qiaopi, remittance letters used by Chinese immigrants to send money and news back home. Many workers who could not write Chinese relied on scribes to compose the letters.
Scenes set in the centralized offices where the scribes worked, called poy kuan, were directly out of the childhood of 74-year-old Sathien Tuntipaiboontana.
“I connected emotionally with that part of the film quite strongly,” he said after watching the first screening of the film in a Bangkok theater with his older sisters and sisters-in-law. Among them was his eldest sister, who is 89 and needed help climbing the stairs to the cinema.
Their father had immigrated to Bangkok from China in search of work, leaving behind a wife and children. He ended up remarrying and never returned to China. But Sathien’s family continued to send remittances to the family left behind in China.
Thitikorn Phanprayoon, a third-generation Thai Chinese, said he decided to see the film after hearing Teochew, the Chinese dialect he speaks at home, in the trailer. It surprised him since most Chinese films are in Mandarin. He plans to return with his parents.
“I felt like I was sitting at home,” he said. “It felt like my family was performing in the movie in front of me.”

"Be among the first! simka.umobile.ua," Ukrtelecom said on Facebook on Thursday.
In comments to Interfax-Ukraine, Ukrtelecom said the company would soon present these new products to users in more detail.
The U Mobile website presents "Fiber+SIM" and "SIM" offerings. Pre-orders can be placed on the site by leaving a phone number.
The day before, the MZU (Mobile Communications of Ukraine) Telegram channel had reported preparations for the launch of a new virtual mobile operator (MVNO) under the U Mobile brand, which would combine fiber-optic network (GPON) services with mobile plans into unified fixed-mobile convergence (FMC) packages for the B2C segment.
According to MZU, the "SIM" plan lineup will include 15 GB or 60 GB of mobile internet, 500 minutes of calls within Ukraine, and 15 SMS messages.
U Mobile plans to bill for a full calendar month - from the 1st to the last day of the month - whereas the three major mobile operators base their plans on a four-week period.
According to the National Commission for State Regulation of Electronic Communications, Radio Frequency Spectrum and Provision of Postal Services (NCEC), mobile operator TriMob, founded by Ukrtelecom, had 60,700 mobile subscribers as of the first quarter of 2026.
Ukrtelecom provided mobile services in 2007-2011 under the Utel brand, later continuing operations through TriMob.
TriMob received Ukraine's first 3G license back in 2005. Its network was based on UMTS/HSDPA technology in the 2100 MHz band. In 2019, the company returned nearly all of its national 3G frequencies to the regulator and focused on providing services only in Kyiv. From 2020, TriMob held a license for the following bands: 1940-1945/2130-2135 MHz. The frequencies were used to provide 3G services within Kyiv.
In May 2025, the NCEC transferred the last radio frequency resources remaining with Ukrtelecom's subsidiary to Vodafone Ukraine.
As reported, Ukrtelecom increased total revenue 12.6% year-on-year in January-June 2026 to UAH 2.78 billion, while EBITDA rose 50% to more than UAH 810 million.
The company currently has more than 95,000 km of fiber-optic network and continues large-scale infrastructure modernization across the country.
In August, Ukrtelecom and Kyivstar, a Ukrainian mobile operator, also began cooperation under an Open Access model, which will involve using part of both operators' networks and will initially launch in Odesa, Vinnytsia and Kirovohrad regions.

Marquinhos received UEFA’s “Respect: Beyond the Game” first award
Kyiv • UNN
The PSG captain supported Gabriel after his decisive miss in the 2026 Champions League final. UEFA recognized this gesture of humanity.
Paris Saint-Germain captain Marquinhos received UEFA’s "Respect: Beyond the Game" award, presented for actions embodying empathy, dignity, solidarity and respect in European football, reports UNN.
Details
UEFA presented Paris Saint-Germain captain Marquinhos with the first "Respect: Beyond the Game" award ("Respect: Beyond the Game" - ed.), recognizing an act of sportsmanship that put humanity above competition during one of the season’s most emotional moments.
Immediately after the 2026 UEFA Champions League final, Marquinhos supported Arsenal defender Gabriel, his fellow Brazilian and opponent that evening.
Instead of joining the celebrations, the PSG captain went to support his colleague, whose missed penalty in the shootout decided the outcome of the season’s match.
"Marquinhos had just won the most prestigious trophy in European club football. And his first instinct was not to celebrate, but to cross the pitch to embrace and encourage his opponent at the most difficult moment of his career. Football is full of moments that seem extraordinary. This moment was also deeply human — and that is precisely why it will be remembered for a long time," said UEFA President Aleksander Čeferin.
The "Respect: Beyond the Game" award is a new annual honor for actions embodying empathy, dignity, solidarity and respect in European football.
Created as part of UEFA’s "Respect" platform, which has promoted positive values in European football for more than two decades, the award is presented to players, coaches, technical staff, referees and fans across all UEFA competitions. It will become a permanent feature of the UEFA calendar.

Paris Saint-Germain defeated Arsenal in a penalty shootout and won the UEFA Champions League for the second consecutive time.

Colombia's new president orders extradition of 5 former peace negotiators to US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:36:25 UTC
01:36:25 KST

Maryam Ashalem de Andres
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Colombia’s new president on Thursday ordered the extradition to the US of five criminal figures who took part as representatives or negotiators in peace processes with armed groups during the administration of former President Gustavo Petro.
US authorities are seeking the five over alleged involvement in drug trafficking, illegal weapons trafficking or possession, and narco-terrorism, according to Colombian media reports.
President Abelardo De la Espriella, who took office on Aug. 5, said the extraditions had already been authorized last year by the previous government but procedures had been suspended because the individuals were taking part in different dialogue processes under the Petro administration.
Among the figures slated for extradition are Geovany Andres Rojas, alias Arana, the alleged leader of the Comandos de Frontera criminal organization, who was arrested on Feb. 14, 2025 while participating in peace negotiations with the government, according to local media.
The extradition order also covers Willington Henao Gutierrez, alias Mocho Olmedo, described as a leader of FARC dissidents, and Carmen Evelio Castillo Carrillo, alias Muneca, a former leader of the Autodefensas Conquistadores de la Sierra Nevada, also known as Los Pachenca. Gabriel Yepes Mejia, alias HH, and Fredy Castillo Carrillo, alias Pinocho, are also slated for extradition but remain fugitives, local media reported.
Mocho Olmedo surrendered to authorities in February 2025 amid fighting between FARC dissidents and the National Liberation Army, or ELN, in the Catatumbo region, while Muneca was arrested in June 2024 during a police operation.
De la Espriella said his administration reviewed the cases and found no “verifiable contributions” or concrete results toward peace that would justify continuing suspending the extraditions.
“Peace negotiations cannot become shelters from justice,” he said, adding that those seeking to move toward legality must demonstrate it through “concrete and verifiable facts.”
The decision marks a shift from Petro’s Total Peace policy, under which his government opened negotiations with FARC dissidents, the ELN, and other armed and criminal groups. Several of those processes were later suspended or stalled amid continued violence.
De la Espriella has pledged a tougher security policy toward armed and criminal groups. He said Wednesday that during his first 16 day in office he had signed more than 30 extradition orders.

Ex-ICE agent charged over shooting is freed by Texas authorities
Christian Castro, accused of carrying out nonfatal shooting in Minnesota, walks free due to extradition lapse.
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer charged with shooting a Venezuelan man and allegedly lying about it during an immigration raid in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail a day after a federal judge refused to order his return to the US state of Minnesota.
The former ICE agent, Christian Castro, had been detained in a county jail in Texas since May, charged in connection with the nonfatal shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis and hitting him in the leg when firing through the front door of his home during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota on January 14.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3ICE kills 26-year-old in Maine: What happened, and who else has ICE killed?
- list 2 of 3Witnesses contest the Trump administration’s account of Texas ICE killing
- list 3 of 3US border security chief withdrawing 700 immigration agents from Minnesota
The immigration sweep was part of a mass deportation effort under United States President Donald Trump. Prosecutors said Castro wrongfully accused Sosa-Celis and another man of assaulting an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.
Castro was freed on Thursday morning from the Carrizales-Rucker Cameron County Detention Center near Brownsville, Texas, a city on the US border with Mexico. A Minnesota judge had issued a nationwide warrant for his arrest in May. Minnesota officials and the state’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension eventually detained him in Texas on May 29. Minnesota authorities then sought his extradition.
Under Texas law, the state cannot hold the subject of an extradition order for more than 90 days. At that point, the suspect must either be transferred or released. The deadline for Castro expired on Thursday.
Upon exiting the detention centre, Castro motioned towards a few camera operators and a reporter crowding around him and quickly got into an SUV that drove off.
In a ruling on Wednesday, District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr wrote that he could not intervene or prevent a county sheriff from releasing Castro given that Texas Governor Greg Abbott, a Republican and close political ally of Trump, had refused to sign the extradition warrant for political reasons. Abbott argued that he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a “fugitive” under the Extradition Clause, lawyers for the state of Texas said.
The governor also said last week that he would not respond to the extradition request, citing ongoing investigations into alleged fraud in Minnesota’s social service programmes, which Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.
Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week to block Castro’s anticipated release. He also sued Abbott to try to force his hand at signing the extradition warrant.
Ellison said Abbott’s inaction unlawfully sidestepped federal extradition to bolster Trump’s deportation campaign. He declared that legal proceedings would persist but omitted specifying what those future actions would entail.
Beginning in December, Trump orchestrated a large-scale deployment of federal agents to Minnesota. The operation lasted less than three months and fuelled protests and allegations of civil liberties violations from residents and watchdog groups. Two US citizens were killed by federal agents during the operation.
Minnesota officials have warned that Castro may flee the US if released, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico.
During those calls, Castro talked “about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released”, according to Minnesota’s lawsuit.
The judge conceded that Castro could indeed flee the country but added that “the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication”.

====================================================================================================

Keto diets may offer health benefits the Mediterranean and other diets don’t
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:32:42 UTC
01:32:42 KST

It’s possible to lose weight following any one of three diets, a new clinical trial has found—but one diet stands out for its substantive health benefits that the other eating regimens just don’t seem to offer.
In the trial, researchers put three popular weight-loss regimes—a low-fat, plant-focused diet, the Mediterranean diet and the ketogenic, or keto, diet—to the test. The Mediterranean diet has long been lauded by nutritionists for its health benefits and is high in healthy fats, plants and whole grains. The plant-focused diet used in the trial is similar and highlights plant-based foods. The keto diet is rather different: it is typically high in fat and very low in carbohydrates, with a little protein thrown in for good measure.
Keto diets are specifically intended to limit your body’s access to sugars, forcing it to consume fat for energy by entering a metabolic state called ketosis. They can be used to treat certain diseases, such as epilepsy, and may have some benefits in other psychiatric conditions such as depression and schizophrenia.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Now, in a new head-to-head clinical study of the three diets, researchers found that people with obesity who lost weight on the keto diet saw better metabolic outcomes than their peers who lost a similar amount of weight on another diet. These benefits included a reduction of liver fat and lower rates of prediabetes.
The trial was small—it involved 55 participants with obesity who were prediabetic and had fatty liver disease. The participants met with a dietician every week, and they got precooked, frozen meals for one of the three diets.
The keto diet that the participants followed was rich in food such as fruits and vegetables, cheese, eggs, meat and fish, says Samuel Klein, the study’s senior author and a professor of medicine and nutritional science at the Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis. The Mediterranean diet, meanwhile, included items such as fish, chicken, legumes, seeds, nuts and olive oil, and the plant-focused diet included beans, rice, and fruits and vegetables.
Klein and his colleagues weren’t interested in whether the diets helped people lose weight. “That’s already been studied in multiple studies, and the differences are quite small between these three different diets,” Klein says. Instead the team assessed the participants’ health before and after they lost a similar amount of weight—about 10 percent of their starting weight.
All three diets had clear health benefits, such as greater sensitivity of muscle tissue to insulin, says Max Petersen, the paper’s lead author and an assistant professor at the Washington University School of Medicine. Blood cholesterol profiles were also similar across all diets.
But the keto diet had “much more profound beneficial effects on the liver,” Klein says. Participants on the keto diet saw a decrease in the liver’s production of triglyceride, a type of fat that is unhealthy in high amounts, and increased liver insulin sensitivity, which helps regulate blood sugar, as well as a reduction in liver fat.
The latter was a critical metric, Klein says: liver fat can have serious complications, including inflammation and cancer. Half of the participants on the keto diet also saw remission of their prediabetes.
The results suggest that reducing the intake of carbohydrates, particularly sugars, can help people lose weight and support their metabolic health, Klein says. “Reducing sugar intake would be a number one thing to do for anybody ... trying to change their diet to improve their health if they have obesity, independent of weight loss itself,” he says.
The study is well designed, says Jeff Volek, a kinesiologist at the Ohio State University, who was not involved with the study. Research by Volek and others has shown that ketosis can help with liver insulin sensitivity, triglyceride production, and more. The study adds to that body of evidence, he says. “It is nice to see these researchers finally coming around on ketogenic diets, as the evidence has been strong for a long time,” Volek says.
Sai Das, a nutrition science professor at Tufts University, who was also not involved in the study, says that the results suggest keto is a “highly promising” choice for people who need to reduce their liver fat and triglyceride levels ahead of surgery, whether for weight loss or any other chronic condition. “This diet offers a better option to do this in a timely manner,” Das says.
The study’s short timeline and small sample size, however, mean more research is needed to better understand the long-term effects of the keto diet compared with those of other diets, she says. On the Mediterranean diet, she notes, participants saw greater reductions in body fat mass and smaller reductions in fat-free mass, which includes muscles and bones.
Klein, for his part, hopes the results inspire future research combining keto with popular glucagonlike peptide 1 (GLP-1) weight-loss drugs such as semaglutide, tirzepatide, and more.
“All medications have costs and side effects,” he says. “How can we use diet in conjunction with medication to enhance the therapeutic effect with the least amount of cost and least amount of side effects?”
The findings were published on Thursday in the journal Cell Metabolism.

West Bank has become 'a lawless land,' says top Catholic in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
16:32:19 UTC
01:32:19 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
The Latin patriarch of Jerusalem, the top Catholic in the holy city, said Thursday that the West Bank has turned into "a lawless land" as the Israeli settlers’ aggression in the region continues, Vatican News quoted the cleric as saying.
The West Bank has now become “a lawless land," Cardinal Pierbattista Pizzaballa told reporters at a Catholic festival in Rimini, northern Italy, adding that the situation continues "without any effective security or legal restraints.”
Speaking at the Meeting for Friendship Among Peoples in Rimini, he urged further diplomatic engagement by the West to stop escalating violence in the Middle East.
“The fact that there is a situation of continuous aggression by settlers is well established," Pizzaballa stressed.
"The West must help raise its gaze somewhat, create perspectives, and also help calm this continuing downward spiral through ever greater diplomatic efforts."
He stressed the need for diplomacy as the "only way" to resolve the conflict "while avoiding the use of weapons, violence and military force.”
On the deteriorating situation in Gaza, Pizzaballa called it "very devastated from a human point of view.”
The two-state solution is "the only way to recognize the right of Israelis and Palestinians to have a home in their own land,” he said.
“Sooner or later the pope will come to the Holy Land — it is only a matter of time. I think it is necessary to prepare the conditions for this visit so that it can truly bear fruit," Pizzaballa added.
He also stressed the need to prevent the dehumanizing logic of war from becoming our “way of thinking, of surviving."
"War steals from young people the most beautiful years of their lives, when it does not take their lives altogether,” he said.
“This is true for Ukraine, but also for the Middle East. War has its own dynamics, and they brutalize you. The other person is exorcized, because if the other is human and close to you, it becomes difficult to strike them.”
He further said they should avoid "reducing peace to a slogan, as well as naive approaches to a complex reality."
Pizzaballa also said the sense of the common good had been lost in the Middle East as institutions seemed to be guided by what is good for themselves or for their own political side.
In a Middle East “so torn apart, burdened by hatred, resentment and hardship,” cultivating hope is not easy, he added.
“We must be realistic because the situation has deteriorated,” he added.
