Persistent financial hardship is linked to later-life brain shrinkage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:00:52 UTC
21:00:52 KST

Money worries can keep us up at night, but could decades of financial stress leave a lasting mark on the brain itself? That’s the question my colleagues and I set out to answer in a new study – and the answer, it turns out, is yes.
Most research on money and brain health looks at people’s financial circumstances at just one point in time. This makes it hard to know whether a few difficult years have the same effect as decades of enduring struggle. For our study, published in the journal Innovation in Aging, we tracked the same people throughout their adult lives to find out.
We used data from the MRC National Survey of Health and Development, also known as the 1946 British birth cohort study. A cohort study follows a group of people born in the same period throughout their lives. This is the world’s longest continuously running study of its kind, tracking thousands of people born in one week in March 1946 – participants who celebrated their 80th birthdays earlier this year.
The study’s origins go back to the economic anxieties of the 1930s, when the Great Depression left many families worrying about money and the cost of raising children – making it a fitting dataset to revisit those same questions decades later. Using this rich resource, we examined the financial circumstances of 2,759 participants at multiple points across adulthood.
Participants reported their household income at ages 26, 43 and 53. We classed those in the bottom 20% of the group on at least two of these occasions as having persistent low income – about one in six people. Separately, we measured financial hardship by asking whether people struggled to manage on their income or had trouble paying bills, at least twice between ages 36 and 53. This applied to about one in eight.
At age 53, participants took tests of verbal memory and processing speed. A smaller group also had brain scans between ages 69 and 71, which let us measure brain atrophy (shrinkage) and ventricular expansion – the widening of fluid-filled cavities within the brain, a recognised marker of poor brain health.
We found that people who had experienced more financial hardship and low income scored lower on the cognitive tests at age 53. These links held even after we accounted for their childhood thinking skills, education and childhood disadvantage. Among those who had brain scans, persistent low income was linked to greater brain shrinkage in later life.
When we looked at how memory changed from age 53 to 69, those who had faced persistent hardship actually showed slower decline over that period. We believe this is because they had already lost more ground by age 53 – they started from a lower point, so there was less left to lose.
We also found that the link between financial adversity and brain shrinkage was stronger for men, for those who grew up in disadvantaged homes, and for carriers of a gene that raises the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease.
For men of this generation – born in 1946, when the male breadwinner model was the norm – the pressure of being the main earner may have made financial stress more acute. Disadvantaged men also had higher rates of smoking and drinking than disadvantaged women.
The finding on genetic risk suggests that people who are already biologically vulnerable may be more susceptible to the effects of financial strain. These subgroup findings are based on smaller numbers within our sample, so we are treating them as suggestive rather than conclusive.
Why would money worries harm the brain?
How might financial hardship affect the brain over time? Chronic stress is known to increase inflammation, which accelerates brain ageing. There is also the simple fact that constantly worrying about money uses up mental energy, leaving less capacity for other thinking tasks – a cognitive load that competes with everything else the brain is trying to do.
We acknowledge that our study cannot prove cause and effect, and the results, drawn from a single generation of British adults, may not apply directly to other populations or countries. But following the same people over many years gives us a clearer picture than studies that only look at a single moment in time.
Financial hardship is increasingly recognised as one of several factors – alongside things such as hearing loss, smoking and physical inactivity – that may shape our risk of cognitive decline in later life. Our findings suggest that reducing chronic financial hardship among working-age adults, wherever they live, could help protect brain health and potentially reduce dementia cases in the future.

The United Nations has strongly condemned those actions, saying that the entry of security forces into a UN facility without the Organisation's permission or approval was unacceptable.
Secretary-General António Guterres called for the Israeli Government to immediately cease its interference with UNRWA installations and to vacate, return and restore all affected premises to the United Nations without delay.
Earlier this month, there was misinformation circulating about the centre, which prompted UNRWA to issue a statement reaffirming its commitment to education and underlining that the agency remains “essential to ensuring that Palestine refugee children and young people can develop the knowledge, skills and opportunities they need to build their futures”.
Roland Friedrich, Director of UNRWA Affairs in the West Bank, told us that the incident was part of a wider effort by the current Israeli Government to end UNRWA's activities in occupied East Jerusalem, following the adoption of what he described as "anti-UNRWA" legislation almost a year and a half ago.
The Kalandia centre provides vocational training to young people from refugee camps across the West Bank. Mr. Friedrich warned that its closure would deprive 340 male youth of their right to education and opportunities for the future.
This interview has been edited for clarity and length.
Roland Friedrich: The situation at the Kalandia Training Centre remains critical. Israeli security forces are still deployed inside the centre, along with Israeli officials from the Municipality of Jerusalem, as they carry out work and alterations to the installation. This is an unacceptable violation – as the Secretary-General has underlined – of the privileges and immunities of the United Nations. The continuation of this situation will very likely deprive 340 male youth from the West Bank of their right to education.
UN News: Can you tell us exactly what happened? What happened to the UNRWA staff who were at the centre?
Roland Friedrich: On Tuesday morning, a large Israeli force arrived and forcibly entered the compound. We had 24 staff on site as we prepared for the new scholastic year, which is scheduled to start next week. Israeli security personnel searched the site, opened the buildings and temporarily held our staff at the site. They were later released. This is an unacceptable violation of the privileges and immunities of the United Nations.
UN News: Were you informed of any reason for the Israeli authorities' entry into the centre or what they were looking for? Do you have any information on the possibility of returning the centre to UNRWA, as requested by the United Nations?
Roland Friedrich: The Secretary-General has been very clear in his demand to urgently restore the situation to the way it was before. The background of what happened goes back to the Israeli anti-UNRWA legislation that was adopted roughly a year and a half ago. We saw the progressive closure of our six schools in Occupied East Jerusalem for 2025, depriving 800 children of education. In December, amendments were made to the anti-UNRWA laws, including a provision to cut water and electricity from UNRWA installations in East Jerusalem, and secondly, to authorize Israeli security forces to seize, our compound, the main headquarters, and the Kalandia Training Centre.
UN News: You talked about the immunities and privileges of the United Nations and its facilities. Can you explain what that means and why it is important to commit to it all over the world, especially in the occupied Palestinian territory?
Roland Friedrich: Any Member State of the United Nations, per its obligations under the Charter, but also through being a party to the general Convention, is obliged to respect the privileges and immunities of the UN. That means, for instance, the inviolability of UN premises, the respect for immunities relating to staff, to vehicles, as is the case anywhere in the world where we operate. What we saw yesterday and what continues to happen is exactly the opposite [of this]. And I think what is important to keep in mind is that this sets a precedent when it comes to making sure that our staff can work in a safe way, are protected anywhere else in the world in a very dangerous context.
UN News: Because we're talking about international law and international obligations, what is the UN planning to do now? What do you hope the international community will do about it?
Roland Friedrich: What we hope is that Member States take the responsibility to exercise pressure, so that we can resume our work at this training centre. The key thing is that we can go back to that centre, operate it, and serve the people that we are mandated to serve by the General Assembly.
UN News: In the context of the Israeli legislation you talked about regarding UNRWA, what can you still do in the West Bank to serve Palestine refugees?
Roland Friedrich: There are two laws. One law is a ban on UNRWA operations and presences in what Israel considers sovereign territory and that applies to our services in occupied East Jerusalem. The occupation of East Jerusalem is not recognized by the UN, nor is in fact the annexation of East Jerusalem. The second law provides for no-contact policy that bans Israeli authorities from being in touch with UNRWA and that has an impact on our operations in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank. However, we can continue to operate both in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, providing critical humanitarian aid in Gaza through more than 11,000 staff members who work every day, providing education, health consultations, shelter and drinking water. Similarly, in the West Bank, we have 4,600 staff on the ground. We continue to provide education. Last year we provided 1.1 million health consultations through 50 health facilities, and we provided together with partners social protection, cash assistance, and food support to more than 270,000 beneficiaries. I pay the highest respect to my UNRWA colleagues on the ground, Palestinian teachers, nurses, social workers in the Gaza Strip and in the West Bank who work under extremely difficult conditions every day.
UN News: What is the main message you would like the international community to understand about UNRWA's presence, its work and the risks it faces in the West Bank?
Roland Friedrich: One thing that we clearly need to see is a restoration of respect for the United Nations at large, and for UNRWA as an agency mandated by the General Assembly by all State parties. Secondly, the humanitarian space in the West Bank overall is shrinking, and that is a trend that needs to be reversed. And thirdly, we need to reverse the trend of forcible displacement in the West Bank. These are dangerous trends because together with settlement expansion, they create a reality on the ground that makes the two-State solution ever more unlikely to be implemented. It is important to pull back from the brink that we're seeing in the West Bank now and return to a credible pathway towards the two-state solution, and eventually a situation where UNRWA as an agency does not have to do its work anymore because the conflict has moved towards a solution.

Shock and devastation remain, a day after Himalayan flood disaster

Shock and devastation remain, a day after Himalayan flood disaster
Amid reports that hundreds of people are still missing in Nepal and China after a floodwater surge slammed into towns and villages on Wednesday, aid teams have been working to reach communities cut off by the disaster.
Key points
- Hundreds remain missing after devastating floods in Nepal and China
- $2 million funding released by UN emergency relief chief
- World Health Organization (WHO) sends medicines, supplies and tents
An initial $2 million has been released from the United Nations Global Emergency Fund (CERF) “to save lives with emergency medical care, shelter, water”, the UN’s relief chief Tom Fletcher said on X.
In Nepal, immediate humanitarian needs are huge in the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading and communities face immense challenges as families cope with loss, displacement and disruption to essential services.
The UN chief pledged swift support.
“The United Nations is mobilising supplies and humanitarian teams and we pledge to support national efforts to deliver emergency aid and support,” Secretary-General António Guterres said.
17,000 children affected
The flash floods have swept away or cut off entire communities, with roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, water systems and telecommunications networks badly damaged, leaving affected areas largely inaccessible and hampering the delivery of lifesaving aid, the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) said on Thursday.
At least 17,000 children have been impacted by the devastating flash floods that tore through Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts.
“Children across Rasuwa and Dhading saw their lives being literally washed away in front of their eyes in a very short span of time, with homes, classrooms, and medical facilities damaged,” said Alice Akunga, UNICEF Representative to Nepal.
“Too many lost their lives and loved ones. With the death toll still rising, we know this tragedy is far from over. Children who have survived the floods now face heightened risks of disease, malnutrition, violence and exploitation.”
For its part, UNICEF is on the ground and scaling up support, “but we urgently need more resources to reach every child in need”, Ms. Akunga said.
Still missing
“UN agencies are deployed to affected areas with food, medical supplies and relief materials in support of the government-led response and stand ready to do more,” the UN office in Nepal wrote on Facebook.
In China, around 560 people remain missing, according to the authorities, while the UN country office on Wednesday reported damage and significant numbers of casualties and destruction in the Tibet autonomous region of China.
Meanwhile, in support of the authorities and the wider response, WHO has dispatched an interagency emergency health kit, containing medicines and supplies sufficient to provide basic health services for up to 10,000 people. The UN health agency has also provided six multipurpose tents to help sustain health service delivery in affected communities.
“These supplies are intended to support frontline health workers as they continue providing critical care and responding to the immediate health needs of affected populations,” the UN agency explained on Facebook.
New deployments
“WHO remains committed to working closely with health authorities and partners to assess the evolving situation, support emergency health services and help ensure that people continue to access the care they need during this difficult time.”
In addition on Thursday, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) and the UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) planned to start deploying staff and trucks carrying relief supplies.
Efforts also continued to rapidly assess the scale of the disaster, in particular from secure satellite imagery and analysis of the area impacted by flooding, provided by the UN platform for the UN Space-based Information for Disaster Management and Emergency Response (UN-SPIDER). Managed by the UN Office for Outer Space Affairs (UNOOSA), the initiative connects disaster management experts with space agencies to help disaster risk reduction, early warning and emergency response activities.
Collapsed glacier
A collapsed glacier high up in the steep-sided valleys of the Himalayas has been cited as a possible cause of the sudden flash-flooding and mudslides that have destroyed entire communities and washed away bridges and roads.
Rasuwa district some 80 kilometres north of Kathmandu in northern Nepal was hit particularly hard, including the towns of Timure, Rasuwagadhi and Syabrubesi, a popular trekking destination among tourists, climbers and pilgrims wanting to access the Langtang valley.
The area was also hit by a 7.8 magnitude earthquake in April 2015, which killed more than 8,800 people. Last October, torrential rains caused fast-moving floods and landslides across eastern and central Nepal, affecting more than 30,000 people.
Growing risk of disasters
UNDRR, the lead UN agency for the coordination of disaster risk reduction, projects that the world will experience 560 medium to large-scale disasters annually by the year 2030.
“Global disasters are projected to increase by 40 per cent between 2015 and 2030, driven by climate change and systemic underestimations of risk,” the agency said.
In addition to the human cost of such disasters, the annual cost is $2.29 trillion and rising, when indirect and ecosystem impacts are factored in, UNDRR said. This figure is nearly 10 times the annual direct losses reported in official figures.

Lebanon: UN warns of growing civilian risks as military activity continues
Unknown

Lebanon: Civilian risks grow as military activity continues, UN says
Damaged roads, disrupted services and ongoing military activity continue to put civilians at risk in south Lebanon as strikes between Israeli forces and Hezbollah continue, according to the UN’s peacekeeping mission in the country (UNIFIL).
Following reports of Hezbollah drone attacks and retaliatory Israeli strikes on Wednesday and Thursday, UNIFIL is urging restraint and renewed political engagement to avoid a further escalation of hostilities.
UNIFIL spokesperson Kandice Ardiel told UN News that while the latest strikes occurred outside UNIFIL’s area of operations, the impact of the conflict continues to be felt across southern Lebanon and along the “Blue Line”.
Find out more about the Blue Line in our explainer here.
UNIFIL is urging all parties to comply with Security Council resolution 1701 – the 2006 agreement intended to cease hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah – and use existing mechanisms to de-escalate tensions.
“It’s in no one’s interest to continue on a military path,” Ms. Ardiel said. “The only solution to this is political and diplomatic.”
Although violence has decreased compared to previous months, UNIFIL has observed a rise in military activity inside its area of operations, including logistical movements, demolitions and projectile launches.
The mission continues to monitor developments closely and report violations, warning that renewed military activity risks undermining the fragile stability achieved in recent months.
Scale of damage harms civilians
UNIFIL remains concerned about the scale of destruction across parts of south Lebanon. According to the mission, several villages and neighbourhoods have suffered severe damage, affecting homes, roads and civilian infrastructure.
The destruction has also restricted the movement of residents, many of whom face difficulties travelling between villages and accessing essential services. Humanitarian organizations and peacekeepers have faced similar logistical challenges while carrying out their work.
To help reduce risks on the ground, UNIFIL continues to coordinate with both the Lebanese Armed Forces and the Israeli Defense Forces, facilitating movement and helping prevent incidents through deconfliction mechanisms.
Peacekeepers regularly accompany certain movements to support safety and ensure humanitarian access where possible.
While peacekeepers continue to carry out their mandate, they have faced occasional delays at Israeli military checkpoints along the coastal road linking UNIFIL headquarters in Naqoura with Beirut.
“Peacekeepers have freedom of movement, and any interruption of that is a concern for us,” Ms. Ardiel said.
Political solution remains essential
With UNIFIL’s mandate set to expire at the end of this year, the UN remains concerned about the potential impact of a security vacuum left behind by its departure.
In a letter published in June, UN Secretary-General António Guterres outlined options for implementing resolution 1701 without UNIFIL’s presence, all of which involve a continued UN presence – albeit a smaller one – on the ground to monitor the Blue Line, plus a strengthened UN political office (UNSCOL) to promote peace and coordinate UN efforts.
UNIFIL continues to stress that a lasting solution cannot be achieved through military means alone. The mission is urging both parties to return to dialogue and implement measures that can restore security and stability for communities on both sides of the Blue Line.
Aid efforts hampered
On the humanitarian front, UNIFIL, in coordination with OCHA, facilitated humanitarian missions to reach those in need.
Since the Hezbollah-Israel conflict erupted in March, 900,000 people have received at least one round of emergency cash assistance, according to UN Spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric.
At the same time, humanitarian needs remain immense, yet available funding is insufficient to meet those needs, he said, noting that the six-month flash appeal requiring nearly $640 million to support people impacted by the escalation of the fighting is due to end in just four days and remains only half funded.
“We call for full respect for international humanitarian law, the protection of civilians, the protection of civilian infrastructure, the protection of humanitarian and aid workers as well as our peacekeepers while stressing that sustained humanitarian support is essential to meet the needs of communities affected by the ongoing hostilities,” he said.

How Widow’s Bay Supports a Mystic Epistemology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Nathan Eckstrand is an editor at the Blog of the APA. The views expressed here are solely those of the author and do not necessarily represent the views of the American Philosophical Association or the Blog of the APA.
Mystical experiences, or non-sensory awarenesses of situations that can’t be accessed normally, are incredibly diverse. They consist of encounters with God, eerie coincidences, feelings of connection with others, awarenesses of spirits, and insights into the world’s nature. Research on near-death experiences shows that mystical experiences can have a profound impact on someone’s life. People come away with a greater sense of purpose or connection to their world. But what is the epistemological status of such experiences? While clearly not scientific facts, are they subjective opinions? Is it reasonable for someone to believe them or the accounts of others? As the main character of Apple TV’s show Widow’s Bay, Tom Loftis deals with this question when confronted with the island’s mystic past, transforming from a skeptic to a believer. His transformation illustrates why it is reasonable, though not necessary, to believe that mystical experiences are true.
Widow’s Bay, named after the island town in which the show takes place, has no lack of mystical experiences. There’s a bell that rings nine times despite being chained up, a book that puts people into trances, and a demon that communicates with the town’s founder. While some supernatural phenomena are presented as empirical, others take place in characters’ minds. The latter qualify as mystical experiences. At the show’s beginning, Mayor Tom Loftis is skeptical about the townspeople’s claim that the town is cursed. He’s more interested in providing a positive experience for a visiting New York Times reporter. Loftis wants Widow’s Bay recognized as “the next Martha’s Vineyard and definitely not cursed,” which will bring more tourists. Of course, it doesn’t help that the local museum—which Loftis obligingly brings the reporter to—is decked out with exhibits about the island’s mysterious history, including references to a possible deal the town’s founder, Richard Warren, might have made with a demon. Yet Loftis dismisses these as local superstitions that he, as a mainlander, knows are absurd. In episode two, Loftis even stays a night in the local hotel to show townsfolk that it is not haunted.
Loftis’s rejection of local mysticism is a clear appeal to scientific realism. The locals only refer to legends to prove their claims of curses and demons, and Loftis finds this unreliable. He wants something he can confirm empirically; anything else is a rumor at best. Yet, even as he rejects the islanders’ superstitions, Loftis appeals to a constructivist view of mysticism to explain them. For him, the superstitious beliefs are part of the island’s culture. Similarly, Steven T. Katz claims that the content of mystical experiences is partly the result of one’s culture. Unlike those who believe all mystical experiences have a common core, Katz says that language, society, and psychology necessarily influence every mystical experience. As Katz’s goal is to explain the origins of such content, he—unlike Loftis—doesn’t question whether it is true. Nevertheless, Loftis draws on Katz’s insight. Loftis believes is the islanders’ similar culture that produces similar mystical experiences, rather than the similar experiences signaling that the superstitions are true. Loftis believes he has a more rational view, given his upbringing on the mainland.
Loftis changes his perspective on mysticism midway through the series when he accidentally takes psychedelic mushrooms, leading him on a drug trip in which—among other things—he recalls his wife going blind when she tried to leave the island. While the hallucinations are mostly comedic, it is true that psychedelics can create or enhance mystical experiences, and neurological studies confirm this relationship. Notably, Loftis’s hallucinations include a revelation confirming Warren’s pact with a demon and indicating that the only way to end the island’s curse is to end Warren’s family line.
Despite no scientific evidence to confirm his revelation, Loftis accepts it as true, indicating a shift in how he views mystical experiences. He begins to accept them, in part because he has had a mystical experience and in part because his experience matches the experiences of others. Loftis embraces what philosophers who study mystical experiences call the Doxastic Practice Approach. Doxastic means “of or relating to beliefs,” and advocates of this theory argue that the truth of one’s beliefs can be established, at least in part, by referring to one’s society. Specifically, supporters claim everyone evaluates and forms beliefs using socially established methods, and no method can justify itself without referring to itself (i.e., it is “epistemically circular”). Epistemologies should not be judged on whether they produce “Truth”—an impossible task—but on whether they are consistent. As long as one does not ignore cognitive or perceptual experiences indicating one’s epistemology is unreliable, one can use socially accepted practices to decide if something is true. For example, Christians can accept the truth of their mystical experiences by referencing Christian scriptures and doctrines. Since every epistemology is circular, there is no reason to privilege epistemologies like scientific realism over those that accept the existence of mystical experiences (assuming those other epistemologies are consistent).
In addition to providing a reason to accept that one’s mystical experiences are true, the Doxastic Practice Approach argues that we can sometimes accept the truth of others’ mystical experiences. This is because: (1) the experience itself argues for its existence, (2) if there is agreement between people in different times and places (e.g., people provide similar accounts of experiences with God), that implies the experience is not simply subjective, and (3) if the experiences have a positive effect upon a person’s life, that testifies to its truth. This last criterion, while perhaps unusual, comes from the pragmatism developed by William James. James says that mystical beliefs have greater truth value the more useful they are. As we can’t assess them scientifically, we should prefer mystical beliefs that lead to the best outcomes. While not arguing that mystical experiences are objectively true, James argues that these criteria provide reasons to accept the truth of both one’s own mystical experiences and those of others.
After his hallucinations, Loftis accepts the mysticism of the islanders. Even though the weird phenomena he’s experienced could be explained by other ideologies, Loftis looks for explanations using the island’s lore, as the Doxastic Practice Approach suggests. Among other examples, he searches the town’s museum to find Warren’s last descendant. Additionally, he accepts the truth of his revelation, not just because he’s had it but because it is confirmed by people throughout the town’s history who’ve had similar experiences. This is illustrated by his new interest in island lore, which describes others who, like Loftis’s wife, went blind after leaving the island. Most importantly, embracing the truth of his revelation leads Loftis to better outcomes. He realizes that to be a good mayor he needs to stop the troubles plaguing the island, and this requires him to accept the mystical experiences of the islanders as true. His improved outlook and actions testify to the truth of the island’s mystical experiences.
Loftis wrestles with the island’s mystical beliefs throughout Widow’s Bay. While initially dismissive, he comes to embrace them as important. By doing so, he effectively adopts the doxastic practices of the Widow’s Bay community, symbolically giving up his mainlander identity. Loftis transforms from a scientific realist who rejects the island’s mysticism to someone who embraces it using the Doxastic Practice Approach. As Loftis’s journey demonstrates, mystical experiences don’t need to be accepted as true by everyone, but that doesn’t mean we should reject them. There are legitimate reasons to believe that mystical experiences, whether encountered by us or others, are still true.
The post How Widow’s Bay Supports a Mystic Epistemology first appeared on Blog of the APA.

Aid reaches hundreds of thousands in Gaza amid severe food insecurity
As hunger deepens across Gaza, humanitarian agencies continue to deliver food and other essential supplies to families in need.
In Gaza, about one in five families say that they are eating only one meal a day, and 50 per cent of them reported that they completely ran out of food at least once in the past month, according to latest UN figures.
This is because of cash shortages, but also because most food items have become exponentially more expensive since the escalation of hostilities in October 2023.
So far this month, three-quarters of households in Gaza have faced difficulties in accessing markets, according to the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP).
The UN on the ground
Yesterday, the UN and its partners collected hundreds of pallets of supplies from the Kerem Shalom crossing – a vital commercial and humanitarian entry point located at the junction of Israel, Egypt, and the Gaza Strip.
The pallets include fruits, vegetables and other food, as well as adult diapers, school supplies and fuel.
So far, partners have provided food parcels and wheat flour to more than 600,000 people as part of the August cycle.
A fragile peace
Despite a ceasefire signed by Israel and Hamas in October 2025, ongoing hostilities and security restrictions hamper local movement and recovery efforts.
Frequent Israeli military strikes continue to kill and displace people across Gaza. More than two million people, almost the Strip's entire population, have been driven from their homes, with most now living in makeshift or fragile shelters.
Around 90 per cent of civilian infrastructure – including homes, hospitals, water plants, and schools – is heavily damaged or destroyed.

UN chief condemns “indifference” as Ebola cases mount in DR Congo

UN chief condemns “indifference” as Ebola cases mount in DR Congo
The Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) requires “urgent” action and funding to rein in its alarming spread, the UN Secretary-General told reporters at UN Headquarters on Thursday.
Key points
- More than 5,600 cases and 2,700 deaths in six affected provinces in DRC since the outbreak began in mid-May
- The World Health Organization (WHO) believes it has slowed its spread, but has not yet managed to reverse the current trend
- Prevention work has already begun in neighbouring Burundi, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
“The challenge is immense,” he said, noting 500 new cases are being reported every week while the humanitarian response remains only 48 per cent funded.
Estimates show current resources will last only weeks, not months, as the epidemic spreads faster than the response to contain it.
“We know how to contain Ebola, how to interrupt transmission and how to save lives,” he underscored, “but we must also overcome another virus: the virus of indifference.”
Watch the UN chief’s press stakeout on UN Web TV:
More funds needed
“Without additional funding, vital operations will run out of money at the very moment they need to ramp up,” he warned, calling for an additional $1.1 billion.
Money, however, is only part of the problem. Ebola is spreading in a region where decades of conflict have displaced entire populations and weakened health infrastructure. In Ituri province alone, one million people have been displaced, and more than 12 million people in the region are in need of humanitarian aid and protection.
Insecurity is also directly hindering the response. More than 40 healthcare workers have lost their lives while treatment centres and ambulances have been attacked. Humanitarian teams must therefore simultaneously confront the virus and the violence while some communities remain difficult to access.
All corners of civil society mobilised
Local artists and social media influencers are joining the fight against Ebola by raising awareness through their respective medium, including renowned Congolese singer and songwriter Lokua Kanza.
A national UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) ambassador, Mr. Kanza called for people to implement preventive measures in a video posted on the agency’s social media account.
The Wedy duo and singer Drigo Eboma have also both published music calling for people to stop the spread, and 15 influencers – each with over 100,000 followers – have used their platforms to raise awareness among young people.
Religious leaders are also on the case, with over 50 of them in Ituri province – the epicentre of the outbreak – being briefed on how to prevent the spread and manage rumours.
Similarly, around 30 former combatants received special training from the UN and local partners on prevention measures and detection of suspect cases before being dispatched to heavily frequented areas north of Ituri province to share this crucial information with the local communities.
Prep work in Burundi
UN humanitarian agencies and partners are continuing to support government-led efforts in Burundi to prepare for the potential spread of Ebola in that neighbouring country.
While Burundi has not reported any confirmed cases, the country remains at higher risk due to its proximity to the affected areas in the DRC and continued cross-border population movements, UN agencies are reporting.
Some of the preparedness efforts are already under way, from strengthened surveillance at points of entry through temperature screening and deployment of thermal scanners to training healthcare providers, including nurses and community health workers, as well as journalists.
Uganda’s outbreak declared over
UN health officials and partners declared on Thursday that the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in neighbouring Uganda is over.
This follows 42 consecutive days without a new confirmed case since the country’s last patient was discharged from care on 16 July.
The 42-day benchmark – equivalent to twice the upper limit of the incubation period for Ebola – is the internationally established criterion for determining that an outbreak has ended.
During the outbreak, Uganda reported 20 confirmed cases of the disease, including two deaths. More than 800 contacts were identified and monitored to stop the spread.
What’s the UN doing?
- UN agencies and partners began expanding the response with 35 additional mobile safe and dignified burial teams and 286 community-based teams high-risk areas, with more than 2,500 volunteers and civil protection personnel, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA)
- WHO has deployed more than 260 experts, delivered over 330 tonnes of essential medical and logistical supplies
- The World Food Programme (WFP) continues to provide assistance and medical evacuations through its UN Humanitarian Air Service (UNHAS)
- The UN migration agency, IOM, launched a regional preparedness plan in June covering 11 countries and has helped to screen more than one million people
- In Burundi, WHO and partners are supporting the national authorities in updating their Ebola response guidelines and strengthening lab procedures for the safe collection and transportation of samples while nearly 30,000 Ebola prevention posters have been distributed in three languages: Kirundi, Swahili and French

Consequences of the Russian shelling of Boryspil district — photo report
Kyiv • UNN
Russian drones and ballistic missiles caused fires at nine locations in Boryspil district. Warehouses and private houses were damaged.
In Boryspil district, warehouses and private houses caught fire as a result of a nighttime attack by Russian drones and ballistic missiles. The aftermath of the shelling is featured in a photo report by UNN.
Details
As reported by Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, the enemy attacked the Kyiv region with strike drones and ballistic missiles throughout the night. A fire broke out at warehouse facilities in Boryspil district as a result of the attack.
The State Emergency Service reported that rescuers were working at 9 locations in Boryspil district.
They included private homes, warehouse facilities, and fires in ecosystems.
Local Telegram channels report that the Rozetka and Fozzy warehouses are most likely on fire.

In Kyiv, the aftermath of the Russian attack has already been recorded in five districts; a school was affected
Kyiv • UNN
Debris fell near a school, a kindergarten, residential buildings and garages. Three people were injured, two of them were hospitalized.
In Kyiv, the aftermath of the Russian attack has now been recorded in five districts, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on social media, UNN reports.
According to him, the Holosiivskyi and Pecherskyi districts have been joined by the Shevchenkivskyi, Obolonskyi and Podilskyi districts.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, debris also fell near one of the schools — the facility's windows were damaged. In the Obolonskyi district, debris fell in a residential area, a park and a parking lot, as well as on the premises of a garage cooperative. There were no fires or casualties. In the Podilskyi district, debris fell on the grounds of a kindergarten. It also fell in the area near a non-residential building.
According to him, three people have been injured so far. Medics hospitalized two of the wounded.

Satellite images show destruction from Nepal-Tibet floods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:54:59 UTC
20:54:59 KST

Satellite images show destruction from Nepal-Tibet floods
A glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday triggered catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-Tibet border.
At least 359 people have been confirmed dead and more than 1,300 remain missing across Nepal and China’s Tibet region after a Himalayan glacier collapse sent a wall of water, mud and rock through border towns and valleys.
Rescue teams are searching for survivors in terrain that is hard to access at the best of times. At least 19 bridges and about 40km (25 miles) of road have been destroyed, further hampering the search.
Nepal Police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle said the death toll is expected to rise further.
Satellite imagery captured by Planet Labs before and after the flood shows how buildings and roads have been washed away.
The imagery also shows large parts of Syapru Besi village submerged in mud.
What happened?
At about 8:40am local time (02:55 GMT) on Wednesday, a large section of glacier broke away high above the Lhende river in Tibet. The falling ice and rock dammed the river and, shortly afterwards, when the blockage gave way, the surge tore through settlements in Nepal’s Rasuwa district, destroying homes, hydropower plants and border infrastructure.
The resulting ice and rock avalanche struck the river about 20km (12 miles) northeast of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing.
Early reports attributed the collapse to a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. But the United States Geological Survey later said the seismic signal was caused by the landslide itself, not an earthquake. The landslide packed enough force to register as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
Where did the floods hit?
Some of the worst damage was in Rasuwa district, on Nepal’s northern border with China. The surge travelled down the Lhende Khola (river) into the Bhotekoshi and then the Trishuli river, which rose by as much as 9 metres (30 feet) in 30 minutes, according to Nepali officials.
Timure and Syapru Besi were among the settlements hit in Rasuwa. Further downstream, the flooding reached parts of Nuwakot and Dhading. Bodies have since been recovered much further south, in Gorkha, Tanahun, Chitwan and the two Nawalparasi districts.
In Tibet, mud and debris struck Gyirong Port in Shigatse.
The Trishuli eventually joins the Narayani, which flows into India’s Bihar state, where it is known as the Gandak.

Iran endures 6 months of US strikes as Trump’s war goals hit ‘dangerous impasse’
‘I don’t think the administration is any closer to finding a way out of this,’ an ex-diplomat says, as Tehran bets time is on its side
The Iran war has reached its endgame: a costly stalemate.
Six months after US and Israeli forces attacked Iran, killing its supreme leader and maiming his son and successor, the Iranian government is under economic siege, but it still holds power and believes it has time on its side.
A threat by US President Donald Trump to impose crippling new sanctions on Iran faces a fundamental problem: Tehran is betting he will not take the final step to break the stalemate – aggressively enforcing secondary sanctions on the countries keeping its economy afloat, foremost among them China and India.
Washington’s latest measures, announced on Monday, mark a new phase in the conflict that began on February 28, shifting the battlefield from missiles and air strikes to Iran’s oil revenues, banks and trading partners.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said the United States will cut off the financial lifelines sustaining Iran’s economy, while a US-led naval blockade restricts Tehran’s oil exports and access to hard currency.
“The [Trump] administration is groping in a sort of desperate fashion to try to find a pathway out of this,” said Aaron David Miller, a former US diplomat and senior fellow at Carnegie Endowment.

Kyiv Endures Hours-Long Drone Attack as Russia Strikes Ukraine From Odesa to Kharkiv
A prolonged Russian drone attack on Kyiv stretched into the morning of August 27, damaging a sports complex, a vehicle and other sites across several districts of the Ukrainian capital, as Russian strikes also hit multiple regions across Ukraine overnight.
Russia launched a massive combined missile and drone attack across Ukraine overnight and into the morning of August 27, repeatedly sending drones toward Kyiv while ballistic missiles and hundreds of UAVs struck cities and critical infrastructure across the country.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia attacked with two Onyx anti-ship missiles launched from occupied Crimea, Iskander-M and North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles fired from Russia’s Bryansk and Kursk regions, and 258 drones of several types.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The drone wave included Shahed attack drones, roughly one-third of them jet-powered, as well as Gerbera UAVs, S8000 Banderol missiles and Parodiya decoys. The main targets were the Odesa, Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Zaporizhzhia regions.
By 9 am, Ukrainian air defenses had destroyed or suppressed one Onyx missile, seven Iskander-M or KN-23 ballistic missiles, three Banderol missiles and 222 Russian drones, according to the Air Force.
Russian weapons reached targets at 15 locations, while debris from intercepted threats fell at another 11. Ukrainian officials said some Russian weapons also failed to reach their intended targets, with assessments still underway.
Kyiv and the surrounding region remained under threat well into the morning as additional Russian drones approached the capital following the overnight barrage.
In Kyiv’s Podilskyi district, debris from an intercepted drone fell in a courtyard between apartment buildings. Another educational facility was damaged in the Shevchenkivskyi district, while the blast wave shattered windows at a municipal medical facility.
A Russian drone also came down in the Holosiivskyi district, damaging a vehicle and sparking a fire that was later extinguished. In central Kyiv’s Pecherskyi district, a sports complex was damaged, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
No casualties were initially reported in the capital itself.
The surrounding Kyiv region suffered more extensive damage. Warehouse facilities caught fire in the Boryspil district, while warehouses were also damaged in the Fastiv district. Private homes were damaged in the Brovary and Vyshhorod districts.
“Also, warehouse facilities were damaged in the Fastiv district, as well as one private house each in the Brovary and Vyshhorod districts. Two people, a 15-year-old girl and a 73-year-old woman, were injured in the Russian attack,” Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said.
Odesa endured more than seven hours of attacks, with residents hearing explosions through much of the night. A 16-story apartment building, two educational facilities, a private home, infrastructure sites, an elevator complex, garages and vehicles were damaged.
“Damage was caused to a 16-story residential building, two educational institutions and a private home. Infrastructure facilities, the territory of an elevator, garages and residents’ vehicles were also damaged,” Odesa Regional Military Administration head Oleh Kiper said.
Three people, ages 24, 25 and 49, were later confirmed injured and hospitalized in moderate condition.
Emergency officials said fires broke out at several locations following the attack.
“As a result of the enemy shelling, fires broke out at several addresses. The facade, roof and windows of a 16-story building, an educational facility, a private house with a garage and vehicles were damaged.”
In Zaporizhzhia, at least three people were wounded as Russian strikes damaged vehicles and buildings and sparked a fire.
“As a result of the attacks, at least three people were injured. A vehicle and several buildings were damaged. A fire broke out. Two men and one woman were injured. They received medical assistance,” regional governor Ivan Fedorov said.
Russia also struck industrial facilities in the Kremenchuk district of the Poltava region and an energy facility in the Myrhorod district, triggering emergency power outages.
“One of the energy facilities in the Myrhorod district was also struck. An emergency power outage occurred. Consumers in seven settlements were temporarily left without electricity,” Poltava regional head Vitalii Diakivnych said.
By morning, parts of Poltava and several surrounding communities were also without power.
In Kharkiv, a Russian drone hit the fourth-floor balcony of an apartment building in the city’s Industrialnyi district.
“During the night, an enemy drone struck the balcony on the fourth floor of a multi-story residential building in the Industrialnyi district,” Kharkiv regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
A 30-year-old man suffered an acute stress reaction, while the building’s facade and windows were damaged.
One person was killed and others wounded in Kherson after strikes sparked fires, including at a two-story store. A woman was killed in Romny in the Sumy region after a residential building was hit, with four other people injured.
In Kryvyi Rih, Russian ballistic missiles struck the city, injuring three people and damaging an industrial facility and civilian infrastructure.
“Two men aged 46 and 58 were injured. Both are in hospital in moderate condition. Doctors are providing them with all necessary assistance. In addition to the enterprise, a primary healthcare center and civilian infrastructure facilities were damaged,” city official Oleksandr Vilkul said.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the assault as another large-scale combined Russian attack targeting both infrastructure and residential areas.
“The Russians struck critical infrastructure in the Poltava, Sumy, and Kherson regions. In the Kharkiv region, they struck residential buildings. In Kramatorsk, a guided aerial bomb hit a high-rise building. Four people were rescued by the State Emergency Service units. Three people were injured in Zaporizhzhia, and two in Kryvyi Rih. An apartment building was struck in Odesa. In Chubynske, Kyiv region, all the necessary emergency services are involved in putting out fires at enterprises following the drone strikes.”
Zelenskyy said the scale of Russia’s continuing missile investment makes additional air and ballistic missile defense support essential.
“Everything that strengthens the protection of our skies effectively saves the lives of Ukrainians every day. To bring down Russia’s desire to keep fighting, we need to effectively bring down the missiles Moscow clings to so much to keep the war going. I am grateful to everyone who understands this and helps.”
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Russia deliberately targeted ports, grain storage facilities, energy and industrial infrastructure during the attack.
“This is state terrorism. It does not show strength; it shows helplessness. Putin cannot and will not achieve anything on the battlefield. Instead, he is betting on terrorizing our cities, ports, and critical infrastructure.”
Sybiha warned that attacks on Ukraine’s agricultural and maritime infrastructure have consequences far beyond Ukraine itself.
“Attacks on grain infrastructure, ports, and maritime routes are especially harmful not only to Ukraine, but to approximately 400 million people around the world. One hectare of Ukrainian agricultural land feeds 18 people globally.”
He called for additional routes, export quotas, grain-storage equipment and international action to protect freedom of navigation, while also urging partners to strengthen Ukraine’s energy resilience ahead of winter.
“Ahead of winter, we also call for additional support packages to strengthen Ukraine’s energy resilience. We value every contribution: air defense, generation capacity, equipment, resources, and energy imports.”
Earlier, Russian forces struck the Kherson Combined Heat and Power Plant (CHP) with a guided aerial bomb, causing serious damage to the facility.
The Kherson CHP plant serves as the primary source of heating for the city and sustained significant damage in the attack.

London to Host Russian Rapper Instasamka, Who Praised Putin and Embraced Pro-Kremlin Rhetoric

London to Host Russian Rapper Instasamka, Who Praised Putin and Embraced Pro-Kremlin Rhetoric
Russian rapper and influencer Instasamka, who has praised Vladimir Putin, embraced increasingly nationalist rhetoric during Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, and publicly targeted fellow musicians over their perceived lack of loyalty to Russia, has announced a November performance in central London.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The artist, whose real name is Daria Yeropkina, is scheduled to perform an 18+ club show at London’s Emerald Theatre on November 14.
The venue sits at 8 Victoria Embankment, while the Eventbrite listing advertises the Russian star’s appearance as an “exclusive club show” running from 11 pm until 4:30 am. Her official website also lists London as part of her 2026–2027 world tour.
The planned appearance comes despite a public record that stretches far beyond the provocative lyrics and social-media scandals on which Instasamka built her career.
Years before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Instasamka explicitly praised Russian leader Vladimir Putin in her song “Bless,” declaring him “the best president” and presenting the statement as a “fact.” The track was released years before the invasion, but the rhetoric did not disappear as Russia’s war continued.
In November 2024, during the third year of the full-scale war, Instasamka and the Russian band Leningrad released a track titled “Russians Forward,” built around the repeated chant “Russians, forward.”
That same period also saw the release of “Pumping Oil,” a track portraying wealthy Russians flying to Courchevel, travelling business class and celebrating what the lyrics call “Russian style.”
Instasamka later told Russian journalist Ksenia Sobchak that she had originally conceived the track as “a gift to Russia,” adding: “Our country—we pump oil. We pump the world.”
Her political positioning became considerably more explicit in 2025. In July, Instasamka publicly attacked fellow performers Dora and Maybe Baby, accusing them of effectively betraying Russia and spreading harmful ideas among Russian youth.
Among her complaints was Dora’s association with music by rapper Face—who left Russia after condemning the invasion—and Ukrainian musician Yurii Kaplan of Valentin Strykalo, who has publicly supported Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Instasamka questioned why artists she portrayed as hostile to Russia were still allowed to perform in Russian cities and appear on state-controlled Channel One.
“Today they perform for Russian people, for our youth,” she wrote, accusing the singers of producing “destructive content” and asking: “What are you doing here?”
Days later, Instasamka appeared at Russia’s Public Chamber, a state-established consultative body, to discuss proposals concerning children and online content. Reports at the time noted that the appearance followed years in which the singer herself had faced pressure and concert cancellations from Russia’s conservative censorship apparatus.
Her transformation—from a performer targeted by Russia’s morality campaign into an artist publicly questioning the patriotism of other musicians—was striking enough that even figures within Russia’s establishment fought over her new role.
The controversy has already followed Instasamka beyond Russia. In April 2023, then-Latvian Foreign Minister Edgars Rinkēvičs placed her on Latvia’s list of undesirable persons, imposing an indefinite entry ban. The decision forced the cancellation of a planned Riga performance.
A claim circulating at the time that Instasamka had donated 900,000 rubles (about $12,000) to the Russian military was later shown to be unsubstantiated, and the singer publicly denied making such a donation.
Her own public rhetoric, however, requires no such disputed allegation. Just weeks before announcing the London show, Instasamka declared that she was leaving the Russian music market, had moved to Dubai, wanted to record her songs in English and intended to pursue a career abroad.
One day later, she admitted that the announcement had been a publicity stunt designed to generate attention for a new release. “I’m not going anywhere,” she said, adding that she would never stop making music for her existing audience.
Now, the performer who praised Putin, released “Russians Forward” during Russia’s invasion, called a pro-Russian song a “gift to Russia,” and publicly questioned whether artists deemed insufficiently patriotic should be allowed on Russian stages is preparing to take one of her own in the heart of London.
Instasamka’s planned London appearance comes as British cultural institutions face growing scrutiny over hosting Russian performers with ties to the Kremlin.
In 2025, Russian soprano Anna Netrebko—long dubbed “Putin’s diva” by critics—continued performing at London’s publicly funded Royal Opera House despite protests from Ukrainian diplomats and activists, who accused European venues of normalizing Kremlin-linked cultural figures during Russia’s war against Ukraine.

1968 seoul residence is reshaped with courtyard, annex and timber frame
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
11:50:40 UTC
20:50:40 KST

Tucked behind a long, narrow alley in Yeonhui-dong, Seoul, Saekdong House by Isak Chung and Jinpyo Hong transforms a residence originally built in 1968 through a combination of renovation and extension. Set deep within a landlocked plot and surrounded by neighboring buildings, the existing single-story house already sat unusually high, with elevated floor and ceiling levels intended to pull in more daylight and preserve views despite its enclosed position.
The architects chose not to correct these peculiarities so much as work with them. The entrance passage becomes a gradual transition from the city into a more secluded domestic world, while another inherited feature — an air-raid shelter beneath the house, typical of older Yeonhui-dong residences built amid tensions with North Korea — is folded into the new spatial sequence rather than treated as an inconvenient leftover.
Saekdong House transforms a 1968 residence in Seoul | images courtesy of Saekdong House
A COURTYARD REPLACES THE OLD LIVING ROOM
At the center of the intervention, the former living room was removed entirely to create an open courtyard, bringing daylight and ventilation into the previously enclosed plan. The building coverage released by this subtraction was then transferred to a new annex in the southern yard, an area that had previously received little light because of surrounding construction. In other words, one room disappears so another can appear elsewhere — a fairly productive bit of domestic accounting.
The existing structure was reinforced with timber framing, while a low-ceilinged internal corridor connects the reorganized spaces. Outside, a jade-green FRP eave protects circulation from rain, and the heavy original roof has been replaced with a lighter, restrained gable. Below ground, the floor of the former shelter was lowered to create usable headroom, with a sunken passage between the courtyard and annex bringing daylight and movement into the lower level.
a central courtyard brings light into the existing house
SAEKDONG TURNS CONTRAST INTO A DESIGN METHOD
The project takes its name from saekdong, a traditional Korean technique in which strips or patches of different colored fabrics are joined together to form a single textile. Chung and Hong translate that principle into architecture, allowing contrasting elements to remain visibly distinct while still belonging to the same composition. Old and new, timber and FRP, enclosed rooms and open courtyards all meet without being forced into visual uniformity.
That patchwork logic extends across scales: furniture and architecture, structure and finish, interior and exterior, main house and annex, as well as natural and constructed elements are treated as separate pieces within one domestic landscape. Rather than smoothing over the house’s oddities, the renovation makes them part of its character, turning a difficult urban plot, an aging structure and even a wartime shelter into ingredients for a home that feels intentionally assembled rather than simply updated.
timber framing reinforces the original structure
old and new elements remain visibly distinct throughout the house
Saekdong House combines renovation, extension and adaptive reuse

Nepal flood fury: How it started

Then came the human toll

PM Modi offers India’s support

Across China: Green computing powers diverse industries in China's Inner Mongolia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:21 CST
20:43:21 KST

HOHHOT, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- At a community health center in north China, an artificial intelligence (AI) system is used to undertake early screening instead of a doctor's traditional clinical consultations.
By leveraging big data and algorithms, the system analyzes basic blood test results to flag potential health risks, offering diagnostic support and enabling early medical intervention.
The Haidong Road Community Health Center in Hohhot, capital of Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, is one of the pioneering clinics showing how technology is reshaping everyday life, thanks to the region's burgeoning green computing infrastructure.
This AI-driven transformation is taking place across multiple sectors. In classrooms at a school affiliated with Inner Mongolia Normal University, smart blackboards respond to voice commands, while AI systems analyze student performance in real time and create personalized learning plans.
At a smart ecological ranch operated by Yili Group, China's leading dairy producer, in Hohhot, tens of thousands of dairy cows wear smart collars and ear tags that monitor vital signs around the clock, turning traditional herding into a precise, data-driven science.
These smart scenes are powered by a robust computing infrastructure. As a key hub in China's national "East Data, West Computing" project, Inner Mongolia is capitalizing on its abundant renewable energy and favorable climate to build a core base for green computing power.
With rich wind and solar resources, the region generated more than 270 billion kilowatt-hours of renewable power in 2025, ranking among the top nationwide. This clean energy provides a stable power supply for energy-intensive data centers.
As of July 2026, Inner Mongolia's total computing power reached 345,000 PFlops, with intelligent computing accounting for 326,000 PFlops -- a unit representing one quadrillion calculations per second. Notably, over 85 percent of the electricity used by regional data centers comes from green power.
The region has developed a dual-hub strategy centered on Hohhot and Ulanqab. The two centers operate in synergy and complement each other, efficiently handling high-intensity AI computing tasks for both industrial and public sectors.
Inner Mongolia's green computing initiative aligns with China's broader national strategy. The country's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) explicitly calls for the coordinated development of green power and computing infrastructure.
Nationally, the results of this green transition are already clear. By the end of 2025, China had built 42 supercomputing clusters, each with more than 10,000 AI acceleration cards. The country's eight national computing hubs now account for more than 80 percent of total intelligent computing capacity.
"Inner Mongolia's practice is a vivid microcosm of China's broader shift toward greener and more intensive computing," said Li Donghong, vice dean at the Institute for Global Industry, Tsinghua University.
By converting clean energy advantage into computing power, the region has not only bridged the gap between eastern China's computing demand and its energy constraints, but also offered a replicable model for the low-carbon development of global AI industry, Li said. ■

Economic Watch: New growth drivers power China's industrial profit surge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:14 CST
20:43:14 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- China's burgeoning new growth drivers are fueling a sustained surge in industrial profits, reflecting the country's accelerating shift toward innovation-driven development.
Profits of China's industrial firms above designated size increased 17.6 percent year on year during the first seven months of 2026, data from the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) showed on Thursday.
These industrial firms with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan (about 2.95 million U.S. dollars) saw their combined profits reach 4.58 trillion yuan in the January-July period, according to the data.
In the three major sectors, mining industry profits jumped 34.9 percent to 666.05 billion yuan, and manufacturing profits climbed 18.8 percent to nearly 3.44 trillion yuan. However, profits in the power, heat, gas and water production and supply sector fell 5.8 percent to 478.42 billion yuan.
Among major industries, the computer, communications and other electronic equipment manufacturing sector saw profits surge 110 percent. Non-ferrous metal smelting and rolling processing jumped 91.8 percent, chemical raw materials and products manufacturing rose 56.6 percent, and coal mining and washing increased 50.4 percent. The petroleum, coal and other fuel processing sector turned from losses to profits.
Yu Weining, an NBS statistician, attributed the robust gains to the rapid expansion of the "AI Plus" initiative and booming demand for computing power, which boosted product demand, pushed up prices and underpinned rapid profit growth in AI-related electronic industries.
Pang Ming, a researcher with the China Chief Economist Forum, said that the remarkable growth fundamentally reflects the accelerated development of new quality productive forces and the synchronized cyclical resonance of the global AI and consumer electronics industrial chains.
Notably, high-end segments represented by integrated circuits, such as memory chips, have seen dividend-driven explosive growth. With the accelerated application of AI, big data, and cloud computing, the market space for the electronic information industry has expanded significantly, driving concurrent growth in upstream components and related manufacturing sectors, Pang said.
Meanwhile, the recovery of export orders and the improved domestic industrial chain support have also provided solid backing for the profitability of industrial firms.
Pang also noted that some traditional industries remain under pressure, highlighting the mismatch between energy costs and demand structure.
The NBS data also showed that in the first seven months, the combined revenue of these industrial firms reached 80.92 trillion yuan, up 6.5 percent year on year, while operating costs increased 5.9 percent to 68.79 trillion yuan.
Yu attributed the relatively fast profit growth to steady industrial production and the rapid expansion of new growth drivers.
Yu highlighted the electronic sector as the main pillar, with profits surging 110 percent and contributing 9.3 percentage points to the overall industrial profit growth.
High-tech manufacturing also showed strong momentum, with profits up 50.1 percent, contributing 9.6 percentage points to overall industrial profit growth. Raw material manufacturing profits rose 55.2 percent, adding 7.1 percentage points.
Yu noted that the profit margin on revenue stood at 5.66 percent in the first seven months, reaching the highest level for the same period since 2023.
However, Yu cautioned that the international environment remains complex and challenging, while the domestic imbalance of strong supply and weak demand is still prominent. He called for further efforts to expand domestic demand, optimize supply, and advance the upgrading of traditional industries, the growth of emerging sectors and the cultivation of future industries to consolidate the foundation for high-quality industrial development.
Pang said that the industrial economy remains in a transition period characterized by the strengthening of new driving forces and the pressure on old ones. Maintaining profit momentum continues to rely on policy support and market demand recovery.
In July alone, profits of major industrial firms grew 11.2 percent year on year, according to the NBS.
Looking ahead, with the ongoing release of policy dividends and the deep stimulation of endogenous momentum, the performance of industrial enterprises is expected to make solid progress toward high-quality development, Pang added. ■

Chinese art dialogue exhibition opens in New Zealand
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:06 CST
20:43:06 KST

Wellington Mayor Andrew Little (2nd R, front) views Chinese painting on display at the opening ceremony of an international art dialogue exhibition by China National Academy of Painting in Wellington, New Zealand, Aug. 27, 2026. An international art dialogue exhibition by China National Academy of Painting kicked off in the New Zealand capital on Thursday in celebration of the 20th anniversary of sister city relations between Wellington and Beijing. (Photo by Meng Tao/Xinhua)
WELLINGTON, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- An international art dialogue exhibition by China National Academy of Painting kicked off in the New Zealand capital on Thursday in celebration of the 20th anniversary of sister city relations between Wellington and Beijing.
The 39 art pieces on display were organized into four sections, namely Observing the Way with a Clear Mind, Figures in Myriad Forms, Scenery of the Four Seasons and Timeless Bronze and Stone Inscriptions. Together, they showcase contemporary creative practices in Chinese landscape, figure and bird-and-flower painting, alongside calligraphy and seal carving, tracing the evolution of these traditions from classical paradigms to present-day expressions.
A Chinese artist also painted a plum blossom on the spot.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Wellington Mayor Andrew Little noted that 20 years ago, New Zealand and China were negotiating in the final stages of a free trade agreement. "It reminds us of the importance of diplomacy and relationships being conducted at all levels," he said, adding that relationships between citizens, people, cities, and communities are very important.
Different cultures have their own distinct histories and traditions, yet feelings for nature, life and beauty can resonate with one another through art, said Yan Dongsheng, chairman of the Artistic Committee of China National Academy of Painting.
"'Embracing Diversity' conveys an open and inclusive cultural spirit," he added. "We choose this as the title of this exhibition in the sincere hope that art can bring different cultures together, enable mutual learning, and enhance understanding through exchange and dialogue."
On behalf of Ambassador Wang Xiaolong, Minister Counsellor Zhang Xinyu at the Chinese Embassy in New Zealand stressed that both China and New Zealand are multicultural nations built on equality, mutual respect and cooperation. "Across mountains and seas, we hope this exhibition could serve as a bridge, channeling the spirit of the Global Civilization Initiative: equality, mutual learning, dialogue and inclusiveness," she said.
After the inaugural leg in Wellington, the exhibition will tour other major New Zealand cities until Oct. 7, including Christchurch, Hamilton and Auckland. ■

China urges Philippines to remove unlawfully "grounded" vessel from Ren'ai Jiao
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:43:01 CST
20:43:01 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese defense spokesperson on Thursday urged the Philippines to tow away a vessel unlawfully "grounded" at Ren'ai Jiao and cease all provocative acts in the South China Sea.
Zhang Xiaogang, a spokesperson for China's Ministry of National Defense, made the remarks at a press conference in response to a media query regarding the Philippine vessel BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57), which recently received a fresh shipment of supplies.
It was reported that the Philippine side has repeatedly attempted to use such resupply missions to smuggle in reinforcement materials in order to permanently anchor the vessel on the reef.
Ren'ai Jiao is part of China's Nansha Qundao, Zhang said, noting that China and the Philippines had reached a provisional arrangement on the humanitarian resupply of living necessities for handling the situation at Ren'ai Jiao.
China would not accept any attempt by the Philippines to deliver construction materials, build fixed facilities or establish a permanent outpost on the reef, Zhang said, adding that China would take measures to prevent such actions in accordance with the law.
He said China remained committed to safeguarding its territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, while upholding peace and stability in the South China Sea. ■

Feature: The ball and the crutches -- Gaza's amputee children reclaim a lost childhood
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:42:47 CST
20:42:47 KST

GAZA, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Eleven-year-old Malak Khader balances on her crutches at the center of a five-a-side football pitch in Gaza City, her eyes fixed on the ball as it weaves between feet and metal poles.
One crutch forward, then the other, she moves cautiously into the game as her teammates pass the ball and coaches call out instructions.
For Khader and the other children here, football is not just a game. It is a way to process loss, regain confidence in bodies altered by war, and piece together a shattered childhood.
Khader lost her right leg during the war. She also lost her entire family after a bombing struck the school where they were sheltering.
"I was trapped under the rubble for hours," she tells Xinhua. "I'm the only survivor from my family."
Pulled from the rubble, the girl underwent multiple surgeries to treat injuries to her abdomen, leg and hand.
Before her injury, she had never played football. But afterward, she found the pitch, a place where, for a few hours, the weight of her new reality lifts.
Every Saturday, she joins other children who have lost limbs or suffered injuries during the conflict, "kicking" the ball across the dusty field.
"Football is the only thing that makes me feel happy and joyful these days," Khader says. "It makes me forget my injury, the tent I live in and the difficult life that has become our daily reality."
On the other side of the pitch, 13-year-old Hanin Ayoub Shaaban Ghanem moves with deliberate precision.
She extends one crutch, nudges the ball with her left foot, and pushes toward the goal in measured strides.
Ghanem lost her right leg during the war, and her sister was killed. Afterward, she withdrew into isolation.
"At first, I would sit alone and feel different from the other children," Ghanem recalls. "I kept thinking about my injury and my sister whom I had lost. I felt that everything had changed suddenly and that I could no longer live as I used to."
Then came football.
"When I started coming to the playground and playing with the other children, I began to feel that I wasn't alone," Ghanem says. "At first, I was afraid I wouldn't be able to keep up with them, but they encouraged and helped me."
"Now I try, I move, and I learn how to play using my crutch and my other leg. I feel that I can do things I never thought I could do," Ghanem says.
"When I play, I feel free, like any other child. I don't think about the injury, the tent or the war. I just want to play, laugh and feel that I can keep going."
Ahmed Badwan, a coach with the Palestine Amputee Football Association, says the group he coaches includes about 15 girls and a similar number of boys. The association currently supports more than 90 amputees across Gaza.
"The goal is not only to teach children how to play football," Badwan explains, "but also to help them overcome the psychological trauma they experienced during the war and after their amputations. We try to help them adapt to their new reality and regain their self-confidence."
According to the Gaza-based social development authorities, over 5,000 amputations have been recorded in the enclave, including 700 among children. About 10,000 children now live with permanent disabilities, while fewer than a quarter of those needing prosthetic limbs have received them.
Badwan dreams of one day taking the children to international matches and championships, so they might see themselves not only as survivors, but also as athletes.
For Khader and Ghanem, such stages may still feel distant. But for now, they keep coming back to the pitch, playing with friends, chasing the ball, and laughing in the dust. ■

Thailand's exports surge 21.6 pct in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
19:42:33 CST
20:42:33 KST

BANGKOK, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's exports grew for the 25th straight month in July, driven by strong global demand for technology-related and digital infrastructure products and a rebound in agricultural shipments, official data showed on Thursday.
Exports, a key driver of the Southeast Asian country's economic growth, expanded 21.6 pct year-on-year last month to 34.79 billion U.S. dollars, accelerating from a 20.8 percent gain in June, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
Industrial product shipments soared 24.2 percent year-on-year, marking the 28th consecutive month of expansion, fueled by sales of video and audio equipment, as well as telephones, computers, and their related components.
Exports of agricultural goods increased for the first time in three months, rising 0.6 percent year-on-year in July, while agro-industrial products fell by 3.3 percent.
The July data also indicated that imports surged 36.7 percent from a year earlier to 38.40 billion dollars, resulting in a monthly trade deficit of 3.61 billion dollars.
For the first seven months of 2026, exports rose 18.2 percent to 231.53 billion dollars, while imports advanced 37.8 percent to 266.89 billion dollars, yielding a trade deficit of 35.35 billion dollars.
Looking ahead, Thai export growth is expected to remain robust in the remainder of 2026, supported by ongoing demand for artificial intelligence-related products, said Nantapong Chiralerspong, director-general of the ministry's trade policy and strategy office.
However, downward pressures from geopolitical tensions in the Middle East and uncertainties surrounding trade barriers remain risk factors that could hamper growth momentum, Nantapong told a news conference.
Last month, the ministry upwardly revised its export outlook to a rise between 5 percent and 11 percent this year, after a 13.1 percent expansion was recorded in 2025. ■
