How a 95 percent drop in Hormuz traffic changed global shipping
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:29:06 UTC
18:29:06 KST

How a 95 percent drop in Hormuz traffic changed global shipping
A crisis in one narrow passage has disrupted an industry that carries about 80 percent of the world’s trade.
Six months into the United States-Israel war on Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz continues to drive one of the worst maritime shipping disruptions in decades.
Traffic through the 33km (21-mile) chokepoint has fallen from more than 100 vessels a day to just five, disrupting the flow of oil, gas and goods worldwide.
Al Jazeera visualises how a crisis in one narrow passage has disrupted an industry that carries about 80 percent of the world’s trade.
About 80 percent of goods move by sea
Almost everything people buy, from the fuel in their cars to the grain in their bread, has likely spent time on board a vessel at sea.
About 80 percent of world trade by volume moves by sea at some point, making maritime shipping essential to the global economy, according to UNCTAD, the UN’s trade and development body.
Not all ships are created equal. Different vessels are built for various purposes, from moving oil to the goods we rely on every day.
- Oil tankers are among the largest ships and carry energy products such as crude oil, refined petroleum, and chemicals. Most crude oil is transported by Very Large Crude Carriers, or VLCCs, which can access a wide range of ports and carry about two million barrels of crude.
- Container ships transport consumer goods such as phones and clothing in stacked steel boxes known as containers. Some are enormous, measuring more than 400m (1,312 feet) long and carrying more than 20,000 containers.
- Dry bulk carriers transport raw materials like grain, coal and iron ore. Lloyd’s List estimates they made about 7,000 Hormuz transits a year, or about 20 a day, before the war.
- General cargo ships carry mixed goods like steel and machinery, while Ro-Ro ships transport wheeled cargo such as cars, trucks and heavy machinery.
The Middle East’s shipping problem
The Strait of Hormuz is a critical chokepoint for global energy trade. It is one of three main gateways in the Middle East, carrying more than one-third of global seaborne crude oil and nearly one-third of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) flows, along with significant volumes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) and refined petroleum products.
“That’s probably the first time we’ve really seen a major constriction of a choke point,” Richard Matthews, director of consultancy and research at Gibson Shipbrokers, a London-based shipbroking and maritime advisory service, told Al Jazeera.
He explained that what makes the Strait of Hormuz different from other chokepoints is “there is no alternative maritime route. There are some pipelines, but there’s no alternative, which is why it’s been so significant in terms of cargo volume.”
Ports along the Gulf are where much of the region’s energy begins its journey to the rest of the world.
What used to pass through the Strait of Hormuz?
According to UNCTAD data, the week before the Iran war began, average flows of crude oil through the Strait of Hormuz accounted for roughly 38 percent of the global total, LPG was 29 percent and LNG was 19 percent.
Crude exports from the Gulf region have dropped by nearly half (47 percent) compared with before the war, down from about 17 million barrels a day in 2025 to roughly nine million bpd as of August 2026. According to Reuters, analysts estimate that five to seven million barrels of Gulf oil a day are currently being disrupted.
Direct exports of crude oil moving via the strait have fallen to an average of just 2.2 million bpd, according to Kpler, a data and analytics company that tracks global commodity markets and trade flows.
The chart below shows the combined crude oil shipments from the Gulf’s largest oil-producing countries – Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran and Kuwait – dropping sharply since the start of the war from roughly 400 million barrels in February to about 200 million barrels in July.
From 100 ships daily to five
Before the war, about 100 ships passed through the Strait of Hormuz each day, more than half of them tankers, carrying tens of millions of barrels of oil.
That collapsed within days of the February 28 US-Israeli strikes on Iran. After the IRGC announced the strait’s closure on March 2, traffic fell to an average of five vessels a day and stayed there through the April ceasefire and the US blockade of Iranian ports.
A June 17 interim agreement lifted the daily average to 20, still only one-fifth of normal traffic, before the US resumed its blockade on July 14 and traffic sank back to five per day.
Today, the strait remains, in effect, closed. From July 15 to August 23, an average of about five vessels a day passed through, marking an almost 95 percent decrease from pre-war traffic levels. What little traffic remains consists mostly of tankers operating under naval escort or with their tracking systems switched off.
The map below shows how the number of vessels passing through the strait plummeted during the first four days of the war.
Before the war, the Strait of Hormuz functioned as one shared waterway, with ships using standard shipping lanes mainly through the centre of the strait, supported by the International Maritime Organization (IMO). These routes were chosen based on port schedules, contracts and safety.
The little traffic now moving through the strait runs through a workaround, with the waterway split into two distinct paths after Iran and Oman agreed to temporary shipping routes, using their respective territorial waters to help vessels pass through. Iranian authorities insist ships use its northern route, which runs along its coastline near Larak and Qeshm islands and connects directly to Iranian ports and terminals.
But in April, the US military placed a naval blockade on Iranian ports to stop roughly two million barrels of Iranian oil from reaching the rest of the world.
Which countries rely most on Middle East oil?
For people and businesses further down the chain, the disruption is being felt through the rising cost of essentials.
Countries which rely heavily on oil, gas and fertiliser from the Gulf are facing higher prices, longer waits for shipments and the need to find alternative suppliers. Even where deals have been struck to keep goods moving, the cost of doing so is being passed through the supply chain.
The countries that rely most heavily on Middle Eastern oil include Eritrea and Madagascar, which each source about 90 percent of their oil from the region, followed by Pakistan which gets 78 percent, Japan (77 percent) and Kenya (77 percent).
Where are ships going now?
Hormuz’s closure has redrawn global shipping flows, pushing traffic away from the Gulf and towards the Red Sea and Southeast Asia, with Singapore and Malaysia emerging as hubs for redirected energy.
Russia’s fuel oil shipments to Singapore and Malaysia, for example, rose 2.5 times month-on-month in July, making the region an increasingly important hub for redirected energy flows.
The table below shows how port traffic changed across countries after the conflict began. Kuwait saw the steepest fall, with daily port calls – when a ship arrives at a port – dropping by 86 percent. Geographically, Kuwait’s only maritime route to the open sea runs through the Strait of Hormuz.
Ukraine saw the second-largest percentage drop, driven by ongoing drone attacks on shipping in the Baltic and Black seas. The United Arab Emirates saw the third-largest percentage drop of 69 percent, with port calls dropping from 78 daily to 24. Qatar, Iraq and Bahrain saw similar declines of about 66-68 percent.
Saudi Arabia saw a smaller drop in port calls – down 15 percent compared with its neighbours, thanks to its network of pipelines and access to Red Sea ports, which handled higher oil shipment volumes, even after Houthi forces declared a naval blockade against the kingdom on July 20.
“Once the Middle East war kicked off, we suddenly saw more ship owners being willing to go into the Red Sea because there were far fewer options to get to the crew they needed to get to. And the Houthi risk just seems to have diminished,” Matthews of Gibsons said.
What happens next?
For those working in shipping, the crisis has already surpassed many of the disruptions of recent years. Matthews, who has worked in the industry since 2009 in the wake of the financial crisis, said even the COVID-19 pandemic was a different kind of shock, one where the path to recovery was easier to see.
He explained: “We’ve gone from having to deal with one conflict or ‘black swan’ event every five years, let’s say, to having probably four of them or maybe five of them since 2020.
“It’s much easier now to disrupt shipping through drones and other sorts of attacks than it was before. Whereas, if you go back 10 years ago, the main threat to shipping was probably Somali piracy, now you’ve got any form, where you’ve got Ukrainian drones hitting shipping or Russian drones hitting shipping, you’ve got the same situation in Hormuz again, and it’s easier for the Houthis to target ships in the Bab al-Mandeb region.”
For consumers, one of the most obvious impacts of the Hormuz crisis has been on oil prices, which are some 20 percent higher than before the war, recovering from highs of more than $130 a barrel in April. However, some experts argue that the price increase is somewhat muted, saying that the oil and shipping markets have been adaptive and resilient.
Matthews explained that, before the war began, oil stocks and inventories were building massively, providing a buffer to supply shocks.
“It’s only around now where we’ve kind of burnt through that buffer,” Matthews said. “So we’re now at the stage where the next six months could look much more volatile and critical in terms of inventories if things don’t change soon.”

Scientists switch on a strange new form of magnetism in an ultrathin material
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:23:20 UTC
18:23:20 KST

Scientists switch on a strange new form of magnetism in an ultrathin material
Researchers found that ultrathin ruthenium dioxide can show signs of an unusual new form of magnetism when its atomic structure is placed under strain.
- Date:
- August 27, 2026
- Source:
- Rice University
- Summary:
- Scientists have found a surprising way to potentially switch on an unusual form of magnetism in ruthenium dioxide, a material that normally appears nonmagnetic. When the material was made into an ultrathin film only a few atomic layers thick and placed under strain, its electrons developed patterns consistent with altermagnetism, a recently proposed magnetic state with promising uses in advanced electronics.
- Share:
A recently proposed form of magnetism known as altermagnetism could eventually help researchers make computer memory smaller, faster, and more efficient. Now, scientists have found evidence that ruthenium dioxide, a quantum material previously considered nonmagnetic in its bulk form, may display this unusual magnetic behavior when prepared as an ultrathin film only a few atomic layers thick.
Rice University physicist Ming Yi, working with Bharat Jalan of the University of Minnesota and Milan Radovic of the Paul Scherrer Institute, reported the findings in Science Advances.
"Ruthenium dioxide was one of the first materials to be proposed as an altermagnetic candidate, but studies on its bulk form didn't return evidence of magnetism," said Yi, an associate professor of physics and astronomy. "Our research shows that its ultrathin form, on the other hand, may be the key in making it magnetic."
Detecting Magnetism Through Electron Spins
To investigate the magnetic state of ultrathin ruthenium dioxide, the researchers examined its spin texture. Spin texture describes how a material's magnetic moments -- the spins of its electrons -- are arranged in space. Those patterns can reveal whether a material is magnetic and, if so, what kind of magnetism it exhibits.
The team measured these patterns using a technique called spin-resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy.
"After analyzing our measurements, including informing our interpretation with theoretical calculations, we found that, in our experimental conditions, the ruthenium dioxide shows spin textures consistent with unconventional magnetism," said Yichen Zhang, the first author on the paper and a recent Rice graduate. "This suggests that bulk and ultrathin ruthenium dioxide, under the right conditions, may have distinctly different magnetic properties."
Atomic Strain May Act as a Magnetic Control
The researchers found that the unusual spin behavior appeared under specific conditions. In particular, the electron structure of the ultrathin ruthenium dioxide had to experience lattice strain, which places pressure on the material's atomic structure.
Without that strain, as in the material's natural bulk form, the electron spins did not show signs of altermagnetism.
"The strain-dependent nature suggests that we may be able to use lattice strain as a tuning knob to induce or control altermagnetism," Zhang said. "This could be extremely useful when thinking about next-generation spintronics and RAM architectures."
The result raises the possibility that researchers could deliberately adjust lattice strain to control magnetic behavior in future electronic materials. Such control could prove valuable for spintronics, a field that uses electron spin as well as electrical charge to process and store information, and for new computer memory designs.
A Longstanding Debate Over Ruthenium Dioxide
The findings also highlight how difficult it can be to identify and describe the behavior of quantum materials. Ruthenium dioxide has been at the center of a lengthy scientific debate as physicists tried to determine whether its bulk form was magnetic. Researchers ultimately reached a consensus that bulk ruthenium dioxide does not exhibit magnetism.
The new work suggests that changing the material's dimensions and placing its atomic structure under strain can produce very different behavior.
"This work shows just how complex these questions can be," Yi said. "The high quality material prep and the careful measurement protocol were critical to our observation of the correct electron spin properties. The results required careful analysis of spin-resolved angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Through this, we were able to determine not only the magnetic state symmetries but a potential way to manipulate it in next-generation quantum materials."
This work was funded by the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0026179, DE-SC0020211, DE-SC0024710), the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation's EPiQS Initiative (GBMF9470) and the Robert A. Welch Foundation (C-2175).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Rice University. Original written by Rachel Leeson. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yichen Zhang, Seung Gyo Jeong, Luca Buiarelli, Seungjun Lee, Yucheng Guo, Jiaqin Wen, Hang Li, Sreejith Nair, In Hyeok Choi, Zheng Ren, Ziqin Yue, Jounghoon Hyun, Tieqiong Zhang, Alexei Fedorov, Sung-Kwan Mo, Hojoon Lim, Adrian Hunt, Iradwikanari Waluyo, Junichiro Kono, Ján Minár, Jong Seok Lee, Tony Low, Turan Birol, Rafael M. Fernandes, Milan Radovic, Bharat Jalan, Ming Yi. Observation of mirror-odd and mirror-even spin texture in ultrathin epitaxially strained RuO 2 films. Science Advances, 2026; 12 (31) DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aec2917

Russia preparing to mobilise 600,000 in new wave, Ukrainian intelligence services say
Russia's General Staff has drawn up a plan to mobilise an additional 600,000 people in 2026-2027, with 300,000 to be called up each year. Most of them are expected to reinforce units fighting against Ukraine and newly formed military units.
Source: a briefing by Defence Intelligence of Ukraine and the Foreign Intelligence Service, which has been released on the President's Office website
Quote: "Ukraine has information that the Russian General Staff has already prepared a scenario for the additional mobilisation of 600,000 people within the specified time frames this year and next.
First and foremost, they plan to bring up to full strength the formations and military units fighting against Ukrainians, as well as units of the Russian armed forces that are currently being formed."
Details: The Ukrainian intelligence agencies said Russia is considering additional mobilisation because of mounting battlefield losses and a slowdown in the recruitment of contract soldiers.
Between January and July 2026, Russia lost around 240,000 personnel, including at least 140,000 killed or otherwise permanently lost. In the same period, 232,000 people were recruited under contract.
As part of preparations for a new wave of mobilisation, Russia is amending its legislation, tightening military registration requirements and expanding recruitment among convicts. People convicted of offences such as trafficking weapons, explosives, radioactive materials and drugs, as well as banditry, involvement in criminal organisations and organising illegal migration, could be allowed to serve.
The Russian leadership has also approved the recruitment of certain categories of female convicts for mobilisation or contract service.
The mobilised personnel could receive between 15 and 60 days' training. Ukrainian intelligence agencies say some may be trained at military training grounds in Belarus.
Internal Russian documents reportedly justify the need for mobilisation in part by growing dissatisfaction with the war in Russia's regions – reaching as high as 69% in some areas – and a decline in the number of people willing to sign military contracts.
Russia has introduced digital call-up notices and is preparing to introduce additional restrictions, including bans on leaving the country, taking out loans and conducting property transactions, as well as the revocation of driving licences and freezing of bank accounts.
Ukraine's intelligence agencies believe that Russian leader Vladimir Putin is most likely to make a decision on additional mobilisation after the State Duma elections on 18-20 September.
Previously: The Wall Street Journal reported that the Russian military had conducted an exercise in Kaliningrad Oblast in July to test procedures for mobilising local residents.

Türkiye orders local private schools to drop foreign names
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:21:22 UTC
18:21:22 KST

The Education Ministry has ordered all local private schools to drop their foreign names and adopt Turkish titles by Oct. 1, 2026, to protect national values and prevent cultural erosion.
The sweeping mandate requires previously licensed institutions to change their current designations to comply with the revised Private Educational Institutions Regulation. Minority schools, international facilities and language courses remain strictly exempt from the new rule and will continue to operate under their established identities.
Authorities will evaluate proposed names based on their alignment with the general goals of Turkish national education. The regulation dictates names must carry a specific Turkish meaning and respect the moral, human and cultural values of the Turkish nation.
The legislative shift aims to prevent cultural degeneration, identity erosion, linguistic alienation and any negative impact on students’ psychosocial development. Officials warned they will reject any names that conflict with these constitutional principles regarding the preservation of national culture.
The measure aligns with a broader state policy to preserve the Turkish language in the public sphere, sweeping across multiple sectors. Local municipalities frequently conduct market sweeps to enforce strict signage rules, penalizing businesses using foreign words on their storefronts or menus.
Inspectors recently intensified their crackdowns in major metropolitan centers, issuing administrative fines to shop owners who fail to replace non-Turkish signs within a given timeframe. The government maintains these linguistic regulations are vital to maintaining a cohesive national identity as globalized branding increasingly penetrates local markets and educational spheres. Schools that fail to submit their new names before the deadline will face administrative action.

Xinhua Headlines: Xi's SCO attendance, state visits to energize regional cooperation, global development
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
17:19:11 CST
18:19:11 KST

* Chinese President Xi Jinping will attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 in Bishkek and pay state visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt from Aug. 30 to Sept. 3.
* Guided by the Shanghai Spirit, the SCO has expanded from six founding members to a 27-nation family, standing out as a model for a new type of international relations.
* In recent years, under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China and Kyrgyzstan have elevated their ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era in the spirit of solidarity and mutual benefit.
* Since the establishment of diplomatic ties in 1956, China and Egypt have worked together to deepen their relationship, and strengthen friendship, solidarity and mutually beneficial cooperation.
BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- From Aug. 30 to Sept. 3, Chinese President Xi Jinping will attend the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit 2026 in Bishkek and pay state visits to Kyrgyzstan and Egypt.
Amid an ever-evolving international landscape, Xi's upcoming trip is expected to foster collaboration among all parties to deepen practical cooperation. By pooling the strengths of the Global South, it is set to advance global governance reform, promote world peace and development, and facilitate the building of a community with a shared future for humanity.
CARRYING FORWARD "SHANGHAI SPIRIT"
Rows of freight trains stand ready at the China-SCO Demonstration Area in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, awaiting departure for Central Asia and Europe -- a striking visual testament to the growing vitality of SCO cooperation.
Guided by the Shanghai Spirit of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diverse civilizations and pursuit of common development, the SCO has expanded from six founding members to a 27-nation family. Demonstrating strong vitality and broad appeal, it has stood out as a model for a new type of international relations.
"Looking back, we have weathered the storms on our journey and emerged stronger because we have adhered to the Shanghai Spirit," Xi said in his speech at the 25th Meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the SCO in north China's port city of Tianjin last year.
Xi has attended every SCO summit since 2013, steadily shaping the grouping's development along the way. He has repeatedly called for carrying forward the "Shanghai Spirit" and forging an even closer SCO community with a shared future.
At the SCO Astana summit in 2024, Xi called for building a common home featuring solidarity and mutual trust, peace and tranquility, prosperity and development, good-neighborliness and friendship, as well as fairness and justice.
To further unlock the organization's potential, Xi told fellow SCO leaders at the Tianjin summit to seek common ground while shelving differences, pursue mutual benefit and win-win results, champion openness and inclusiveness, uphold fairness and justice, and strive for real results and high efficiency.
Also at the Tianjin summit, the organization mapped out a strategic blueprint for its development over the next decade and ushered in a new stage of high-quality development. Over the past year, China has implemented the major initiatives proposed by Xi and contributed to regional development through concrete actions.
Seven cooperation platforms -- covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, higher education, vocational and technical education, and artificial intelligence -- have been launched, generating more than 160 projects. Meanwhile, steady implementation of the action plan for high-quality development of economic and trade cooperation continues to drive trade growth between China and SCO member states.
In the process of building an SCO community with a shared future, China has been both an architect and a driving force, said Sayfiddin Juraev, a professor of political science at Tashkent State University of Oriental Studies.
It is also at the Tianjin summit that Xi proposed the Global Governance Initiative, a vision that has rallied broad support across the international community.
Xi's vision consistently shapes not only the SCO's current agenda but also its long-term operating strategy, Sheradil Baktygulov, director of the Kyrgyz Institute of World Politics, told Xinhua. "The SCO's values of peace, equality, and mutually beneficial cooperation are reaching the global level."
NEW CHAPTER OF PARTNERSHIP
China and Kyrgyzstan, linked by mountains and rivers and united by close bonds between their peoples, are good neighbors, good friends and good partners, said Xi during talks with Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov in Beijing on Feb. 5, 2025.
Last year marked a high point in China-Kyrgyzstan diplomacy, with the two leaders meeting three times. Key engagements also included their back-to-back meetings on the sidelines of the second China-Central Asia Summit in the Kazakh capital of Astana in June and the SCO summit in Tianjin in August.
Kyrgyzstan's most valuable advantage is that it is a neighbor of China, Japarov has said. Invoking the ancient Chinese proverb -- "Amity and good-neighborliness are invaluable to a country" -- he noted that the saying aptly captures the essence of Kyrgyzstan-China relations.
Since establishing diplomatic ties more than 30 years ago, China and Kyrgyzstan have been supporting each other amid shifting global dynamics.
In recent years, under the strategic guidance of the two heads of state, China and Kyrgyzstan have elevated their ties to a comprehensive strategic partnership for a new era in the spirit of solidarity and mutual benefit, and are working together to build a China-Kyrgyzstan community with a shared future featuring good-neighborliness, friendship, and shared prosperity.
Practical cooperation between the two countries is gaining strong momentum, as seen in the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway project, with construction well underway.
In a congratulatory letter to the commencement ceremony of the project in December 2024, Xi said that the construction of the railway is a strategic decision made by the three governments to promote regional connectivity, prosperity and stability, which also reflects the shared aspiration of the three countries to open up this strategic corridor.
Located in Central Asia, Kyrgyzstan was among the first countries to actively participate in Belt and Road cooperation. Projects such as the Chinese-built new North-South highway and the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan highway enhanced regional connectivity and facilitated economic exchanges.
For years, China has been one of Kyrgyzstan's most important trade and investment partners, with two-way trade amounting to 27.2 billion U.S. dollars in 2025, up 19.8 percent year on year.
From pure honey to fresh orchard fruit, high-quality Kyrgyz agricultural goods are becoming household favorites across China. Meanwhile, on the streets of Kyrgyzstan, sleek Chinese new-energy vehicles are quickly becoming a familiar sight.
At the Irkeshtam Port on the China-Kyrgyzstan border, 24-hour freight clearance operations have helped speed up the flow of goods, streamlining cross-border trade for businesses on both sides.
The port also serves as a key gateway for Chinese exports, ranging from machinery to home appliances, as they travel onward to markets across Central Asia and Europe.
The bond between China and Kyrgyzstan runs deeper than trade -- it is also reflected in the growing exchange between their peoples.
In Bishkek, the Luban Workshop is helping train a new generation of skilled professionals. Its curriculum standards in areas such as smart water management and electrical equipment have been incorporated into Kyrgyzstan's national education system.
The two countries have also maintained close coordination on the international stage, working together within multilateral platforms such as the United Nations and the China-Central Asia mechanism.
"We are witnessing one of the most meaningful and fruitful periods in the history of Kyrgyz-Chinese bilateral relations," said former Kyrgyz Foreign Minister Alikbek Jekshenkulov. Xi's upcoming visit will represent not only another milestone, but also an opportunity to elevate bilateral ties to a new level, he added.
A MODEL OF FRIENDSHIP
Since the establishment of diplomatic ties in 1956, China and Egypt have worked together to deepen their relationship, and strengthen friendship, solidarity and mutually beneficial cooperation.
"China-Egypt relations have become a model of amity, solidarity and cooperation among developing countries, as well as a benchmark for collective cooperation between China and Arab states and between China and Africa, thereby advancing steadily toward building a China-Egypt community with a shared future in the new era," Xi said on May 30 in a congratulatory message to Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on the 70th anniversary of diplomatic ties.
Strong political trust and close engagement between the two leaders have been instrumental in driving bilateral ties. For over a decade, Xi and Sisi have met more than 10 times, providing strategic guidance for the continued expansion of bilateral cooperation.
In 2014, the two countries elevated their relationship to a comprehensive strategic partnership. In 2016, Xi paid a state visit to Egypt. In 2024, Egypt became the first Arab country to include the goal of building a community with a shared future in a bilateral joint statement.
A major symbol of this partnership is the China-Egypt Suez Economic and Trade Cooperation Zone. In January 2016, Xi and Sisi jointly inaugurated the second phase of the zone; it has since developed into a flagship project of China-Egypt industrial cooperation.
By the end of June this year, the zone had attracted more than 200 companies, brought in over 4.7 billion U.S. dollars in investment, created more than 10,000 direct jobs and supported tens of thousands of additional job opportunities.
Beyond economic cooperation, cultural exchanges have brought the two peoples ever closer together. Chinese language education has been introduced into Egypt's national education system, while growing interest in Chinese culture has encouraged more Egyptians to explore China.
The exchange runs both ways: the Grand Egyptian Museum has become a magnet for Chinese tourists, while the Shanghai Museum's exhibition on ancient Egyptian civilization gave Chinese audiences a closer look at Egypt's rich cultural heritage in return.
Egypt and China have developed a partnership rooted in mutual trust and understanding with remarkable resilience and vast potential for further development, said Osama El-Gohary, assistant to the Prime Minister of Egypt and chairman of the Information and Decision Support Center.
Under the guidance of the two heads of state, Egypt-China ties are poised to reach new heights, delivering greater benefits to both peoples and contributing to global development, he said.■

The services sector remained optimistic, although its confidence indicator eased slightly to +5.2 percent from +6.2 percent in the preceding quarter. ■

World Athletics mourns passing of Chinese high jump legend Zheng
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
17:18:33 CST
18:18:33 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 27 (Xinhua) -- World Athletics mourned the passing of Chinese high jump pioneer and former world record-holder Zheng Fengrong, who died on Tuesday at the age of 89.
"Zheng made athletics history in Beijing in November 1957 when, aged 20, she cleared 1.77-meter to set a world high jump record," read the obituary published by the sport's global governing body on its website on Thursday.
Zheng's performance added one centimeter to the world record of 1.76m shared by 1956 Olympic champion Mildred McDaniel of the United States and Romania's Iolanda Balas, making her the first Chinese athlete to set a world record in athletics and the first female athlete in China to set a world record in any sport.
Although Zheng's world record was broken by Balas with a 1.78m clearance in 1958, she went on to improve China's national record to 1.78m in June 1963.
Hailed as "the swallow who announced that the spring of China's sports has arrived", Zheng also emerged as one of the country's leading athletes in combined events, winning gold medals at the Chinese National Games as well as the Games of the New Emerging Forces.
After retiring from competition, Zheng remained closely involved in sport and served as vice-president of the Chinese Athletics Association. She was awarded the Olympic Orders of the International Olympic Committee in 1995 in recognition of her contribution to the Olympic movement and was selected as one of eight former Chinese athletes and coaches to carry the Olympic flag during the opening ceremony of the 2008 Olympic Games in Beijing. ■

EU wants to revive a plan to use frozen Russian assets for Ukraine – FT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
12:14:15 EEST
18:14:15 KST

EU wants to revive a plan to use frozen Russian assets for Ukraine – FT
Kyiv • UNN
Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, among others, are calling on the European Commission to resume work on using more than €200 billion in Russian assets. Belgium fears legal and financial risks.
EU countries, including Sweden, the Netherlands, Spain and Poland, are calling on Brussels to resume efforts to use frozen Russian sovereign assets to finance Ukraine "in response to concerns that Kyiv will face a new funding crisis," the Financial Times reports, UNN writes.
Details
Plans to finance Ukraine using more than €200 billion in Russian central bank assets held in the EU under sanctions collapsed last winter, as Belgium, where most of these assets are located, blocked the initiative, the publication notes.
"But a letter from a coalition of states to the European Commission calls on the EU executive to resume work on the concept," according to four people familiar with the document, and "requests clarification on any progress in alternative legal and technical frameworks that could provide a solution to Belgium's veto."
"Now is the right time to start a new discussion on how we can continue to use Russia's frozen assets for the benefit of Ukraine and ourselves," said Swedish Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard. "It is a fair and sensible way to ensure that Ukraine can defend itself and all of Europe," she said.
One source said it was "a call for the European Commission to carry out the technical work" to use the assets and ease Kyiv's budgetary needs. "The letter is expected to be sent on Thursday," the publication writes.
"The €90 billion loan is a manifestation of the EU's commitment to supporting Ukraine, but it is clearly insufficient," Stenergard said.
"We [need to] make sure that not just one or two member states bear responsibility for this," said a person familiar with the document.
In December, EU countries agreed to "continue work on ... creating a reparations loan based on cash balances linked to Russia's blocked assets." But there has been no communication on the issue since then, so countries are now requesting a progress report, sources said.
Belgium blocked the plan last year over concerns that it would have to assume responsibility for any repayment of the assets in the event of legal challenges from Russia.
"No one has yet proposed a new offer that would not face the same political barriers that existed in December," said an EU official familiar with the internal discussions. "We do not have a magic white rabbit to pull out of a hat," he added.
"But we can experiment with and fine-tune the same legal proposals, and if the political environment changes, perhaps they will be adopted," they added.
Belgium still has the same concerns as last year, fearing retaliatory legal action from Russia and warning of risks to financial markets from touching sovereign assets, the publication writes.
"Nothing has changed since the debates and the disaster last time," one source said.
The call to return to the proposal concerning immobilized assets comes amid intensifying debates over the size and financing of the EU's next seven-year joint budget. Some diplomats suggested that additional funding for Ukraine could become part of these discussions and increase pressure on countries to find alternative sources of cash.
Euroclear declined to comment, the publication writes.

Russians Shift to Cash Over Banks for First Time Since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:13:56 UTC
18:13:56 KST

- Category
- World
Russians Shift to Cash Over Banks for First Time Since 2022
In August, 37% of survey respondents in Russia identified cash as the best way to store savings, marking the highest share recorded since October 2022, as reported by The Moscow Times.
By contrast, 36% selected bank accounts or deposits, reaching the lowest point since December 2022 and representing the first time since then that paper currency surpassed bank deposits in popularity.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
An additional 11% of respondents opted for a combined approach, keeping part of their money in banks and part in physical cash. This shift comes as Russian banks experienced massive capital outflows between February and July, during which citizens withdrew nearly 2.6 trillion rubles ($32.5 billion), pushing the total amount of cash in circulation past 21.5 trillion rubles ($268.75 billion).
Herman Gref, head of Sberbank—which holds nearly half of all personal bank savings in the country—previously highlighted a "significant outflow of funds from the banking system into cash" in July.
Multiple domestic economic shifts contributed to the resurgence of physical currency. Tax adjustments introduced in January raised value-added tax (VAT), extended it to card payment processing, and lowered the annual revenue threshold for VAT exemption from 60 million rubles ($750,000) to 20 million rubles ($250,000), pushing more business operations into the informal economy.
Widespread mobile internet outages in the spring further increased demand for physical bills, while ongoing public discussion regarding a potential freeze on bank deposits fueled consumer hesitation.
Economists from the Bank of Finland attribute the shift to broader economic instability and tax avoidance, while local analysts also point to interest rates falling toward inflation expectations.
Average top retail bank deposit rates declined from a peak of 22.3% in late 2024 to 12.9% in early August, nearly aligning with household inflation expectations of 13.7%.
Despite shifts in how savings are held, most households maintain no financial reserves. Overall, 58% of survey respondents reported having no emergency funds to cover basic expenses in the event of job loss, while only 37% indicated they had sufficient cash reserves.
Russian authorities have reduced public access to information about the country’s remaining financial reserves. The Moscow Times reported on August 13 that the government had stopped publishing official figures on cash reserves held in its single treasury account, a key financial cushion for unallocated budget funds.
Russia’s Federal Treasury removed daily operational data covering ruble deposits placed with commercial banks, money market transactions, and the total amount of cash available across different levels of the budget system.

The warning, delivered by Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova at a news briefing in Moscow, was the strongest of is kind yet from Russia to Britain, a NATO member state and a staunch ally of Ukraine.
Zakharova said London was "one step away" from becoming legally complicit in what she called "terrorism" against Russian civilians, something she said would have "catastrophic consequences" unless Britain changed course.
"We have repeatedly warned that any British military installations and equipment in Ukraine and beyond its borders could be targeted in response to Ukrainian strikes on Russian territory carried out using British weapons," she said.
"We propose that the British leadership once again carefully analyse the situation and immediately, in the most resolute and unequivocal manner, abandon the hostile, aggressive line, which can only ... create the risk of the conflict escalating to an entirely new level," she said.
Zakharova issued her warning a day after Russia accused Ukraine of firing British Storm Shadow missiles at a shopping centre in the Russian-controlled city of Donetsk in eastern Ukraine in an attack which it said wounded civilians, including children.
The Kremlin said on Monday that Britain was methodically adding "fuel to the fire" after London announced it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow cruise missiles, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia. France has already given its assent to license the technology for the European missile. REUTERS

From E coli to amenity gaps: What CAG found beyond the railway makeover
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:06:39 UTC
18:06:39 KST

From E coli to amenity gaps: What CAG found beyond the railway makeover
Abhishek Mishra / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 27, 2026, 14:46 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Vande Bharat to E. coli: What CAG found behind Indian Railways’ big makeover (PTI file photo)
NEW DELHI: Indian Railways is in the middle of one of its biggest modernisation drives, spanning station redevelopment, new trains, electrification and record capital investment. A recent CAG audit, however, shows that alongside this expansion, gaps remain in some of the most basic passenger amenities at stations.For years now, the story of Indian Railways has been told through images of transformation.There are sleek Vande Bharat trains gliding out of revamped stations, glossy artist's impressions of redeveloped railway hubs, new concourses, lifts, escalators and futuristic terminals. The government has steadily raised capital expenditure on the national transporter, presenting the Railways as one of the central pillars of country's infrastructure push.The makeover is visible. But the latest audit findings of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India show that ensuring basic passenger amenities remain available and functional across the network continues to be an important part of that transformation.In a report tabled in Parliament on August 12, the CAG examined passenger amenities and sanitation at non-suburban railway stations and found significant gaps in the basics.
Of 512 stations covered by the audit, 458 had deficiencies in one or more essential passenger amenities. Water samples collected from coolers at eight stations were found contaminated with E. coli, a marker that raises serious concerns about faecal contamination and water safety.
Amenities gap at railway stations (Source: CAG)
The latest CAG reports, including those on passenger amenities, railway finances and compliance, raise a larger question about the makeover that we keep talking about: Is the transformation merely about building new assets, or is it also about making the everyday railway experience safer, cleaner, more reliable and financially sustainable?
What the CAG found at railway stations
Indian Railways is not a conventional transport system. It is the daily infrastructure of a country on the move.Millions pass through its stations not as occasional tourists but as workers, students, migrants, families and small traders. For many, the railway journey begins long before boarding a train. It begins with finding the platform, locating a toilet, getting drinking water, sitting in a waiting area and navigating a crowded station.That is precisely where the latest audit becomes very important.The CAG's Report No. 31 of 2026, focused on passenger amenities and sanitation at non-suburban railway stations, was tabled on August 12.The findings suggest that while major infrastructure projects may dominate the narrative around railway modernisation, there continues to be significant variation in the availability of basic passenger amenities across the stations examined.The audit found deficiencies at nearly nine out of every 10 stations examined.The gaps ranged across basic amenities such as toilets, urinals and drinking-water facilities. In other words, the issue was not necessarily the absence of a grand redevelopment plan. It was ensuring that facilities passengers encounter every day are available and functional consistently.The audit underlines that station modernisation has two components: creating new infrastructure and ensuring that routine passenger amenities remain available and functional.
Water quality emerges as a key concern
Perhaps the most striking finding in the audit concerns drinking water.The CAG found E. coli contamination in samples collected from water coolers at eight locations. The presence of such bacteria raises concerns because contaminated drinking water can pose a serious public-health risk.The finding was particularly important because access to safe water is among the most basic services expected at a railway station.The finding has now prompted a special response from Indian Railways.The Railways has launched a special drive to clean and disinfect drinking-water tanks and filters. Zonal Railways have also been advised to undertake comprehensive inspections of drinking-water infrastructure and rectify deficiencies wherever they are found.Importantly, the exercise is not being limited to a one-time cleaning drive. The Railways has directed that station-wise deficiencies and the action taken to address them be monitored.That changes the nature of the response.The issue is no longer simply whether a station has a drinking-water facility. The bigger question is whether the entire system behind that facility, tanks, filters, pipelines, coolers and monitoring, is functioning properly and delivering safe water consistently.It is a crucial distinction.A water cooler installed at a station is an infrastructure achievement. Ensuring that the water remains safe every day is a maintenance and governance challenge.The new cleaning and inspection drive also underlines the broader problem identified by the CAG.Modernisation is not simply about creating infrastructure. It is about maintaining it.A water cooler installed at a station is only as useful as the quality of the water flowing through it. A new toilet is only as useful as its cleanliness and upkeep. An escalator that frequently stops working or a waiting hall that is not maintained does not become useful merely because the infrastructure exists.The challenge for Indian Railways is increasingly shifting from construction to maintenance.
The missing link in the makeover
India's railway modernisation programme has been built around large numbers.New lines, doubling and electrification projects, station redevelopment, signalling upgrades and new rolling stock have become the visible markers of the transformation.The latest financial audit, Report No. 30 of 2026, was also tabled on August 12 and examines the finances of the ministry of Railways for the year ended March 2025. Its significance lies in placing the makeover against the larger question of financial capacity and the resources available to sustain such an ambitious transformation.The numbers show the scale of the continuing investment push. For 2026-27, railway capital expenditure is budgeted at Rs 2.93 lakh crore, with budgetary support from the Centre expected to finance around 95% of that spending.This represents a fundamental shift in how railway modernisation is being financed.The network is no longer relying only on internally generated resources to fund its massive expansion and upgrade plans. Government support has become the financial backbone of the capital programme.That has enabled Indian Railways to build faster. At the same time, the growing asset base makes maintenance, upgrade and efficient operation increasingly important.
Record spending, 98.4% operating ratio
The answer lies partly in the operating ratio, a measure of how much of every rupee earned is consumed by working expenses. A lower operating ratio leaves more room for investment and financial flexibility.For 2026-27, the operating ratio is budgeted at 98.4%, after a revised estimate of 98.8% for 2025-26, as reported by Parliament and PRS Legislative Research.The margin remains narrow.The modernisation drive is also being supported by a substantial increase in central budgetary support. Government support is expected to finance around 95% of railway capital expenditure in 2026-27, while the operating ratio remains above 98%.
Building big, maintaining better
The CAG's findings bring an old problem into a new context.The audit places renewed focus on maintenance, an increasingly important issue as the Railways adds and upgrades infrastructure across a very large network.The transformation of Indian Railways will not be judged only by whether a station redevelopment project is completed on schedule. It will also be judged years later by whether the facilities created continue to work as intended.The CAG examined precisely these everyday indicators — drinking water, toilets and urinals, seating, platform shelters, accessibility and sanitation — making the report as much about service quality as infrastructure availability.The findings highlight the importance of pairing asset creation with regular maintenance, inspection and service monitoring.The former is visible. It can be photographed, inaugurated and counted.The latter is harder. It requires regular inspection, accountability, maintenance contracts, quality checks and systems that continue to work long after the inaugural ceremony.The Railways' latest drinking-water drive points in that direction. The focus on comprehensive inspection, rectification and station-wise monitoring suggests an attempt to make maintenance more systematic rather than waiting for individual problems to surface.The real test will be whether that monitoring continues after the immediate response to the audit findings.The challenge of maintaining standards across a vast networkThe latest findings also underline the challenge of ensuring uniform service standards across a railway network of India's scale.At one level are the flagship projects: High-profile trains, major stations and corridors receiving substantial investment. These are the symbols that shape public perception of a changing railway system.At another level are hundreds of ordinary stations where the provision and upkeep of basic amenities remain equally important.The CAG's examination of 512 stations and its finding of deficiencies at 458 suggests that ensuring minimum standards consistently across the network remains a work in progress.That is where the true test of the makeover lies.Indian Railways is too large and too geographically diverse for transformation to be measured only through a handful of showcase projects. The success of the modernisation programme will depend on whether improvements can eventually become the standard across the network rather than remain concentrated at major stations.The passenger boarding from a smaller city experiences the Railways through the condition of the local station.That station is where the promise of transformation ultimately becomes visible.
A financial makeover still in progress
The railway modernisation programme is also taking place against a difficult financial backdrop.Passenger and freight revenues remain central to the financial health of the system. Yet recent budget analysis has pointed to revenue estimates falling short of targets, even as the Railways continues to undertake large capital investments.According to the 2026-27 analysis by PRS Legislative Research, freight revenue in 2025-26 was estimated to be 5.1% below the budget estimate, while passenger revenue was expected to fall short by 13.8%.
Freight down, passenger revenue misses target
This does not mean that the railway transformation has stalled. Far from it. The scale of capital expenditure remains historically high.It does mean, however, that central budgetary support remains a major pillar of the current modernisation programme.The question is whether the investments being made today will eventually create a more efficient railway system, one that can carry more freight, attract more passengers, reduce congestion and improve revenue generation.That is the economic logic behind modernisation.The CAG's latest findings add another dimension: modernisation must also ensure that spending translates into reliable passenger amenities and services.
The real makeover begins after inauguration
There is another lesson in the CAG audit.One of the most important parts of railway transformation is creating systems capable of looking after the infrastructure once it is built.A station redevelopment project has a beginning and an end. A maintenance programme does not.It requires continuous supervision.The Railways' decision to launch a special drive for cleaning and disinfecting drinking-water tanks and filters, inspect infrastructure and monitor station-wise deficiencies is therefore significant.The Railways will now have to ensure that the response goes beyond corrective action after contamination is detected. The larger goal is preventive systems, regular water testing, routine cleaning and disinfection, replacement of ageing infrastructure, clear responsibility for sanitation, and stronger monitoring of passenger amenities.The same principle applies across the network.Modernisation must become a process rather than an event.The CAG's findings have arrived at an important moment because Indian Railways is entering a phase where the story can no longer be told only through the scale of capital expenditure. The network has already seen major investments and ambitious announcements.The next question is whether these investments are producing a railway that works better every day.
From showcase projects to everyday reliability
There is no doubt that Indian Railways is changing.The infrastructure pipeline is enormous. Capital spending remains high. Stations and trains look different from what they did a decade ago. Electrification, new corridors and capacity expansion are reshaping the network.The CAG audit does not erase those changes.Instead, it adds another dimension to the modernisation story: the importance of ensuring that basic passenger services improve alongside major infrastructure creation.A transformed railway will ultimately be judged both by its new assets and by the consistency with which its everyday facilities work.It must be judged by outcomes.The latest audit reports offer precisely that reminder.The CAG's passenger amenities report was tabled in Parliament on August 12, alongside the latest reports on railway finances and compliance. Together, they offer a snapshot of a system undergoing one of its most ambitious periods of investment while still grappling with persistent questions of service delivery, maintenance and financial sustainability.
Record capex, heavy government support: The financial reality behind Railways’ makeover
The new drinking-water drive shows that the Railways is responding to at least one of those concerns. But whether the effort translates into consistently safer and better-maintained facilities across stations will determine its real impact.
The railway makeover, in other words, is real. But seems unfinished.The CAG report does not negate the scale of the transformation underway in Indian Railways. Capital investment remains at record levels, stations are being redeveloped and capacity is expanding. What the audit adds to that picture is a reminder that the next phase of modernisation will also depend on maintenance, consistency and ensuring that facilities already created remain functional, accessible and safe.The Railways' response to the water-quality findings, including inspections, filtration upgrades and station-wise monitoring, shows that corrective action has begun. The larger test will be whether these systems can help close the remaining amenity gaps across a network that serves millions of passengers every day.For millions of passengers, transformation will ultimately mean something simple: a clean station, a functioning toilet, safe drinking water and a journey in which the infrastructure created for them continues to work as intended.
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

Türkiye to bring 200 young climate negotiators to Istanbul ahead of COP31
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
09:01:24 UTC
18:01:24 KST

The simulation will take place on Yassıada Island, officially known as the Democracy and Liberties Island, situated in the Sea of Marmara. (AA photo)
Two hundred young delegates from Türkiye and abroad will gather in Istanbul for a six-day simulation of U.N. climate negotiations, as Türkiye prepares to host COP31, organizers have said.
NextGenCOP30.5, organized by the Cemre Foundation in partnership with the Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Ministry, in cooperation with Istanbul Technical University and with support from the University of Cambridge, will run from Aug. 27 to Sept. 1 on Democracy and Freedoms Island.
Participants, including students from Cambridge and Oxford universities, will be divided into six negotiating blocs reflecting the economic and political interests represented in U.N. climate talks. They will negotiate emissions reductions and the energy transition, climate finance and loss and damage, and adaptation and resilience.
The simulation aims to give young people practical experience of climate diplomacy, including defending national interests, building coalitions, managing red lines and making concessions under pressure. Unexpected climate-crisis scenarios will also force delegates to reassess positions and seek new alliances.
“We do not want young people to watch the climate debate from the sidelines. We are inviting them to take their seats at the table,” said Furkan Gökgöz, chairman of the Cemre Foundation.
The event will also promote Türkiye’s “Zero Waste” vision. As part of its sustainability program, organizers will implement food and energy-saving measures, ban single-use plastics and use digital documentation. Participant badges will be made from seed paper that can be returned to nature.
The official opening on Aug. 28 is scheduled to include Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister and COP31 President Murat Kurum. Sessions will cover climate finance, the circular economy, sustainable agriculture, climate technology, entrepreneurship and artificial intelligence in climate solutions. Academics from Istanbul Technical University, Bogazici University and Cambridge are also expected to participate.
The simulation will conclude with a plenary vote on a common text, the “Antalya Agreement.” Adoption will require support from at least four of the six blocs, replicating the coalition-building and compromise required in multilateral climate negotiations.
Alongside the negotiation-focused Blue Zone, a Green Zone will showcase climate technologies and business models. Ten climate-focused startups, five from Cambridge’s entrepreneurial ecosystem and five from Türkiye, will present their work through pitches, exhibitions, demonstrations and networking.
The six-day program will prepare young people not only as informed participants but as future climate negotiators and leaders, while connecting climate policy discussions with practical innovation ahead of COP31.

Malaysia’s former PM Ismail Sabri charged with concealing assets
Ismail Sabri, 66, pleaded not guilty to a charge that allege he failed to provide a complete declaration of assets.
Former Malaysian Prime Minister Ismail Sabri Yaakob has been charged with failing to declare tens of millions of dollars worth of assets, becoming the country’s third former prime minister to face criminal charges after leaving office.
The 66-year-old pleaded not guilty at the Kuala Lumpur Sessions Court on Thursday to a charge that alleges he failed to provide a complete declaration of assets to Malaysia’s anti-corruption agency.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Anwar Ibrahim: Malaysia between the superpowers
- list 2 of 3Malaysia vows not to return Myanmar refugees if lives at risk
- list 3 of 3Malaysia’s Anwar puts non-aligned stance in focus with remarks on Taiwan
He is accused of concealing holdings worth about $40m, spread across nine currencies, as well as bars of gold and silver.
His lawyer, Amer Hamzah Arshad, said at a media conference that the charge was essentially a failure to comply with a notice to declare certain assets.
“We will be studying the charge and as we informed the court, we are raising certain concerns about the propriety and legality of the charge, but we won’t go into detail here,” he said.
The judge set bail at 300,000 ringgit ($74,504) and rejected the request to confiscate his passport, finding no evidence of flight risk.
He is due to return to court on September 29 . If convicted, he faces up to five years in prison.
Ismail Sabri was PM for 15 months, from August 2021 to November 2022 – Malaysia’s shortest prime ministerial term.
Last March, Malaysia’s anti-corruption agency said he had submitted an assets declaration after being ordered to do so as part of its investigation into alleged corruption and money laundering.
He is the third former prime minister to be prosecuted in recent years over alleged corruption-related activities.
Former Prime Minister Najib Razak is serving a reduced six-year prison sentence after his conviction in a case tied to the multibillion-dollar looting of the 1MDB state investment fund. He was sentenced last year to a further 15 years in his second and largest graft trial linked to 1MDB and still faces other proceedings.
Another former prime minister, Muhyiddin Yassin, is currently on trial on corruption and money-laundering charges.

Taiwan: Proposed judicial caning referendum indicates further erosion of human rights protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:54:36 UTC
17:54:36 KST

Ahead of the meeting of the Central Election Commission on 28 August regarding a proposed referendum on introducing judicial caning as a criminal punishment in Taiwan, Amnesty International Taiwan’s Director, E-Ling Chiu, said:
“It is both disturbing and disgraceful that the Legislative Yuan has chosen to advance a referendum proposal on judicial caning that clearly breaches international human rights law.
“This proposal is part of a broader pattern that has emerged in recent months. Human rights-related budgets have been cut, the work of independent institutions such as the National Human Rights Commission has been obstructed and the functioning of the Constitutional Court has been undermined. The advancement of a referendum seeking to legitimize cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment further contributes to the erosion of the human rights protection framework that Taiwan has spent decades building.”
Amnesty International’s Deputy Regional Director Sarah Brooks added:
“When public anger over crimes is exploited for political gain at the expense of human rights, everyone stands to lose.
“Amnesty International opposes any legislative proposal to introduce judicial caning in Taiwan and calls on the government to reaffirm its commitment to Article 7 of the ICCPR and the absolute prohibition of torture and other cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment or punishment.”
Background
On 14 August 2026, Taiwan’s Legislative Yuan approved a referendum proposal asking voters whether the government should enact legislation introducing judicial caning as a special criminal punishment for offences including sexual assault, child abuse, high-value fraud and aggravated fraud. The proposal comes amid growing public anger over these offences fuelled by a series of highly publicized cases.
Shortly after the proposal was approved, Amnesty International Taiwan joined civil society organizations in issuing a joint statement expressing concern that judicial caning would violate human rights protections and contravene internationally recognized standards prohibiting corporal punishment.
The caning proposal is one of three referendum initiatives currently under consideration by Taiwan’s Central Election Commission. The Commission is scheduled to deliberate on the proposals on 28 August before deciding whether they may proceed to a nationwide vote. If the Central Election Commission approves, the referendum will be held in November 2026, alongside a national election.
The International Review Committee in May of this year confirmed that corporal punishment constitutes cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment in violation of the right to personal integrity and human dignity in Article 7 ICCPR. Amnesty International opposes corporal punishment in all circumstances and has consistently called on governments worldwide to abolish punishments such as caning, flogging, whipping and other forms of corporal punishment that are incompatible with the absolute prohibition of cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

Hong Kong lowers heat stress warning system thresholds after calls for revamp

Hong Kong lowers heat stress warning system thresholds after calls for revamp
Labour Dept says updates include automatically raising alert level when temperatures in multiple parts of the city reach 35 degrees Celsius
Hong Kong labour authorities have unveiled changes to the system that sends out warnings to workers about overexertion during very hot weather, reducing the threshold so higher-tier alerts can be issued more easily following intense criticism of the mechanism.
The Labour Department said on Thursday that two new conditions would be introduced to the Heat Stress at Work Warning system starting Friday.
The system has three warning levels – amber, red and black – which alert employers and staff to the severity of heat stress if they are working outdoors or indoors without air conditioning.
The first change will lower the threshold for triggering a higher-tier warning if the Observatory has already issued the extremely hot weather special alert, ensuring a quicker response.
The second change will automatically raise the warning level by one tier – from amber to red, or from red to black – when measured temperatures generally over Hong Kong reach 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) or higher.
The revamp follows criticism over a lack of higher alerts earlier this month, when the city grappled with record-breaking temperatures.

Taking the plea off the table, it is highly probable that the defendants will be facing the death penalty at their trial in 2028.

Wu said the sharp upward revision of Taiwan’s economic growth forecast this year to 11.05% by the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting, and Statistics on Aug. 14 likely had limited influence on the survey, as consumers tend to assess the economy based on their daily experiences. He said stock market performance can also shape perceptions of economic conditions, with rising markets making people feel more optimistic.
All six CCI sub-indexes remained below 100, indicating a pessimistic outlook. Wu explained that US economic conditions, Federal Reserve policy, AI infrastructure investment, and developments in the US-Iran situation will remain key factors affecting Taiwan’s economic and market outlook.

The report cites Article 15 of the Irish Constitution in explaining the legal advice, saying officials were told that only the Oireachtas has the right to raise a military force on Irish territory.
When asked about this, a Royal Navy spokesperson told me:
“The UK and Ireland regularly cooperate on shared security challenges. We do not speculate on potential operational tasking of Royal Navy vessels.”
The Irish Times also reports that the French frigate Aquitaine was stationed in Dublin Bay, just outside the 22-kilometre limit, on 1 July while dozens of European heads of government were visiting Ireland. The ship reportedly provided air defence while Irish military aircraft and naval vessels were also deployed to secure the area.
The report says a separate legal issue arose over whether a foreign warship positioned outside Irish territorial waters could take lethal action against an airborne threat over Ireland, such as a hostile drone or hijacked aircraft. Under Irish Defence Forces rules of engagement, known internally as COD 6, only Irish military officers can authorise the use of force in such circumstances, according to the newspaper.
As a workaround, an Irish naval officer was reportedly placed aboard the French ship as a liaison officer and given responsibility for providing final authorisation if lethal force was required. The Irish Times reports that this could have included authorising the use of long-range anti-aircraft missiles against an airborne threat.
European warships are reportedly expected to continue providing air defence during major events for the remainder of Ireland’s EU presidency. According to the report, next week’s meeting of EU defence and foreign affairs ministers in County Wicklow will be supported by a Royal Navy air defence warship operating in the Irish Sea.
The Irish Government has not publicly confirmed the French frigate’s earlier security role. The Irish Times reported that Ireland’s Department of Defence referred questions to An Garda Síochána, while a Garda spokeswoman said the force had no knowledge of Operation Fianna, the military security operation mounted for Ireland’s EU presidency.

How is the flood of information drowning human intellect?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:41:14 UTC
17:41:14 KST

Topic: Contemporary Psychology, Technology, and the Culture of Reading 
  
 Introduction: The Paradox of the 21st Century: We live in the richest era in history in terms of access to data. With just a few touches on the screen, we have access to libraries, articles, and analyses from all over the world. But why, despite this unprecedented abundance of information, do we feel that human society is becoming more superficial, more bored, and more oblivious day by day?
 
 What was predicted by thinkers two or three decades ago has today become our tangible, everyday reality: the ruthless encroachment of data on the privacy of thought and thought. We live in the age of information bombardment; an age in which the boundary between “knowledge” and “noise” has disappeared.
 
 1. From intellectual nourishment to brain "self-eating": The human brain has an amazing and flexible structure. Reading and learning are the engines of activation and development of this vital organ. But unlike cloud memories and digital hard drives, the brain's deep processing capacity is not unlimited.
 
 When data inputs exceed the brain's tolerance threshold, a reverse and destructive cycle begins: the phenomenon of cognitive self-eating.
 
 At this stage, the brain not only loses the ability to analyze and organize new data, but also, due to the lack of opportunity for "memory consolidation", slowly forgets the deep archive of knowledge and fundamental concepts that it had previously stored. We read more, but we understand less and forget faster.
 
 Daily data flood ──> Unstable concentration ──> Inability to analyze ──> Analysis of mental archive (decline of wisdom)
 
 2. Entering the World of “Post-Literacy”: New global analytical reports show that this crisis is not regional or limited to a specific culture; it is a pervasive and transnational phenomenon. We are rapidly moving into what experts call the “post-literacy era.”
 
 
 What is true literacy? Literacy is not simply the ability to read words; it is the possession of systematic, coherent, contextual, and in-depth knowledge about a subject.
 
 
 What is post-literacy? A state in which active readers have given way to “passive consumers.” In this age, people consume a vast amount of headlines, short messages, social media posts, and instant information, but they have lost the ability to understand complex texts, analyze long arguments, and connect concepts.
 
 3. The decline of art and the rise of “shallow artists”: The impact of this information overload is not limited to memory or general literacy; literature and art are also major victims of this trend.
 
 As today’s audience becomes bored and preoccupied with receiving a quick dopamine hit from social media, their tastes change. This change in tastes creates a damaging feedback loop:
 
 The consumer audience loses the ability to appreciate deep, complex, and layered works.
 
 The market and algorithms push artists to produce “simplistic,” “marketable,” and “quick-to-consume” works.
 
 As a result, a new generation of creators is emerging: superficial, shallow, and possibly meaningless.
 
 Art, once a haven for deep thought and the nurturing of human wisdom, has itself become a product of the same noise factory.
 
 4. Solution: Renaissance of classic media and "digital abstinence": To escape this cognitive swamp, one cannot hope for algorithms or newer technologies; because the essence of modern technologies is designed based on capturing momentary attention and fragmenting human concentration.
 
 The antidote to this crisis is a conscious return to classical principles: escaping the rigidity of the screen: reducing the distance from smartphones and the non-stop Internet is the first step to recovering the attention span.
Taking refuge in paper media (books and newspapers): Reading on paper allows the brain to think linearly, patiently and deeply. Unlike social networks, books do not contain "notifications" and distracting links; books invite you to "silence of thought".
 
 Slow Reading: Instead of accumulating information at hand, returning to original texts and reading them repeatedly re-waters the roots of wisdom in the mind.
 
 Conclusion: A choice for the future of humanity: We stand at a civilizational crossroads: do we want to be beings with a huge accumulation of worthless data and fragmented minds, or patient humans with deep wisdom and coherent thought?
 
 Saving thought, art, and literacy in today's world is a revolutionary act. This revolution begins with closing a tab in the browser, putting away your mobile phone, and opening a real book. Wisdom does not grow in the noise of data; wisdom is born in silence and depth.
MNA

Greece reports 232 West Nile virus cases, 19 deaths
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-27
08:38:49 UTC
17:38:49 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
27 August 2026•Update: 27 August 2026
Greece has reported 232 locally acquired West Nile virus cases and 19 related deaths during the 2026 transmission season, health authorities said Thursday.
Seventy-five new cases were diagnosed in the week ending Aug. 26, marking a sharp rise in infections, according to the National Public Health Organization’s latest epidemiological surveillance report.
The outbreak is nearly three times larger than during the corresponding period last year, Greek daily Tovima reported.
Of the confirmed patients, 165 developed complications affecting the central nervous system, including encephalitis, meningitis or acute flaccid paralysis.
Another 67 experienced mild symptoms or showed no neurological complications.
All 19 people who died were over 65, with a median age of 85. The victims ranged in age from 66 to 92.
Eighty-nine patients remain hospitalized across the country.
Deputy Health Minister Marios Themistokleous said mathematical models suggest that 2026 could become a record year, potentially exceeding the severe 2018 outbreak, when Greece registered 317 cases and 59 deaths.
Health authorities expect the current wave to peak within the next one to two weeks, although new infections are likely to continue through at least the end of September.
Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis said “there is no reason to panic,” stressing that the healthcare system is not under pressure.
A significant share of infections has been detected in the Attica region, where municipalities have intensified mosquito-control measures.
Authorities in Pallini are using a digital risk map to monitor storm drains and installing special traps targeting female mosquitoes.
In Filothei-Psychiko, emergency nighttime spraying was conducted within a 300-meter (984-foot) radius of a confirmed case.
Health authorities urged residents, particularly older people, to continue taking precautions against mosquito bites throughout the fall.
